The BPL is a public report identifying individuals and legal entities involved in money laundering or terrorist financing. All Mexican individuals and companies are required to immediately suspend any and all acts, operations or services with people or entities on the BPL.

With reports from EFE, Infobae, El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Volaris will be the first Mexico-based airline to offer passengers Starlink satellite Wi-Fi
World.content:
Low-cost airline Volaris will soon become the first Mexican carrier to offer Starlink satellite Wi-Fi on board its flights.

Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite network, is known for allowing users to browse the Internet as if they were on the ground. In the sky, users can text, make video calls, listen to music, work remotely, or watch streaming content.

First, we changed the way Mexico flies. Now, we’re changing what flying feels like. The fastest Wi-Fi in the sky is coming aboard with @Starlink Book here: https://t.co/YO6KQwZld5 pic.twitter.com/eL6T5xjTOV — Volaris (@viajaVolaris) July 14, 2026

Starlink’s advantage is that it operates via satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO), much closer to the planet than older systems, shortening data travel distance, cutting response time delay, and using flat smart antennas to track moving connections.

Volaris expects to have Starlink’s Internet available across its entire fleet by 2027. But it has not specified whether access will be free for all passengers, linked to a loyalty program, or have an additional cost.

The rollout will encompass more than 150 Airbus A320 and A321 aircraft, on both domestic and international routes.

This announcement is part of a broader strategy by Indigo Partners — Volaris’s holding company — which also includes JetSMART, Wizz Air, Frontier, and Cebu Pacific. Collectively, these airlines plan to install Starlink on more than a thousand aircraft worldwide.

Unlike other connectivity models, the service won’t be managed by the airline, but directly by Starlink through its own system.

Beyond improving passenger experience, the technology seeks to improve communication between aircraft and ground personnel, anticipate maintenance needs before they become failures and better react to unforeseen events.

Said Volaris head Enrique Beltranera, “The airline’s ultra-low-cost model goes hand in hand with an exceptional travel experience, which continues to evolve in line with our customers’ expectations.”

With reports from Aviación Online and ADN 40

World.title: Trump re-imposes his tariffs, but Mexico gets a pass
World.content:
The U.S. government imposed new tariffs on 80 countries effective on Friday, but Mexico escaped relatively unscathed.

Taxes on Mexican goods replace the 10% duty U.S. President Donald Trump dictated in February after the Supreme Court invalidated the broad-based tariffs he had applied last year. Those original replacement tariffs were valid for only 150 days, prompting Friday’s new levies.

U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer informed President Claudia Sheinbaum of the pending decision during a Thursday morning meeting at the National Palace.

Afterward, Mexican Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard explained that the 10% tariff does not affect approximately 80% of the products Mexico exports to the U.S.

“Mexican products that comply with the terms of the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact (USMCA) will remain tariff-free,” Ebrard said.

The other 20% involved previously established sectoral duties — including those applied to specific non-USMCA goods, steel and vehicles — that were already set at 10% and therefore will essentially be unchanged.

There is a possibility that Mexico could be subject to an “excess capacity” tariff — an obscure provision of a 1930 trade law that applies to countries that “put undue burdens on U.S. imports.” This is likely to be addressed during ongoing USMCA negotiations.

The new U.S. tariffs seek to address what the Trump administration claims are unfair trade practices in an effort to restore some of the rates struck down by the Supreme Court.

The USTR conducted investigations seeking to establish that some countries had failed to take steps to curb forced labor, with the alleged worst offenders now facing a 12.5% tariff rate. However, the forced-labor compliance requirements do not affect Mexico, Ebrard said.

Sheinbaum reiterated this news during her Friday morning press conference.

“All products we exported within the USMCA have zero tariffs, with the exception of steel, some vehicles and products exported outside the treaty,” she said. “Mexico remains exactly the same as we were a week ago.”

The US Trade Representative’s Mexico City agenda

In addition to meeting with Sheinbaum, Greer was in Mexico City to participate in bilateral talks as part of the ongoing review of the USMCA.

Greer and Ebrard discussed topics ranging from steel and aluminum and derivative products, automobiles, economic security, labor, agriculture and electronic payment services.

Sheinbaum said her meeting with Greer served as “an assessment of how far the talks have come, to learn more about what the U.S. is proposing, and to consider the timeline.”

With reports from El Economista, El Financiero and Atlantic Council

World.title: 900 more troops arrive in Mazatlán after a series of targeted attacks
World.content:
A contingent of 900 Mexican Army troops arrived in the early hours of Thursday at the port of Mazatlán, Sinaloa, as part of a security reinforcement in response to a series of armed attacks in recent weeks.

City Clerk Moisés Ríos Pérez said the newly arrived soldiers bring the total number of troops for the enhanced security operations to more than 1,300.

Ríos explained that the Public Security and Defense Ministries, and other authorities involved in daily security meetings, are working on accommodating the new troops before defining their operational deployment.

“Nine hundred arrived at midnight yesterday; we are struggling to relocate them at the moment,” Ríos told local media. “But we’re hoping that with this new number we can now deploy them throughout the municipality . . . to prevent more [violence].”

The security reinforcement, a joint effort among federal, state and municipal authorities, comes in response to a surge in violence that has marked the start of the summer holiday season in the port city and tourist destination.

Between July 12 and 18, local media reported Mazatlán recorded seven homicides and one femicide, in addition to a shooting and suspected explosive attack on a home. On July 17 and 18 alone, six armed attacks were reported in less than 24 hours, leaving four dead and three wounded. Days later, between July 22 and 23, five more people were murdered in less than a day.

Investigations by the State Attorney General’s Office (FGE) are underway to clarify the homicides and to identify the victims and the perpetrators.

The climate of violence stems from the conflict between factions of the Sinaloa Cartel following the arrest and extradition two years ago of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, the former leader of the criminal organization.

Since September 2024, Mazatlán has been the scene of armed attacks, kidnappings, disappearances, and murders.

Some of the new personnel will be stationed in areas such as Germán Evers and Urías, while another group will guard the federal highways leading to Durango and Nayarit. The effort aims to protect both residents and tourists arriving at the destination during peak season.

With reports from Infobae, Noroeste and Los Noticeristas

World.title: Sheinbaum touts improved security perception amid 54% drop in Morelos homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🎤 Cuernavaca cabinet meeting: Sheinbaum held her Friday presser in Morelos, spotlighting a 54% murder-rate drop under Gov. Margarita González, credited to the federal Plan Morelos.

Sheinbaum held her Friday presser in Morelos, spotlighting a 54% murder-rate drop under Gov. Margarita González, credited to the federal Plan Morelos. 📊 Security perception improves: INEGI’s Q2 survey showed 59.8% of respondents feel unsafe in their city, down from 61.5% in March and 63.8% in December.

INEGI’s Q2 survey showed 59.8% of respondents feel unsafe in their city, down from 61.5% in March and 63.8% in December. 🚨Temoac mayor murder: Federal agents are aiding Morelos prosecutors probing the killing of Mayor Valentín Lavín Moreno, who had alleged ties to local crime groups; his in-laws were arrested Thursday.

Federal agents are aiding Morelos prosecutors probing the killing of Mayor Valentín Lavín Moreno, who had alleged ties to local crime groups; his in-laws were arrested Thursday. 📰 Oaxaca journalist killing: Federal prosecutors took over the case of slain journalist Alejandro Leyva at Oaxaca’s request; Sheinbaum tasked the AG with meeting Leyva’s family.

Federal prosecutors took over the case of slain journalist Alejandro Leyva at Oaxaca’s request; Sheinbaum tasked the AG with meeting Leyva’s family. ⚖️ Ruffo arrest not political: Sheinbaum denied persecution claims over ex-Baja California governor Ernesto Ruffo’s arrest, tying it to a 12-month fuel theft probe involving his company, Ingemar.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Cuernavaca, the capital of the state of Morelos, continuing a practice begun in January of holding regional Security Cabinet meetings on the road to highlight local challenges.

Located just south of Mexico City, Morelos is the third-smallest entity in the republic, with a population of just under 2 million residents.

Morelos is grappling with corruption and organized crime challenges, though murder rates have dropped by 54% since Governor Margarita González was sworn in on Oct. 1, 2024 (the same day Sheinbaum took office).

Officials credited Plan Morelos — a joint federal-state security strategy implemented in April — and state-level efforts for reducing high-impact crimes across the state.

President touts improving public perception of security

Sheinbaum highlighted improvement in the public perception of security as reflected in the quarterly survey conducted by the national statistics agency INEGI, saying the results indicate that the public is noticing the advancements her government is making.

So far this year, Mexicans’ perception of insecurity dropped in both the first and the second quarter.

INEGI reported that 63.8% of those surveyed felt unsafe in their city in December, while 61.5% said they felt unsafe in March. That number fell to 59.8% in the latest survey.

The president acknowledged that perception sometimes changes gradually, often depending on whether one or one’s family have been victims of a crime.

“But it also depends on what you hear or read,” she said. “The important thing is that we are delivering results … and the population sees that.”

Federal authorities take over two high-profile murder cases

In stark juxtaposition to the public perception survey, Sheinbaum and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch offered updates on the investigations into Wednesday’s shocking murders.

With regard to the murder of Valentín Lavín Moreno, the mayor of Temoac (just 80 kilometers east of Cuernavaca), Harfuch said federal agents are working closely with Morelos prosecutors “to clarify the events and apprehend those responsible.”

Harfuch added that Lavín, who was shot to death in his City Hall office, was under investigation for possible links to two local crime groups. Lavín’s in-laws were arrested on Thursday, accused of having ties to organized crime.

A few hours before the tragic events in Temoac, journalist Alejandro Leyva was shot to death in the state of Oaxaca.

Federal prosecutors have taken over the case at the request of the Oaxaca authorities, Harfuch said, declining to elaborate further.

Sheinbaum has directed Attorney General Rosa Icela Rodríguez to meet with Leyva’s family and will also consult with journalists. “We have committed to several meetings in hopes of reassuring them that impunity will not be permitted,” Rodríguez said.

Sheinbaum denies Ruffo arrest linked to politics

In response to a question regarding opposition figures accusing the Sheinbaum administration of political persecution, the president denied that federal prosecutors are targeting political opponents.

Addressing the recent arrest of former Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo — a member of the National Action Party (PAN) — Sheinbaum said Ruffo was ensnared in a 12-month fuel theft investigation in which eight others were arrested.

“[Ruffo] is the primary shareholder [of Ingemar, the company accused of criminal activity], but he was not the ‘target’ … and the investigation is ongoing,” she said, adding that any others found to be involved will be pursued equally.

Sheinbaum said the investigation seeks to prove that Ingemar was illegally importing fuel (and evading taxes) and was fraudulently distributing it. “This has nothing to do with politics,” she said.

With reports from Milenio and Infobae

World.title: Michoacán priest douses crowd with pressurized holy water, sparking online debate
World.content:
A Catholic priest in the western Mexican state of Michoacán has gone viral after a video showed him using a pressure washer to spray holy water over a crowd during a patron saint festival.

The footage, widely shared across TikTok, Facebook and Instagram, shows Father Rubén Pérez Rubio standing in the bed of a white pickup truck during celebrations honoring Saint James the Apostle in Contepec, a Michoacán municipality of about 35,000 near the Querétaro border.

Holding a pressure washer (hidrolavadora in Spanish) he directs a stream of holy water (agua bendita) toward dozens of parishioners gathered outside the church on Wednesday.

The unusual method allowed the priest to reach a large crowd at once, with attendees — including women, children and elderly worshippers — reacting with laughter, raised hands and applause as they received the blessing.

“May my magnanimous mercy pour out its grace upon you all,” the priest says in Spanish in the video.

Local accounts cited by El Universal and other media outlets say the approach was intended to ensure no one was left without holy water during one of the municipality’s most important annual religious celebrations, which draws large numbers of residents and visitors.

The video quickly went viral, generating thousands of comments and sparking debate about the balance between tradition and innovation in religious practice.

Some social media users praised the priest’s creativity and practicality, saying the method helped engage the community and adapt to large crowds.

Others questioned whether using a pressure washer diminished the solemnity of a ritual typically performed with a traditional aspergillum.

Additional criticism focused on what some described as a waste of holy water and a lack of reverence.

Still, many commenters framed the act as a lighthearted moment that reflected a more accessible and modern approach to religion.

As of Friday, Pérez Rubio had not publicly commented on the viral video.

Saint James the Apostle, or Santiago Apóstol in Spanish, is honored across Latin America and Spain as a patron of pilgrims and towns whose July 25 feast day blends Catholic ritual with local tradition.

In Michoacán, patron saint festivals for him typically feature special Masses, processions through the streets, music and cultural activities.

With reports from El Universal, El Heraldo de México, Luz Noticias and N+

World.title: The Mexican historical figures behind San Miguel de Allende’s iconic landmarks
World.content:
San Miguel de Allende’s colonial streets and centuries-old architecture bear the names of some of Mexico’s most prominent historical figures. From leaders of the revolution to artists and architects, San Miguel is a living history lesson around every turn. So when you are strolling the gardens in San Miguel’s parks or walking down some of its most historic streets, here are the prominent figures that give their names to San Miguel’s most iconic sites.

Ignacio Allende

Ignacio Allende, a leader of the Mexican Revolution against Spain and the namesake of San Miguel de Allende, is the most prominent Mexican historical figure born in San Miguel.

The son of wealthy Spanish colonists, Allende enlisted with the Spanish army in Mexico before joining the underground independence movement. Eventually, Allende was named lieutenant general of the Revolutionary Army with Miguel Hidalgo y Castillo serving as Captain General.

The two succeeded in winning early victories, but were pushed back towards Guadalajara after failing to march on Mexico City. Hidalgo and Allende, despite greatly outnumbering the royalist forces, were defeated at the Battle of Calderon Bridge in Jalisco. This caused the insurgent troops to oust Hidalgo as their leader and install Allende as the head of the revolution.

Allende attempted to move north towards the United States in the hope of making powerful allies with the Americans. However, he was ambushed by royalist forces and taken to Chihuahua, where he was tried and executed by firing squad on June 26, 1811.

San Miguel de Allende was named after him when it became a city in 1826. The Plaza Ignacio Allende in Centro and the Instituto Allende on Salida a Celaya bear his name. Municipalities in six other Mexican states, including Chihuahua, Nuevo León and Jalisco are named after him.

Benito Juárez

Benito Juárez is one of the most famous historical figures in Mexican history, becoming the first Indigenous president after winning the Reform War and helping to fight off monarchist troops during the French invasion. Benito Juárez Park, about two blocks south of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel, is named after him.

Juárez walked nearly 30 miles to Oaxaca City when he was young to find work, eventually becoming a lawyer. He became the governor of Oaxaca in 1847, but was later exiled by the dictator Antonio López de Santa Anna and he fled to New Orleans, Louisiana.

Juárez later returned as a member of the Reform Party, but was imprisoned as Mexico began to fracture in civil war. After the conservatives won early battles, the liberals regrouped and were able to triumph. Juárez then became the first Indigenous president after assuming the role in 1861.

His problems were far from over, however, as the French — at the invitation of Mexican monarchists — invaded central Mexico and installed Austrian royal Maximilian as emperor. After fleeing north and narrowly escaping death, Juárez received a massive loan from the United States that reinvigorated the Republican troops, eventually forcing the French to flee.

Juárez once again assumed the role as the leader of Mexico, and executed Maximilian despite pleas for clemency. Juárez served for over 14 years as president before dying of a heart attack while still in office in 1872.

Zeferino Gutiérrez

The towering pink facade of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel is, by far, the most iconic landmark in San Miguel. It was designed by iconic stonemason Zeferino Gutiérrez, a highly respected master of his craft despite never being trained as an architect.

Gutiérrez, whose previous work only involved steps and altars of local churches, used postcards of iconic European castles to design the iconic facade. He used pink lava stone, which has retained its color to this day and helped transform San Miguel into a world-renowned tourist destination.

Gutiérrez was given a home in San Miguel for his work on the church and continued to design and build places of worship. He designed the original Mercado Ignacio Ramírez on the town’s Civic Plaza, which was later replaced with the iconic statue of Ignacio Allende on a horse.

The typhus epidemic swept through San Miguel during the height of the Mexican Revolution, killing Gutiérrez in 1916. In January 2020, Zeferino Gutiérrez Park opened in San Miguel just north of the Fabrica la Aurora art center, becoming the largest park in the municipality.

Ignacio Ramírez

Ignacio Ramírez was one of the most prominent liberals of the La Reforma movement, which aimed to create a liberal democracy in Mexico and advocated for the separation of church and state.

The Ignacio Ramírez Cultural Center in the Centro neighborhood bears his name, along with the Mercado Ignacio Ramírez just north of the Civic Plaza.

Ramírez was born in San Miguel de Allende and was raised on liberal values before studying at university in Querétaro. He began publishing liberal newspapers and worked a slew of governmental positions before participating in the reform movement.

When the government of Benito Juárez eventually won power, Ramírez was given a spot in the cabinet where he continued to push for liberal reforms. He was forced out of the capital when the French marched into Mexico City, but continued to publish liberal ideals in hiding. Ramírez was imprisoned by the monarchist government upon his return to Mexico City, but was freed when the empire fell in 1867.

Under President Porfirio Díaz, who seized power in a military coup, Ramírez was named Minister of Justice and was elected to the Supreme Court. He died in 1879 at 60 years old.

Ángela Peralta

Located in the heart of Centro near the Ignacio Ramirez Cultural Center stands the Ángela Peralta Theater, one of the cultural icons of San Miguel.

Peralta, one of the greatest operatic singers in Mexican history, made her debut at just 15 years old in Mexico City before relocating to study in Italy under the bank of a wealthy financier. She made 32 curtain calls in Europe and North Africa, where she was dubbed the “Mexican Nightingale,” before returning to perform in Mexico at the invitation of Maximilian.

After another stint in Europe, Peralta returned to Mexico City, but was involved with an affair with a local entrepreneur, causing many in the city to boycott her performances. She left the city and recovered her reputation before embarking on a tour of northern Mexico. The tour was a success, but on an elaborate visit to Mazatlán, Peralta — along with most of her troupe — contacted yellow fever. Perlata died on Aug. 30, 1883 at the age of 38.

On top of her singing, Peralta was a composer, pianist and harpist. Amphitheaters and theaters across the country are named after her in tribute.

Pedro Vargas

Pedro Vargas, an actor and singer born in San Miguel de Allende, was one of the key figures of the golden age of Mexican cinema from 1936-1956. His former home and his statue sits on the street Salida Real a Querétaro. The house is now a luxury estate, next to the popular lookout of the Parroquia.

Vargas, nicknamed “The Nightingale of the Americas,” left San Miguel at just 14 years old for Mexico City, where he studied at the National Conservatory of Music. Although his career began in the opera, he transitioned into popular song and appeared in over 70 films, eventually performing for U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt at the White House in 1942. Vargas also performed extensively throughout Mexico and at major venues in the United States, including Carnegie Hall and Madison Square Garden.

Throughout his career, Vargas performed lyrical pieces, boleros and ranchera ballads written by some of Mexico’s most celebrated composers, including Agustín Lara. Vargas died in 1989 at the age of 83 in Mexico City.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Feelings you can only experience in Mexican Spanish
World.content:
I was raised in a bicultural environment. Not because either of my parents was from abroad, but because I went to a bilingual school my entire life. Most of my teachers were either from the United States or the United Kingdom — so yes, growing up, I learned how to count pennies and quarters, as well as Mexican pesos.

However, I was often curious as to how to translate the use of usted, for example, which in English does not exist. At a very early age, I remember being unable to express in English some of the feelings I spoke about at home, which were inherently of a Mexican traditional upbringing. Culturally, there were literally no words that could transmit the warmth of an apapacho or the joy of cotorreo in English. As the editors probably know, I often misuse prepositions (I hope it brings them some relief to know I also experience this in Spanish).

Beyond my grammatical imperfections and translation confusions, here’s a handpicked guide to some of my favorite feelings you can only experience in Mexican Spanish — from an imperfect Mexican writer to an ever-supportive readership.

Cotorrear

Cotorrear comes from the word cotorro, meaning parakeets, which are widely known for being talkative and outspoken animals. Cotorrear, thus, implies a noisy conversation in which friends and family members talk over one another excitedly, about anything and everything, all at once.

People, however, do not cotorrean with their bosses or the police (that would be, to say the least, suspicious). You do so with your close inner circle, because although it is a leisurely talk, it’s usually not just small talk. People cotorrean about their issues, about politics and about how their car landed again at the mechanic.

Apapachar

As happens with most Mexicanisms, apapachar comes from Náhuatl, the official language of the Mexica Empire. It translates as people allowing others to care for them with tender displays of affection, such as Grandma’s hug, a nice, warm soup made by Mom, or even just going to a dear friend’s house to talk about a recent loss. “Ser apapachada, apapachado” implies allowing oneself to be vulnerable to a loved one, especially when you’re feeling ill or down emotionally.

Chacharear

Chacharar is just fun. It’s what you do when you’re on vacation and land in the Pueblo Mágico’s wondrous mercado de artesanías, or go on a Sunday stroll to La Lagunilla market. The word comes from cháchara: “something small, unimportant and of little value,” as defined by the Dictionary of Mexican Spanish. I think the best translation is simply “a trinket.”

Chacharear, however, is not like window shopping. You actually get to feel and touch the trinkets in the market, and even get to discuss a lower price with your vendor (oh, the glorious thrill of regateo!). Also, when you’re chachareando, it doesn’t mean you will actually buy any of the things that caught your eye! Actually, you probably won’t — you just do it for the joy of contemplating useless things you don’t need, but you somehow find interesting or amusing.

Achicopalarse

You know when someone is so sad, they actually round their back in a crestfallen way? They’re probably achicopalada, achicopalado. The term comes, again, from Náhuatl achikopa, which has been translated as “feeling inferior.” However, in contemporary Mexican Spanish, the term is used as simply “feeling down.”

You’ll probably feel achicopalada when your boyfriend just dumped you, or when you failed the test you studied so hard for. Or even when your parents unfairly grounded you. People can even feel achicopalados when the sky is heavy with dark clouds, or the weather isn’t that nice, too.

Desconchinflarse

When the blender breaks down, the air conditioner doesn’t work, or the TV screen refuses to turn on, that’s when you know your appliances are desconchinfladas. And it’s sad. Because they’re not beyond repair, they’re simply waiting for you to take them to the shop to be fixed — and maybe you’re just too busy (or lazy) to go.

However, desconchinflarse does not only apply to hardware. Whenever you hurt your leg or possibly strain an ankle, you can also say your foot is desconchinflado. You don’t get to go to the hardware store to repair one of those, though (please, go see a doctor).

Petatearse

Petatearse is possibly the only feeling in Mexican Spanish that every person on planet Earth (and beyond) will eventually face. It comes from the Náhuatl word petate, a rug, and it translates literally as dying. When people in the ancient Mexica Empire died, they were wrapped in a handmade ritual mat before their funeral ceremonies. So whenever you hear someone “se petateó,” it literally means they passed.

However, you would never hear anyone say their grandmother “se petateó.” That would just be disrespectful and rude. Petatearse is a verb people use as slang when referring to someone they don’t know in a mischievous Mexican way. So no, if you receive the news of a dear friend who just lost a family member, do not say “se petatearon.” Please. Ever.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband
World.content:
October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A tentative October 2, 2026 court date has been set in the attempted murder case against Elvira Mulholland, who is accused of shooting her husband during a domestic dispute in 2024.

Mulholland appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Friday, represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones. She remains out on High Court bail.

The defence informed the court that Mulholland is also currently on trial in the Magistrate’s Court for an alleged robbery arising from the same incident. That trial, which began in April, is scheduled to continue on August 3.

Justice Nanton adjourned the attempted murder matter until October 2 for a case management conference, by which time the lower court proceedings are expected to have concluded. A firm trial date could then be determined.

Police allege that on October 25, 2024, Mulholland followed her husband, Jeffrey Mulholland, along the Coastal Road, ran his pickup truck off the road and shot him with his own licensed firearm following a struggle.

She was committed to stand trial in the High Court after a preliminary inquiry concluded in July 2025.

World.title: Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation
World.content:
Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder case against Collin Francis Jr. could take a significant turn when it returns to the High Court on Tuesday, July 28, 2026.

Francis had previously been found unfit to enter a plea and was ordered to undergo psychiatric evaluations every six months for two years. However, Justice Nigel Pilgrim was informed on Friday that only one evaluation had been completed.

The June 29, 2026 report, prepared by psychiatrist Dr. Denethia Usher, found that Francis is now stable, taking his medication and considered fit to enter a plea. The report also noted that his condition had improved while he was away from marijuana.

The prosecution indicated that the Director of Public Prosecutions’ office was prepared to proceed to trial. Justice Pilgrim, however, said he would not allow the case to proceed to trial based solely on the single evaluation.

The judge asked whether the prosecution would consider accepting a guilty plea, but the Crown said instructions would first have to be obtained from the DPP.

Francis is charged with the 2019 murder of 60-year-old Nestor Vasquez Jr., who was fatally injured while the two men were detained in a cell at the Queen Street Police Station.

The matter was adjourned until Tuesday for the prosecution to indicate how it intends to proceed.

World.title: BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’
World.content:
BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton today sentenced 31-year-old Belize Defence Force (BDF) volunteer soldier Mark Anthony Nolberto to 17 years, 10 months, and 3 weeks in prison following his conviction on two counts of rape against a 17-year-old girl.

Justice Nanton ordered that the sentences for both counts run concurrently. In addition to his prison term, Nolberto must undergo counseling as well as medical and psychiatric treatment while incarcerated. Upon his release, he will be legally required to report his residential address to the Commissioner of Police and the Department of Human Development.

The convictions stem from an incident where Nolberto struck the minor with a metal cup, forced her into his residence, subjected her to physical and sexual assault, and recorded the act on his mobile phone—video footage that was later extracted by police and presented as evidence in court.

In delivering the sentence, Justice Nanton classified the harm as severe and noted the high degree of offender culpability, pointing to the victim’s age, the violent nature of the attack, and Nolberto’s lack of remorse throughout the trial. Starting from a 19-year baseline, the judge deducted two years for Nolberto’s prior lack of a criminal record and community service, added one year to reflect the overall severity of the crime, and credited 40 days for time served on remand.

Defense attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington had requested a suspended sentence, but Justice Nanton rejected the plea, citing statutory laws that restrict suspended sentences to offenses carrying maximum terms of three years or less. Under Belizean law, rape carries a mandatory minimum sentence of eight years in prison up to life imprisonment. The prosecution was led by Crown Counsel Joseph Perez.

Following the sentencing, Nolberto maintained his innocence as he was escorted from the High Court, telling reporters that he refused to cover his face because he believed the conviction was “unjust.”

World.title: What is your child doing this Summer? Making memories, Learning new skills or scrolling social media?
World.content:
What is your child doing this Summer? Making memories, Learning new skills or scrolling social media?

By Zoila Palma: With schools closed for the summer break, children and teenagers across Belize have more free time on their hands.

For parents, this can be a valuable opportunity to encourage their children to explore new interests, develop practical skills and build meaningful relationships.

But it also raises an important question: How are our children spending their summer vacation?

Across the country, organizations, churches, schools and community groups offer summer camps and activities designed to keep young people engaged and learning.

From Youth in Agriculture Summer Camps that introduce children to farming, livestock and food production, to Vacation Bible Schools that focus on faith, values and fellowship, there are opportunities for children to learn outside the traditional classroom.

Sports camps, arts programs and other youth activities also allow children to discover talents and interests they may not have had the chance to explore during the school year.

Summer is also a chance for children to gain experiences that cannot always be taught in a classroom.

A child who participates in an agriculture camp may learn how to care for animals, grow food and understand where the food on their plate comes from.

Another child attending a Bible school may strengthen their faith and develop important values, while sports and creative programs can teach teamwork, discipline and confidence.

These experiences can help shape a child’s character and expose them to possibilities that could influence their future.

Parents can also use this time to consider how much time their children are spending on social media, video games and their phones.

Technology has its benefits, but unlimited screen time can quickly consume an entire summer if there are no boundaries.

Instead of allowing children to spend hours scrolling through TikTok, Instagram or other platforms, parents can encourage a healthier balance that includes reading, learning, helping at home, spending time outdoors and participating in activities that challenge them.

Summer vacation should not mean that learning comes to a complete stop.

Are our children taking advantage of every opportunity to learn something new, make friends and develop skills, or are they spending most of their days online?

A summer filled with new experiences, learning and positive activities can create memories that last a lifetime—and perhaps even inspire a child to discover a passion that shapes their future.

World.title: International News: Western Europe records hottest June ever as extreme heat fuels wildfires
World.content:
International News: Western Europe records hottest June ever as extreme heat fuels wildfires

By Zoila Palma: Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record in 2026, with extreme temperatures affecting large parts of the region and contributing to wildfires, drought and serious health risks.

According to the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the region recorded an average temperature of 20.74°C, which was 3.05°C above the 1991–2020 average and surpassed the previous record set in June 2025.

The heatwave continued into July, with Spain’s Fabra Observatory in Barcelona recording 40.5°C on July 8, the highest temperature recorded there in more than a century. France also issued widespread heat alerts amid high fire danger caused by drought, extreme temperatures and low humidity, while devastating wildfires affected parts of France and the Iberian Peninsula.

Temperature records were broken across several European countries during June.

Germany recorded 41.7°C in Coschen on June 28, while Hungary reached 40.7°C, Austria 40°C and the United Kingdom recorded 37.3°C in southern England. France experienced its hottest day on record on June 24, with temperatures reaching 43.8°C in Palluau, while Spain’s Bilbao reached a record 42.7°C for June.

Health officials warned that prolonged extreme heat, particularly when nighttime temperatures remain high, can place severe stress on the body. Older adults, young children, pregnant women, outdoor workers, people experiencing homelessness and those living with chronic illnesses are among those most at risk.

The extreme heat was also accompanied by widespread dryness, worsening drought conditions and increased wildfire activity across parts of Europe.

World.title: International News: Former President Hernández to return to Honduras after Trump pardon, challenge local charges
World.content:
International News: Former President Hernández to return to Honduras after Trump pardon, challenge local charges

By Zoila Palma: Former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández is set to return to Honduras on Sunday and seek the dismissal of separate fraud and money-laundering charges that were not covered by the pardon he received from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Hernández, who was released after Trump pardoned his 45-year prison sentence for cocaine trafficking in the United States, said he expects to begin legal proceedings in Honduras in early August.

He maintains his innocence and has argued that the local case was politically motivated, adding that he has already requested that the arrest warrant against him be dropped, Reuters report.

The former president faces the Honduran charges in connection with the Pandora II case, which investigated alleged corruption and the misuse of state funds.

Hernández, who governed Honduras from 2014 to 2022, was extradited to the United States in 2022 and convicted in 2024 after prosecutors accused him of facilitating the trafficking of hundreds of tons of cocaine.

He served less than two years of his sentence before Trump’s pardon.

World.title: International News: More than 21,000 Venezuelans displaced 1 month after earthquakes
World.content:
International News: More than 21,000 Venezuelans displaced 1 month after earthquakes

By Zoila Palma: One month after twin earthquakes devastated northern Venezuela, more than 21,000 people remain displaced and living in temporary shelters, while families continue searching for missing loved ones.

Humanitarian organizations warn that the disaster is quickly becoming a long-term recovery crisis that could take years to overcome.

More than 5,200 people have died and nearly 17,000 others have been injured, while the World Bank estimates the earthquakes caused $19.6 billion in direct physical damage.

Entire neighborhoods remain in ruins, with schools, hospitals, roads and businesses struggling to reopen.

Nearly 18,000 homes were reportedly destroyed or left uninhabitable, forcing thousands of families into shelters, schools, sports facilities and temporary camps, Latin Times reports.

Although formal search-and-rescue operations ended weeks ago, families in the hardest-hit areas, including La Guaira and neighboring states, continue to search for answers about missing relatives.

Aid workers say survivors are also facing shortages of housing, clean water, medical care and essential services, while overcrowded shelters and damaged infrastructure raise concerns about public health risks.

World.title: Ministry of Health and Wellness and Pan American Health Organization discuss Tobacco Control Bill
World.content:
Ministry of Health and Wellness and Pan American Health Organization discuss Tobacco Control Bill

By Zoila Palma: This week, the Ministry of Health & Wellness continued discussions with the visiting Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) country mission team on the next steps toward advancing the Tobacco Control Bill in Belize.

On July 20, 2026, a meeting was held by Minister of Health & Wellness, Kevin Bernard, along with the Ministry’s management team.

Discussions focused on public sensitization of the Tobacco Control Bill, tobacco taxation, and strengthening national capacity to support its implementation.

The Ministry says that it remains committed to working closely with PAHO and other partners to identify the support needed and determine the next steps toward the successful adaptation and implementation of the Tobacco Control Bill in Belize.

World.title: Hitman’s appeal denied
World.content:
Simone Campbell-Collymore, whose confessed killer Wade Blackwood had his appeal rejected on Friday.

THE Court of Appeal on Friday upheld the sentence and conviction of killer Wade Blackwood, who in 2021 was sentenced to life in prison after confessing to being the trigger man in the 2018 murder of 32-year-old businesswoman Simone Campbell-Collymore.

The then 24-year-old, in a confession, detailed how he had been subcontracted to kill Campbell-Collymore in a $2-million murder-for-hire plot hatched by her then husband Omar “Best” Collymore.

Thirty-six-year-old taxi driver Winston Walters was also killed during the incident which took place outside Campbell-Collymore’s Forest Ridge apartment in Red Hills, St Andrew, on January 2, 2018.

The two men involved in the shooting that day were identified by the police, from closed-circuit television footage in the vicinity, as Blackwood and a now-deceased Corporate Area don who went by the name Jim.

Blackwood, who had been held by cops in April 2018, had pleaded guilty in January 2021 to two counts of murder and one count of illegal possession of firearm before the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment for his role in the murders, ahead of the other individuals involved in the plot, with 35 years on each count of murder before eligibility for parole, and eight years and six months for illegal possession of firearm. Those sentences, however, were to run concurrently, making it so that he would serve 35 years before applying for parole.

Friday, the Appeal Court, which heard the matter over two days, in handing down its decision ruled that based on the fact that Blackwood was resentenced on February 9, 2024, after a plea agreement was reached, the basis of his appeal was obsolete.

Blackwood, through his attorney Shenieka Sparks, in supplemental grounds of appeal filed this year, had contended that a discount for his guilty plea was “unreasoned and inadequate”.

He further argued that the sentencing judge had erred in setting 30 years as a starting point to arrive at his ultimate sentence. According to Blackwood, compared to other similar cases, the discount was “out of parity”.

The Jamaica Observer was told that when Blackwood was advised of the decision of the Appeal Court he accepted that he would not continue challenging his sentence and a notice of abandonment was filed on his behalf.

As such, Blackwood will serve 20 years before he is eligible for parole, as was the sentence imposed on following his plea deal.

In February 2024, Blackwood — who testified against his co-accused following a deal with prosecutors — claimed he was pressured into committing the act by Jim, who was supposedly the leader of a gang his brother had been involved with.

Blackwood claimed that Jim, in levelling death threats at him and his family, told him that he had to carry out the killing to repay his brother’s debt for a firearm that had been seized by the police.

Blackwood, in negotiating with the prosecution, had 15 years shaved off his sentence, which now makes him eligible for parole after 20 years.

At the end of the substantive trial, Collymore, who was slapped with two life sentences, was also sentenced to one year and six months for conspiracy and ordered to serve 46 years and six months before becoming eligible for parole. His co-conspirators Dwayne Pink, Michael Adams, and Shaquille Edwards were also handed life sentences.

In the highly publicised incident, Campbell-Collymore and Walters were ambushed and shot dead outside the apartment complex where she lived with her then husband and children.

The Crown, at the close of its case, established that Collymore ordered the hit to claim his wife’s multimillion-dollar life insurance policies from which their two children were entitled to 15 per cent each while Collymore was entitled to 70 per cent of the benefits.

He was also listed as trustee for the children and their portion. Those policies were taken out by the couple three months before the murders.

Collymore was collared by cops at Norman Manley International Airport while attempting to flee the island a day before his wife’s funeral.

Earlier this month, Collymore, alongside his co-accused Pink, Adams, and Edwards, appeared before the Home Circuit Court again where they are all facing charges of illegal possession of firearm, shooting with intent, and conspiracy to murder with respect to an unnamed woman the businessman was in a relationship with at the time he orchestrated his wife’s death.

A new conspirator, Carey Jonas, is also named on the indictment with respect to the new matter.

On Thursday, Edwards, who had entered into plea negotiations with the prosecution and pleaded guilty to the new charges, was sentenced to six years and nine months for his part in that crime.

Edwards, however, has already spent more than seven years in custody and is set to be released.

World.title: No ease in honey shortage
World.content:
President of the St James Bee Farmers Association Dennis McKay with two bottles of honey, on Tuesday.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — The nation could be facing a severe honey shortage by the end of the year as the long-term effects of last October’s Hurricane Melissa continue to cripple the beekeeping industry, according to president of the St James Bee Farmers’ Association Dennis McKay.

He said even the intense heat now being felt across the country pales in comparison to the lingering effects of the Category 5 storm.

“It’s not so much the heat that is the crisis for the bees. Probably the major problem at this time is the impact of the hurricane and the trees that are missing. The storm turned down all the trees that provide the nectar and the pollen that support the bees. They are unable to get the nectar, so they cannot get enough nectar to store that we can get honey,” McKay told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

He explained that this period would ordinarily be the height of the honey-producing season, when beekeepers harvest their largest volumes. However, with many nectar-producing trees destroyed and only now beginning to recover, bees are gathering just enough food to sustain their colonies rather than building honey reserves.

“As the bees get the little nectar, it is only enough to feed them, not enough to store. So that is the major crisis as it relates to where the beekeeping and the honey business is going to go,” he said.

The dramatic decline in production has left many farmers with only a fraction of their usual harvest.

“A man used to get maybe 100 bottles from an apiary, [now] he only gets four bottles,” McKay said, adding that even large commercial operators who previously sold honey by the drum are now only able to provide a few bottles.

“He’s not getting enough that he can be selling by the drum, like before,” he added.

McKay also noted that many beekeepers suffered another devastating blow when they lost entire colonies during the hurricane.

“We are heading into a honey crisis,” he warned.

According to McKay, the dwindling supply has already sent up retail prices.

“Right now, honey used to be selling for $3,000 a bottle. I went into a supermarket and see it for $4,800, before tax added. This is the middle of the honey season; this is a time when everybody get honey,” he said.

McKay predicted that prices could climb even higher by Christmas.

“Going down to December, you might be paying $7,000 per bottle,” he cautioned.

While some damaged trees are beginning to regenerate, McKay said recovery is likely to be gradual and warned that another major weather event could worsen the situation.

“The existing trees now that are coming up, they may blossom next year, or we might have to start talking about importation of honey,” he said.

However, he expressed concern about relying on imported supplies, arguing that consumers cannot always be certain of their authenticity.

“I am seeing online where honey is made without bees. It’s only when you buy your local honey [that] you can have certain confidence that at least it come from bees,” McKay said.

Following the hurricane, the Government distributed sugar to beekeepers to help sustain weakened colonies. McKay said the assistance was useful when nectar was scarce.

“Bees don’t make honey with sugar. They use the sugar syrup to feed their young. As soon as trees start to blossom they don’t want that sugar water anymore,” he underscored.

He also suggested that support programmes should have included replacing lost colonies, noting that while some districts still have flowering trees, many of the bees needed to pollinate them and produce honey were wiped out during the hurricane.

“We have to be concerned because some people depend on that for a living,” McKay said.

World.title: Job scam victims repaid in court but case not closed
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — Decarlos Christie, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud, has repaid a total of $200,000 to two women who fell prey to a job scam.

With the payment, part of his case has been resolved but he has been remanded as he still owes one of the women $57,000. There is also a third alleged victim.

Decarlos, who is jointly charged with his brother Bryan Christie, appeared before Judge Kaysha Grant-Pryce in the St James Parish Court on Wednesday. Two of three complainants attended the hearing. One was repaid the full $52,000 she had paid while another received $148,000 of the $205,000 of which she was allegedly defrauded. Judge Grant-Pryce has directed that efforts be made to contact the third complainant

Following Wednesday’s guilty plea Decarlos was admonished and discharged in relation to the matter involving the complainant who received full restitution. He is expected to pay the outstanding balance owed to the second complainant by July 29, when the matter will next be before the court. While he was remanded in custody, his brother’s bail was extended.

During the hearing Decarlos maintained that his brother, Bryan, used his personal information without his knowledge or consent to carry out the transactions while he was in custody in St Ann on unrelated matters. Decarlos insisted that he had no involvement in the alleged scheme.

According to the allegations, in January the first complainant was introduced by telephone to a man identifying himself only as “Mr Campbell”, who claimed to be offering overseas job placement opportunities. She was allegedly instructed to deposit $52,000 into a bank account registered to Decarlos Christie.

Police say a second complainant later deposited $205,000 into the same account for the same purpose, while a third complainant transferred $10,000. Investigators allege the complainants were subsequently assured they would travel to Kingston as part of the overseas employment programme. However, the promised arrangements did not materialise, prompting reports to the police.

During the investigation, police reportedly found that Decarlos’s bank card and account information were in Bryan’s possession, leading to the former being charged. Police further allege that Bryan was the individual who communicated with the complainants while posing as “Mr Campbell” and offering the overseas job opportunities.

World.title: Hill wary of call for ganja amnesty
World.content:
HILL...I have to remind you all that ganja is a Schedule 1 drug. It’s the same thing as fentanyl, the same thing as cocaine

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — While a key stakeholder in the cannabis industry continues to call for an amnesty to regularise farmers operating outside the regulated sector, Minister of Industry, Investment and Commerce Senator Aubyn Hill has sounded a cautionary note. He pointed to the complex international legal landscape in explaining his stance on the matter.

“I have to remind you all that ganja is a Schedule 1 drug. It’s the same thing as fentanyl, the same thing as cocaine. It’s in the same category as heroin. It is seen as a bad drug,” the minister stressed.

He was addressing a Westmoreland Chamber of Commerce and Industry meeting at the Hotel Commingle in Savanna-la-Mar on Wednesday. He gave a breakdown on the implications for international trade and travel.

“Even today, because it’s a Schedule 1 drug, if you fly in the airspace of the United States, you are illegal. You can be taken out. You see what happened to those guys out there in the sea? That can happen to a ganja plane flying in the airspace of the United States, legally,” warned the minister.

He further emphasised that strict compliance with international drug laws is essential to maintaining Jamaica’s standing in global trade.

Hill was responding to questions posed by Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) board member Verald Vassell, better known as Ras Iyah V. The Westmoreland ganja advocate — who served on the CLA board from 2016 to 2021 and returned in 2024 — has consistently pointed to the need for an amnesty to transition illicit farmers into the legal medical cannabis industry.

During Wednesday night’s meeting Ras Iyah V highlighted what he said was continued harassment farmers face at the hands of the police.

“As the minister in charge of the CLA, what are the plans? Because I know the regulation has been amended recently. But what are the plans, the road map, and if you can explain how this is going to work? Because, as for me, I see a certain approach that creates a glut in the market, and then there is no market… Can you explain what is the road map going forward to bring our ganja farmers from being considered illegal into the legal industry? Because most of these farmers have been out-financed,” stated Ras Iyah V.

Acknowledging the concerns raised by the advocate, Hill outlined recent legislative changes aimed at easing operational restrictions for small-scale cultivators.

“Under my leadership with the permanent secretary and the people in the ministry, we changed the law. Because the very small farmer was constantly complaining of being put upon, [saying] they can’t get their things done. And we said, ‘Alright, you must have a fence of… five feet,” relayed Hill.

The minister pointed out that these regulatory adjustments provide greater flexibility for traditional farmers and workers trying to satisfy compliance requirements.

Addressing the issue of a market glut, Hill attributed the surplus to the initial surge of interest following the decriminalisation of cannabis.

“Understand that the glut that is developing is because when ganja was decriminalised, the euphoria that came around it encouraged people to go into it. Everybody was in it. There was one firm in Canada that seemed to have made a lot of money and then the thing collapsed. But that euphoria took a lot of people in,” the minister said.

Under the Dangerous Drugs Act, which came into effect on April 15, 2015, provisions were implemented for the possession and smoking of ganja; the use of ganja by those of the Rastafarian faith; and the use of ganja for medical, therapeutic, and scientific purposes.

“Our law allows people who use ganja for their religious practices to be exempt. But they have to go through a process,” explained Hill.

Regarding ongoing police enforcement, he noted that while adults are permitted to possess up to two ounces of ganja without criminal charges, the police must act whenever boundaries are breached.

World.title: Market Bag: Soup vendor Bulbie shops for staples as prices fluctuate
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Shoppers at the Coronation Market will encounter a mixed basket in terms of prices this week.

Persistent dry conditions continue to impact farming, pushing up the prices of some produce including tomatoes at $150 per pound, Scotch bonnet peppers at $350 per pound, sweet peppers at $400 per pound, bananas at $1,400 a dozen and lettuce at $700 per head.

Plantains ($700 for three) also continue to be a pricey commodity.

Still, other food items held steady or declined, including onions at $200 per pound.

In this week’s episode of Market Bag, popular soup vendor Nicardo “Bulbie” Sayer joins host Carlysia Ramdeen as he shops for the fresh ingredients behind his signature Bulbie Soups, a favourite among soup lovers.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Rajindra Campbell signs with Nike
World.content:
Rajindra Campbell signs with Nike

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica’s 2024 Olympic shot put bronze medallist Rajindra Campbell has signed a contract with Nike.

The 30-year-old Campbell, who has always highlighted the plight of non-track athletes in surviving financially, made the revelation via social media earlier this week.

“The work behind the scenes is paying off, and I’m still building. The season isn’t over yet; the best is still to come. Happy to announce I will be continuing my journey as part of the Nike family, Nike Athlete,” Campbell posted on Instagram.

“From the indoor season to now, 2026 has been all about growth, consistency and progress. Every competition has been another opportunity to improve and compete with the best in the world,” he added.

Campbell was one of four Jamaicans who tried to switch allegiance to Turkey in 2025, citing the lack of financial support from Jamaican athletics administrators.

However, world governing body World Athletics rejected their applications.

In announcing the decision, the panel said approving the applications would undermine the intent of World Athletics’ eligibility and transfer-of-allegiance rules.

It found the requests were part of a coordinated recruitment effort by the Turkish Government, operating through a state-funded club, offering lucrative contracts to attract foreign athletes and enable them to compete for Turkey at major events, including the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

In 2024, Campbell accused the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) of not caring about athletes, pointing to an eight-year US$40 million ($6.4 billion) Adidas contract which was turned down when the JAAA extended its contract with longtime sponsors Puma.

“I don’t believe that they really understand that it is challenging. For one, track and field, we are not sprinters, obviously, and as you can see, I am still unsponsored,” he said at the time.

World.title: $1.5-b pothole rescue
World.content:
Water has settled in this pothole on Fairdene Avenue in St Andrew on Thursday.

AS motorists across the island continue to face gaping potholes, minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan has told the Jamaica Observer that the Cabinet on Monday approved a further $1.5-billion spend for patching and sheeting work on main roads across the island to bring some well-needed relief to drivers.

This brings the money allocated to tackle the persistent pothole problem to $3.1 billion for this fiscal year.

According to Morgan, the additional allocation was necessary based on the scope of the problem. He told the Observer that the money initially allocated for the pothole patching programme is already being spent.

“We are engaged in a $1.6-billion programme patching the roads. It’s really sheeting in many cases. Cabinet just approved another $1.5 billion to do more roads. We are doing the $1.6 billion now and then, before the end of the year, we are going to spend another $1.5 billion on road rehabilitation,” said Morgan.

But even as the minister promised relief, motorists across the Corporate Area were pointing the Observer to several roads where potholes are making driving almost impossible.

In downtown Kingston, where many large potholes pockmark the streets, motorists pointed to one on Orange Street, close to its intersection with Heywood Street, which they said is a source of frustration for many.

While an Observer news team was in the area on Thursday, motorists and pedestrians urged the team to take as many pictures and videos as possible to expose the failure of authorities to maintain roads.

In response, Morgan said that area could be fixed as early as next week as it is schduled for priority repairs.

He underscored that his ministry is responsible for fixing main roads through the National Works Agency, and not streets or lanes.

“Not all the roads are mine. I am strictly responsible for main roads; I am not responsible for avenues, lanes, and I am not responsible for crescents. I am not responsible for any of those community roads. None at all. My roads are roads like Washington Boulevard, Constant Spring and Barbican Road.

“Roads like Liguanea Avenue, Paddington Terrace, roads in Cherry Garden, and a lot of the community roads in downtown Kingston are not mine — they belong to the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation — but I have been getting blamed. Parish councils get a billion dollars a year and they need to fix those roads,” argued Morgan.

However residents of several Corporate Area communities only want their roads fixed, with no concern over which agency will do it.

On Fairdene Avenue in Ackee Walk, St Andrew, residents and passing motorists expressed their displeasure at the state of the road, which is littered with very deep and wide potholes..

“It is treacherous. It is dread. When the rain falls, pedestrians get splashed easily all the time. They need to fix the roads properly and done,” said one motorist.

He was supported by another motorist, who charged that the condition of the roads in Corporate Area forces drivers to make detours into areas where they would rather not drive.

In the meantime, one motorist complained about damage to his vehicle by the potholes.

“The road stay very bad, man. The road need to fix. It a mash up mi front end and we have to drive on the roads every day,” lamented the motorist.

World.title: Grief turns to protest in Troy
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents in Troy, Trelawny, on Thursday protesting againt the arrest of a man in connection with fatal mobbing following murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

TROY, Trelawny — Still mourning the murder of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke on Tuesday residents of the usually quiet district took to the streets on Thursday after one of their own was reportedly arrested by the police in connection with the mob killing of the man believed to have attacked her.

According to residents the man was taken into custody by the police who are probing the death of Shani and the fatal attack on the suspected child killer Delroy Coke, and the brutal beating of his father.

The placard-bearing residents used debris to block the Troy main road — which links part of south Trelawny to northern Manchester — as they charged that the police had no reason to arrest the man, whose identity has not been released.

The residents also expressed their anger at the murder of Shani.

“We want justice. Protect our children. Children are the future. Let us protect them. The justice system failed us. We want justice for the brutal murder of Shani,” some of the placards read, while other called for the freeing of the man they said had been taken into custody.

Some of the protesters also took to social media platform TikTok to express their frustration and disgust.

“We a protest, because the police lock up a man and we want him to be freed…. We want justice,” one of the protesting residents told the Jamaica Observer.

Shani partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday. Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on the father and son in the community.

Residents told the Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father was left with major wounds.

When contacted head of the police Area One Assistant Commissioner Glenford Miller said the investigators are seeking those involved in the mob attack.

“I know we are investigating to know who were the persons involved in that mob killing. I cannot say at this time if we have made any arrests,” Miller said mid-morning on Thursday. Subsequent efforts to get a further update were unsuccessful up to press time.

A heavy pall of gloom and anger clouded over Troy on Thursday with one resident telling the

Observer that the community remains grief-stricken.

“The whole of Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” said the resident who requested anonymity.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday, Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

On Wednesday relatives remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night [Tuesday] we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” her aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

World.title: We’ve fallen in love with drones, but they’re not the sole answer
World.content:
They are not. But nor are they mere bit players.

The enthusiasm for drones is understandable. According to the Kyiv Post, on July 9 alone “Ukraine said it struck 14 Russian vessels overnight in the Sea of Azov, including 12 tankers allegedly belonging to Moscow’s sanctioned ‘shadow fleet.’ Ukraine’s drone commander said a total of 35 ships had been hit over the previous 96 hours, while Ukrainian forces also targeted 45 military sites in occupied Crimea and southern Ukraine.”

It’s as if Ukrainian drones are everywhere. And not only is Ukraine using them to hit Russian targets without causing devastating losses to human life the way, say, missiles would; it’s also able to do so at enormous distances.

Drones hit Russian shadow vessels in the Black Sea. They hit Russian shadow vessels in the Mediterranean. They hit Russia’s oil refineries. They hit Russia’s Baltic Sea oil terminals. They’re causing constant problems for the Russian military, and have hit Russia itself. Earlier this month they even struck an oil refinery in Siberia.

In fact, Ukraine’s drones have become such a success that they’re triggering increasingly loud demands for NATO’s European members to shift their focus to these mostly small and cheap weapons. Look at how drones have helped Ukraine shift the course of the war! Look at how much you can achieve at relatively small expense! Drones are the future! Our governments are behind the curve! That’s how the argument goes.

But while drones are indisputably part of the future of warfare, they’re also still experimental and lack clear rules of engagement.

World.title: Trump administration rejects UN farm declaration over gender references
World.content:
The plan, which is completely voluntary, was finally adopted by delegates on Friday. It advises countries to address issues such as biodiversity, animal welfare, emissions and how to prevent the spread of disease.

The word gender only appears once, to explain the numerous mentions of women and equality throughout the document. The goal is to promote equal opportunities for women farmers as well as their nutrition.

“The cross-cutting themes of gender, youth and inclusion are considered essential to ensure that the transformation leaves no one behind,” the agreement states.

But for Washington, the word is too ambiguous. The U.S. administration made its stance clear back in March, when a working group drafted the plan, and again in June, explaining its red lines in a statement.

“It is the policy of the United States to recognize two sexes, male and female. To achieve this, we will use clear and accurate language,” the statement said. For the U.S., focusing on inclusion comes “at the loss of recognizing hard work, excellence, and individual achievement.”

On climate change, the U.S. does not accept the term but prefers to narrow the focus to “specific environmental threats” facing livestock, it said.

World.title: Governments criticize EU’s cash-for-reforms model in new budget
World.content:
It’s yet another thorny issue to solve for the EU's 27 countries racing to reach a deal before the start of 2027, when national elections are due in France, Italy, Poland and Spain, which could make discussions even more difficult.

Major contributors to the budget including Italy, France and Spain, and net recipients of EU funds such as Hungary, Malta and Poland, spoke out against the cash-for-reforms model during Wednesday's meeting. Critics say that the approach could increase the power of national governments at the expense of regions, and result in the EU imposing reforms with no political backing.

“We don’t want [the Commission’s] recommendations to become impositions,” said an EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this article, was granted anonymity to speak freely.

On the other hand, Netherlands defended the plan during the meeting, according to the diplomats. Other fiscally conservative states, such as Sweden and Denmark, have long argued that conditionality could help poorer EU countries become economically more efficient

But two EU diplomats from the rival camp argued that their real motivation is to slow down payments to less affluent regions.

The RRF model

The cash-for-reforms model was tested in the EU’s post-Covid recovery fund, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), where payouts were linked to judicial and pensions reforms among others.

World.title: World chess chief steps aside after EU sanctions
World.content:
Arkady Dvorkovich, president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), talks to media during the pre-tournament press conference on June 16, 2026. | Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

Arkady Dvorkovich stepped aside temporarily after the EU accused him of supporting policies that threaten Ukraine’s sovereignty.

Arkady Dvorkovich, Russia’s former deputy prime minister and president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), suspended his duties Thursday evening after the European Union sanctioned him.

In its latest sanctions package, the EU accused Dvorkovich of “supporting actions or policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.” The FIDE chief pushed back, stating “unequivocally” that he considers the decision “unlawful and unfair.” “I am confident that justice will prevail,” he added.

Dvorkovich became FIDE’s president in 2018, drawing criticism over his closeness to Vladimir Putin’s regime. The Russian president appointed him as deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2018.

Dvorkovich said the decision would remain in effect for as long as he is subject to EU and Swiss sanctions. FIDE Deputy President Viswanathan Anand, a former world champion, will take over his duties. In 2022, Anand told AFP that Dvorkovich had “clearly demonstrated that he is independent of Kremlin influence.”

Under Dvorkovich’s leadership, FIDE’s Ethics and Disciplinary Commission largely overturned a 2024 ruling that had temporarily suspended the Chess Federation of Russia and reprimanded him for “improper association” with an organization or person whose activities conflicted with FIDE’s objectives or interests. The reprimand against Dvorkovich was rescinded.

World.title: China strikes back at EU sanctions targeting defense, tech firms
World.content:
A Bundeswehr truck with the logo Rheinmetall is seen in Unna on July 21, 2026. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images

The announcement came a day after the EU added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong entities to its sanctions list, barring European companies from doing business with them.

BRUSSELS — China announced it will add export restrictions on 14 EU defense and technology companies after the EU added 14 Chinese businesses to its Russia sanctions lists.

This marks Beijing’s most direct and forceful response yet to EU sanctions listings, which it denounced as “egregious.” Recent studies estimate that up to 90 percent of sanctioned goods still reaching Russia transit through China.

Germany’s rapidly expanding defense company Rheinmetall is among 14 firms that Chinese exporters are now barred from supplying with dual-use goods — products that have both civilian and military applications — China’s Ministry of Commerce said Friday. The list also includes Czech truckmaker Tatra, Dutch naval engineering firm IHC Merwede, and several optics and laser companies.

Exporters may apply for licenses permitting certain shipments when they are deemed “truly necessary.”

The announcement came a day after the EU added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong entities to its sanctions list, barring European companies from doing business with them. Most are not high-tech defense firms, but logistics companies that help Russian importers obtain Western technology.

World.title: Polish conservatives split ahead of 2027 election
World.content:
That clash at the top boiled over on Friday when Kaczyński expelled Morawiecki and some three dozen MPs for refusing to abandon an internal grouping in PiS that has been widely seen as Morawiecki’s attempt to build his own splinter party.

Kaczyński announced the expulsion after a midnight deadline he had given Morawiecki and his group to sign loyalty declarations.

“Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign and at the same time everyone knew what the consequences of not signing were. And so they made the decision they made,” Kaczyński told a press briefing at PiS’s headquarters in Warsaw.

Morawiecki’s allies are now expected to establish a separate caucus in the Polish parliament, the 460-seat Sejm.

The departure of Morawiecki’s followers is going to reduce its parliamentary contingent to 140-145 seats, making it the second-biggest caucus after Tusk’s Civic Coalition.

While PiS was ahead of Civic Coalition in polls last fall, support has now dropped to 26 percent, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls, behind the Civic Coalition on 32 percent.

World.title: EU signals relief over new US tariffs as Trump respects transatlantic truce
World.content:
“The EU notes positively the fact that this outcome is in line with the U.S. tariff commitments agreed under the EU-U.S. Joint Statement,” said Olof Gill, deputy chief spokesperson for the European Commission.

While Brussels cautiously welcomed these new tariffs, it is still conscious that more investigations — looking at alleged industrial overcapacity in Europe and pharmaceutical pricing policies — are under way, meaning cumulative duties could ultimately breach the 15 percent cap. Those probes are conducted under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, a tool used by Washington to take action against unfair trade practices by other countries.

“Looking ahead, the EU expects the U.S. to continue abiding by the terms of the EU-U.S. Joint Statement, including as regards any remedies under additional Section 301 investigations,” Gill added.

The new U.S. tariffs follow a five-month investigation into efforts to crack down on imports of goods made with forced labor — a measure specifically combating manufacturing from America's trade rivals in Asia.

The EU’s own forced labor regulation will only apply from Dec. 2027. This is the justification cited by the U.S. Trade Representative for applying a 10 percent tariff on goods coming from the bloc.

The EU’s foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas struck a less diplomatic note, pushing back against Washington’s reasoning to impose the tariffs.

“We had a deal with America and we have kept to that deal, that side of the deal. That's why this is a negative surprise that this agreement is not kept,” she told Reuters on the sidelines of a meeting with ASEAN countries in the Philippines.

“If you compare our labor laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labor conditions for our employees, so it's not really grounded.”

World.title: Merz seeks to revive political fortunes with cabinet reshuffle
World.content:
“These personnel changes follow a clear guiding principle,” he added. “We want a government that works with the greatest enthusiasm and joy, while also reflecting the diversity of our society and political landscape. We are a reform-oriented government, and we intend to continue demonstrating that.”

Merz has often been publicly criticized for surrounding himself with men at top adviser level. With the appointment of Nina Warken, the current health minister, as chancellery chief he is putting a woman in charge of the chancellery’s inner workings for the first time in Germany’s postwar history.
