The position is of strategic importance as it is key to behind-the-scenes brokerage work, for example when mediating between the chancellery and ministries as well as with lawmakers and at state level.

“She is assertive, and she is also well-versed in security policy issues, which are, after all, coordinated here in this house,” Merz said of Warken. “She will therefore be one of the most important — if not the most important— pillars of support for me in the day-to-day work of the government, as well as my primary point of contact.”

The cabinet reshuffle allows Merz to make a political reset before crucial regional elections in September. Polls show that the AfD has a chance of winning an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and is poised to perform well in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin later that month.

To fend off the rise of the far right, Merz has promised to bring much-needed reforms, for example to the pension system, through parliament this fall. In doing so, he would show voters that the political center is indeed the only viable option to get things done, or at least that’s how the thinking goes in the government.

The current general secretary of Merz’s CDU, Carsten Linnemann, is set to take over as health minister from Warken. He will be tasked with bringing one of the key reforms, the health reform, through parliament later this year.

World.title: 'I do not want to replace models with AI': Fashion designer Steven Passaro plans industry revamp
World.content:
One of the most anticipated names at this year's Paris Fashion Week may not be one you've heard before.

 

Steven Passaro has earned praise and recognition from LVMH, the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode, and the French Ministry of Culture, to name just a few.

The French-Portuguese fashion designer graduated from the prestigious Duperré School of Applied Arts in Paris and the University of the Arts London. Before launching his eponymous label, he honed his craft at renowned fashion houses including Hermès, Loewe and Christian Dior.

In an exclusive interview with Euronews Culture, the visionary designer reflected on his creative process, his work, and the evolving landscape of the fashion industry.

Euronews Culture: You initially studied architecture. How did that experience influence your transition into fashion design?

Architecture was kind of my first love. I really developed my mindset around visualizing 3D thanks to the constructions we do in architecture. To me, it was natural to keep the skills of what I've been learning in architecture and translate them into fashion.

Your collections feature strong, structured silhouettes and rigid forms. What draws you to this approach?

The way I see it is there are two ways to dress the body.

In the West, they cut fabric to shape a body, and in the East, they have more of this approach to wrap the body with fabric. I really wanted to have this conversation in duality in the silhouette design.

I really wanted to build a language that you can evolve and adapt season after season.

The architecture allowed me to have this kind of tension between the two, where you sometimes have very strong, almost sculptural aspect in the silhouette, but also some fluidity.

The Spring-Summer 2026 collection called Moonlit Lover explored "toxic love" - secret love affairs, late-night obsessions, and illusions that end up hurting more than they heal. The Fall-Winter 2026 collection called Ethereal Shift delved into personal transformation, letting go, and finding meaning in a chaotic world. Where do you seek get your inspiration from?

The collection is always a continuity of the story of the previous season. In French we say "le fil rouge" [guiding thread] - to me, there is no break [between the collections].

I really wanted to build a language that you can evolve and adapt season after season. It's one big main theme, and each one is a different angle to describe the subject. There is a phase of transformation from a point A to point B, but I think it's very intuitive work at the end of the day.

There's some inspiration on psychology, on spirituality. Also what's happening in the world right now.

The last collection we just presented - I call it the “glimpse” - because it's that moment where you're going to step into something, you really want it, but you're also very afraid of it. It's the feeling I have towards the world right now, with all the political aspects, where there's a very good thing happening in the world, but also a very bad thing. It's this in between tension of “I want to, but I'm afraid to”.

So, hopefully, the next season will be a bit lighter.

Your design process differs from that of many traditional fashion designers. You rely heavily on digital 3D modelling before creating physical prototypes. What led you to adopt this approach, and what advantages does it offer?

At the London College of Fashion, we had a Department for Technology in Fashion, where you can learn about all this technology around the industry, and what people will use in the future.

I came across the software and it was like "Oh, that feels like what I was doing in architecture, but for fashion." I’ve always been a huge nerd, so to me, it was kind of natural to experiment with it.

The calculation became clear when I started to understand that I can make a pattern in two hours compared to by hand, when it takes me two-three days, or even more.

I like the craftsmanship a lot, so to me it was like "Okay, I'm going to save time on the pattern, to be only digital, and then have the time and the resources for the craft."

When you do couture and bespoke tailoring, you need time, and be hands on the [sewing] machine and fabric, so the advantage of using the 3D modeling technology was obvious for me.

Innovation and sustainability are both central to your work. How do your collections reflect your vision of environmental responsibility, and what practical measures do you take to make your design process more sustainable?

It is a very important topic for me. The entire phase of product development is thought with this idea in mind of how we can do less harm to the environment.

There is a lot of education that has to be done today for the consumer. Passaro on the presence of ultra-fast fashion

By using the "Style3D" software, we are able to do virtual sampling and virtual pattern cutting on a digital avatar. This, therefore, reduces the waste.

We use fabrics sourced in Europe that are from LVMH.

Such an approach allows us to focus on the craftsmanship. There's a lot to learn and we always try to improve the process in this sense.

In 2025, Shein opened a retail space inside BHV in Paris, a move that sparked significant public criticism. BHV described the partnership as a “strategic mistake” and ended the collaboration. What are your thoughts on the growing presence of ultra-fast fashion brands in traditional retail spaces and online?

There is a lot of education that has to be done today for the consumer.

People don't know how to consume actually good, because if you buy a t-shirt for €3, which I don't even know how it's possible to make as even the fabric does not cost this price per metre, after three washes is going to be dead. If you buy a t-shirt for maybe €15-20, you're going to have, perhaps, 10-20 washes, so it's going to be cheaper at the end for you.

Now in Europe, even in France, we have a new rule for ultra-fast fashion, which I think is important. There need to be regulations to protect the people and the environment. It's a very difficult topic to discuss because different people have different budgets to afford garments.

Many major luxury fashion houses are increasingly using AI to create campaign imagery and photoshoots. What is your stance on this?

When it's big brands or big corporations using it, I find it quite questionable, because they are the ones with the big budget for models, for photographers, stylists and everything else.

If they start replacing a human behind the images with only AI, then a lot of people going to lose jobs. I do not want to replace models with AI. I think it's nice to gather people, exchange ideas - you get more creative.

Listen to the feedback, but not too much. On launching own luxury fashion brand

If the big brands stop paying models, who is going to pay? Smaller brands. We cannot afford the fees anymore as the modelling agencies double or triple the fees, compared to a year before, for example.

The responsibility is at the different levels of the process. It's image reputation, industry and impact on other people as well.

You used to give lectures at the French Institute of Fashion, one of the world's leading fashion schools. What is the most valuable piece of advice you would give to young designers hoping to launch their own clothing brand today?

Do not run. It's pointless to run. Even if you have the checklist of “I want that magazine, I want that press, I want to be with the fashion week” or whatever - it's very tough.

You need to be smart on the product design. Make sure you find your audience. You need the right people that surround you: friends, acquaintances you make on your journey and business partners.

Listen to the feedback, but not too much. You need to have kind of a filter.

Take your time. Do not rush. The point is a marathon - not the sprint.

That would be my best advice.

Steven Passaro at the photoshoot for the Spring-Summer 2027 "A Glimpse" collection Sebastien Giraud / Steven Passaro

Watch the video in the player above for more from Steven Passaro.

This interview was edited for brevity and clarity.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns of 'massive' Russian attack within 48 hours
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned of a "massive" new Russian attack on Ukraine.

 

In a post on X, the Ukrainian leader said intelligence suggested Moscow had "readied missiles" for an attack "within the next 48 hours."

"Please take care of yourselves and pay attention to air raid alerts," he wrote.

It comes after Ukrainian authorities said Russian missile strikes on the Kyiv region on Friday killed at least 10 people and injured around 100 more. The strikes reportedly hit an arms exhibition where representatives of the Ukrainian defence industry were present.

A further five people were killed following guided aerial bomb strikes in Slovyansk, per Zelenskyy.

Latvia's foreign minister confirmed that the Latvian consulate in Slovyansk was damaged in the attacks.

Responding to the news in a statement posted to social media, Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said the strike on the consulate "underscores Moscow’s utter disregard for international law."

"Latvia has our full support," she added.

Zelenskyy to meet with Trump

Zelenskyy is due to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington next week as the US and Ukraine continue to discuss peace proposals to end the war, which began following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he had spoken with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, about efforts to end the conflict.

"A good and important conversation about how to energize diplomacy and bring peace closer," he said.

Earlier this week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov sat down with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) foreign ministers' summit in the Philippines.

Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, second from right, attends a meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. AP photo

According to the Kremlin, Lavrov used the meeting to warn Washington against continuing arms sales to Kyiv.

"Lavrov briefed his American counterpart on the actual situation along the front line and emphasised that it would be unacceptable to further arm the Kyiv regime," a statement from the Russian foreign ministry read.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Rubio said the pair had a "good," "frank" conversation but declined to go into more detail.

Asked specifically about the Kremlin's statement, Rubio said: "We sell arms via PURL, which is an initiative we have through NATO and that's what we're involved in. There's been no change to our policy in that regard".

"We want a peace deal. We want the war to end," he added.

World.title: Tunisia marks Saied's emergency measures anniversary amid deadly power crisis
World.content:
Five years after President Kais Saied suspended parliament and assumed emergency powers, Tunisia is marking the anniversary of 25 July 2021 amid its worst infrastructure crisis in memory, with between 150 and 200 people reported dead since power cuts began more than a week ago during an exceptional heatwave that has also brought severe water shortages.

 

The death toll was reported by the Organisation of Young Doctors in Tunisia. The Tunisian authorities have not confirmed or responded to those figures.

At least five deaths directly linked to power cuts — including a cancer patient — were reported by local media in the opening days of the crisis, when power failures caused home medical equipment including oxygen devices to stop working.

President Saied ended his public absence to acknowledge the crisis on Saturday, describing the pace of outages as "not normal" and saying those responsible must "assume their responsibility," without announcing specific measures.

The state electricity and gas company, STEG, attributed the outages to record demand driven by what its director general Faysal Tarifa described as "excessive use of air conditioning," telling local media that national consumption reached a record 6,000 megawatts on Tuesday.

He said the controlled outages were a "preventive measure" to protect the national grid and prevent total collapse, and urged citizens to use no more than one air conditioning unit during peak hours between 1 pm and 5 pm.

The date has long carried significance in Tunisia's national calendar — it was the day the republic was proclaimed in 1957. Since 2021 it has split the country into two camps: those who regard the day as a moment that rescued the state from paralysis, and those who call it a coup against the constitution and elected institutions.

On that evening, Saied invoked Article 80 of the 2014 constitution to announce a series of exceptional measures: parliament's powers were frozen for 30 days, the immunity of all its members was suspended, Prime Minister Hichem Mechichi was dismissed, and Saied assumed executive authority, which he exercised with a government he appointed himself. The public prosecution service was placed under his direct supervision.

Those decisions set in motion a political restructuring that culminated in 2022 in a new constitution establishing a presidential system.

Power centralised with the presidency

The 2022 constitution gave Saied considerably broader powers than those set out in the 2014 text, assigned the president primary responsibility for setting state policy and narrowed parliament's role substantially. The document was approved in a referendum held on 25 July 2022, but with turnout far below that of previous elections, after most opposition parties boycotted the process.

Between Saied's emergency declaration and the adoption of the new constitution, he governed by decree, stripped parliament of its legislative and oversight role and dissolved it definitively in March 2022.

In September 2021, Presidential Decree No. 117 formalised his assumption of wide executive and legislative powers.

In 2022, Saied announced the dissolution of the High Judicial Council. Dozens of judges were dismissed by presidential order — a move described by judges, opposition parties and human rights organisations as an assault on judicial independence. Legislative elections held at the end of 2022 recorded a first-round turnout of just 9%.

Protesters hold pictures of detained journalists and the sentences handed down against them during a demonstration against Tunisian President Kais Saied in the capital, Tunis, Friday 5 June 2026. (AP Photo/Anis Mili) AP Photo

From early 2023, judicial proceedings multiplied against opposition figures, politicians, businesspeople and journalists. Among the most prominent detained are octogenarian leader of the Ennahda movement Rached Ghannouchi, opposition figure Chaima Issa and activist Jawhar Ben Mbarek.

Courts have handed down prison sentences against several of them which opposition groups and international human rights organisations have described as politically motivated. The Tunisian authorities say the cases are unrelated to political activity and concern acts they regard as threats to state security.

Saied and his supporters argue that the period before his emergency measures was defined by paralysing inter-party conflict and institutional deadlock, and that the new political framework has restored state effectiveness.

Saied has repeatedly framed his project as a response to popular demand, saying in a December 2025 address to the nation that "social justice is the primary condition for stability and for further creation of wealth and employment opportunities," and that work was under way to "overcome all obstacles and inherited and fabricated difficulties."

Critics — including domestic opposition groups and international organisations — say the changes have weakened the separation of powers and the rule of law.

Persistent economic difficulties, limited growth

The promises of economic renewal that accompanied the July 2021 measures have not translated into meaningful improvements in the main indicators. Economic growth has remained modest, private investment cautious, and access to external financing restricted.

International financial institutions, including the IMF, have warned that rising public debt and weak growth are constraining the state's ability to fund investment.

IMF negotiations stalled for an extended period, financial support programmes slowed, and European and US assistance has become increasingly tied to economic and political conditions.

The Tunisian authorities describe their approach as one of "self-reliance" — reducing dependence on external actors and mobilising domestic resources. A community-owned companies project has been a centrepiece of that strategy, though it has yet to produce measurable results.

The Tunisian Forum for Economic and Social Rights said in a statement published this week that it was following "with great concern" the worsening electricity and water crisis across all of Tunisia's regions since the start of July, noting that the National Meteorological Institute had described temperatures as exceeding seasonal norms by between 8 and 14 degrees Celsius.

Unemployment, emigration and rising costs

Unemployment stood at 15% in the first quarter of 2026 and is particularly acute among young graduates. More than a decade after the revolution whose demands included work, freedom and national dignity, job opportunities remain scarce. The cost of living has risen sharply — inflation has exceeded 5% this year — while wages have not kept pace.

Irregular migration attempts across the Mediterranean have continued. Inland regions remain significantly underdeveloped compared with coastal areas. According to available figures, 65 suicides and suicide attempts were recorded in the first six months of 2025.

Initial criticism from the US, EU and international rights organisations following Saied's emergency measures gave way to a gradual thaw from 2023, driven largely by European interest in Tunisian cooperation on irregular migration.

Tunisian President Kais Saied, right, shakes hands with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni at the Carthage presidential palace in Tunis, Tunisia, Tuesday 6 June 2023. Slim Abid/AP

A memorandum of understanding on a strategic partnership between Tunisia and the EU was signed in July 2023, covering the economy, energy and migration.

Relations with Algeria have grown closer, with frequent high-level visits and enhanced security cooperation.

Relations with Morocco broke down in 2022 after Tunisia hosted Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali at the TICAD summit in August of that year. Both countries withdrew their respective ambassadors after that. Tunisia has also expanded cooperation with China and Russia.

Tensions arose with several African governments after Saied gave a speech in February 2023 describing what he called a "criminal scheme" to change Tunisia's demographic make-up through irregular migration from sub-Saharan Africa.

The remarks were condemned by the African Union as discriminatory and prompted Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea and Mali to organise evacuations of their nationals from Tunisia after migrants were subjected to attacks.

Freedoms narrowing

After the 2011 revolution, Tunisia was regularly cited as a regional model for press freedom and political pluralism, ranking higher in international freedom indices than at any point under former presidents Habib Bourguiba and Zine El Abidine Ben Ali.

Human rights, trade union and media organisations have repeatedly warned that this space has contracted since July 2021, citing the arrest of journalists, activists and bloggers.

One case involved a death sentence handed down against a man over Facebook posts; the sentence was later reversed following a presidential intervention.

Bassam Tarifi, president of the Tunisian Human Rights League, told domestic outlet Anbaa Tounes this week that he was raising "an alarm signal" about prison conditions in the country amid the heatwave, calling for urgent intervention.

Decree 54, on combating offences related to information and communication systems, has been at the centre of that debate. Critics argue it can be applied to prosecute journalists. The authorities say its purpose is to combat disinformation and protect public security.

World.title: Revealed: The best 'trip-maxxing' routes for a four-city European break
World.content:
Why settle for one city when you could visit four? Introducing ‘trip-maxxing’, a new travel trend which is seeing travellers swapping week-long stays in a single destination for multi-city adventures that squeeze in more sights, cultures and experiences.

 

While doing so much might seem unrealistic – and unaffordable – it’s actually entirely possible to do it on a budget. New research from FlixBus has revealed that a number of routes across Europe offer easy connections and affordable stays.

The travel company looked at destinations across the continent served by its network, identifying four-stop routes with journeys under five hours a piece.

Routes were ranked based on the shortest overall travel time, and each stop was scored using a range of travel factors, from average hostel prices and ratings, to the cost of an affordable night out – that’s a low-cost meal and three beers.

The research also looked at the density of attractions and nightlife within 5km of the city centre, as well as the number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites within 100km.

Each city was given a score out of 10, with each route awarded a total out of 40 based on our four key ranking factors – nightlife, culture, budget and accommodation.

Ten routes made the trip-maxxing list – and these are the top five.

Route 1: Berlin - Prague - Vienna - Budapest

This central European route topped the list, with a score of 28.8 out of 40. Flixbus found that each city delivers across all categories, with no destination acting as a gap-filler.

Berlin, the first destination, had the best score overall for nightlife and also boasts rich history and culture, and is an excellent walking city.

Accommodation here is well-priced, and there’s a vast amount of things to see and do per square kilometre – something matched by very few cities in Europe.

Next up is Prague, less than five hours from the German capital by bus. The capital of Czechia is home to a beautiful Gothic old town, an impressive hilltop castle, and Charles Bridge, a medieval stone arch bridge that crosses the Vltava river. It’s also a very affordable city, ideal for budget travellers.

Vienna is also under five hours by bus and is an entirely different experience to Prague. Walk around the famously pretty city, famous for its slower pace of life, relaxing coffee houses, and endless culture. Don’t miss the Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien or a visit to the Vienna State Opera, and wander streets flanked by striking imperial architecture.

This trip comes to a close in Budapest, under four hours from Vienna. Visits to its world-famous thermal baths and ruin bars, built inside crumbling courtyards, are a must do. The city is bisected by the Danube river, crossed by the 19th-century Chain Bridge and the architecturally impressive Fishermen’s Bastion offers sweeping views of the Hungarian capital below.

Beautiful Budapest features on two of the trip-maxxing routes Ervin Lukacs/Unsplash

Route 2: Berlin - Prague - Bratislava - Budapest

This route was awarded the highest budget score of any route in the ranking, scoring 28.1 overall.

While three of the destinations are the same as the first route, it’s Bratislava which stands out as a relatively unexplored destination.

Bratislava, around four hours from Prague, is often overlooked in favour of larger European cities, but Slovakia's capital has plenty to recommend it.

Wander its charming cobbled Old Town, climb up to Bratislava Castle for sweeping views across the Danube, and stop off at one of the city's many independent wine bars and restaurants.

It may not be the obvious choice for a standalone city break, but as part of a multi-city trip, it's well worth adding to your itinerary.

Route 3: Berlin - Prague - Wroclaw - Kraków

This trip, with two of the same stops as the top two on the list, has one of the fastest total travel times in the whole ranking, at just 11.7 hours. It’s also been awarded a budget score of 8.6, which makes up for it offering three countries rather than four.

After Berlin and Prague, it’s a three-hour journey to Wroclaw, Poland’s third-largest city.

Spread across a network of islands linked by more than 100 bridges, Wroclaw is home to a beautiful market square that rivals Prague's, but with far fewer crowds. Wander through the university quarter, explore the historic Cathedral Island and keep an eye out for the city's famous bronze gnome statues, hidden throughout the streets.

The journey ends in Kraków, around three hours further east. Poland's former royal capital is home to one of Europe's best-preserved medieval centres, with the vast Rynek Główny market square surrounded by Gothic churches, colourful townhouses and lively cafés.

While the city is packed with history, it's also a great place to experience Poland's food and nightlife. Around an hour away, the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum is a must visit.

Krakow, Poland's second largest city, is packed full of rich history and culture Kevin Perez Camacho/Unsplash

Route 4: Amsterdam - Dortmund - Berlin - Prague

Scoring 27 overall, this route topped the rankings for culture and is ideal for travellers who want to begin in western Europe before making their way east.

Amsterdam kicks things off with some of Europe's best museums and nightlife. Spend time exploring the Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum and Anne Frank House, before wandering the UNESCO-listed canal district and the independent shops, cafés and bars of the Jordaan neighbourhood.

Just over two hours away is Dortmund, one of the route's biggest surprises. Once known for coal and steel, the German city has reinvented itself as a cultural hub, with attractions including Phoenix Lake, built on the site of a former steelworks, alongside a growing food and bar scene.

Finish the trip with stops in Berlin and Prague, both packed full of culture and fun nightlife.

Route 5: Frankfurt - Berlin - Prague - Vienna

With an overall score of 26.9, and a nightlife score of 7.7, this route is a great option for travellers flying into one of the continent’s best-connected transport hubs before heading east through four of central Europe's most fascinating cities.

Frankfurt is far more than Germany's financial capital. The Museum Embankment is home to one of the country's finest collections of museums, while the restored Römerberg Square offers a glimpse of the city's medieval past.

Frankfurt is so much more than just a financial hub Steven Wei/Unsplash

Finish the day with a glass of traditional apple wine in the Sachsenhausen district before catching the bus east, to Berlin, then Prague and, finally, Vienna.

Although this route has the longest travel time in the top five, at around 13 hours, the journeys are spread across several days, making it an easy way to experience four very different European capitals.

World.title: Iran military says it targeted US bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
World.content:
Iran's military said on Friday that it had targeted US military bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait in retaliation for Washington's latest strikes on the country.

 

"This morning, the fuel tanks, large equipment warehouses and silos, and the barracks of the US terrorist army forces at the Isa Air Base in Bahrain were targeted by Arash kamikaze drones," the Iranian army said in a statement carried by state TV.

The US has not confirmed that any of its facilities or personnel were targeted.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guards also claimed they had targeted an Amazon data centre in Bahrain, according to state media. Neither the US tech giant nor Bahraini authorities have commented on the claim.

An explosion and warning sirens were reported in Bahrain on Friday, although it was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were connected.

Bahrain later said it intercepted and destroyed "a number of Iranian aerial aggressions", accusing Tehran of targeting civilians.

The Iranian army also claimed it had carried out drone attacks against Jordan, targeting "aircraft hangars, aviation maintenance hangars and a barracks" at Al-Azraq base.

Jordan's military said it had intercepted seven missiles and six drones fired by Iran on Friday, saying the operation "resulted in no casualties or material damage".

In a separate statement, the Iranian army said it had also launched drones targeting US equipment warehouses at Camp Udairi, as well as American military personnel stationed at Camp Doha and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the military's ideological arm, separately claimed they had targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, saying they destroyed an ammunition depot and inflicted casualties among US personnel.

They also said they had struck equipment storage silos at Camp Udairi in Kuwait and a US Fifth Fleet watchtower in Bahrain.

Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, warned US personnel in the region on Friday that Iran had "prepared free, one-way tickets to hell for you".

"For every proud citizen of the Islamic Republic of Iran who is martyred, one American service member will be sent to hell," he was quoted as saying by the state broadcaster.

World.title: ICC chief prosecutor removed from post over sexual misconduct allegations
World.content:
Member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) removed chief prosecutor Karim Khan from office on Friday, diplomats told the Associated Press, marking the first dismissal of a chief prosecutor in the court’s history.

 

The ICC's 125 member states voted by a large majority to remove Khan from office following allegations of sexual misconduct, which he has repeatedly denied.

The move marks the first-ever removal of an ICC chief prosecutor. Khan had been temporarily suspended in June while the allegations were reviewed after an internal report found he had committed serious misconduct, a finding he strongly rejects.

According to documents seen by the Associated Press, Khan had a sexual relationship with the woman and allegedly tried to discourage her from pursuing her complaint.

An independent oversight report found that he had committed "serious misconduct", though Khan denies the allegations.

Related ICC chief prosecutor suspended pending proceedings on sexual misconduct allegations

Khan's removal comes as the ICC faces mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump administration, which has already imposed sanctions on him and a dozen other ICC employees.

The sanctions were imposed in response to the ICC's arrest warrants for senior Israeli officials, including Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza, as well as the court's investigations into US personnel in Afghanistan.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the United States was launching a “comprehensive campaign to crush the threat that the International Criminal Court poses to US sovereignty”.

Rubio said the US would pressure member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organisations that cooperate with the court and deny its employees entry to the United States. Countries that “benefit from the US security umbrella” are to be urged to reject the court’s jurisdiction over US citizens.

Khan’s removal has no immediate impact on the arrest warrants already issued. Decisions on whether they remain in force are made solely by ICC judges.

World.title: Trump and Zelenskyy to meet in Washington next week
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday, a White House official said, amid renewed efforts to end the war with Russia.

 

"President Zelensky is slated to meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday," the White House official told AFP on condition of anonymity on Friday.

Zelenskyy said this week he had spoken with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff and the US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as part of efforts to revive stalled talks aimed at ending the four-year war.

US-led efforts to end the war have stalled as Washington shifted its focus to the conflict with Iran.

Trump and Zelenskyy have had a tense relationship, ranging from a heated Oval Office clash in February 2025 to warmer ties in recent months.

This week, the Ukrainian president met right-wing US influencer and Trump ally Laura Loomer, in another sign of improving relations.

The 33-year-old conservative commentator, who has millions of social media followers, has recently softened her stance on Ukraine.

"This is everyday for every Ukrainian, I feel like such an a**hole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last five years," she said of the experience.

Trump reposted one of Loomer's social media posts about her Zelensky meeting on Thursday with the caption: "Very good!!

Zelenskyy is due to meet Trump on the same day as a memorial service in Washington for US Senator Lindsey Graham, a longtime supporter of Ukraine who died earlier this month at the age of 71.

Trump is due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the same day as Zelenskyy.

World.title: Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day
World.content:
From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.

Nature's own firefighters

Sometimes the best climate solutions have four legs. From goats and sheep in the United States to donkeys in Spain, grazing animals are helping reduce wildfire risk by clearing dry vegetation that can fuel fires.

Carefully managed grazing not only slows the spread of potential wildfires but can also create access paths for emergency crews. It's a simple yet effective example of how working with nature can help communities become more resilient to a changing climate.

Keeping cities cool: Reclaiming the right to a livable future

Young voices and urban innovators are driving change in the fight against extreme heat. Climate activist Che Chen is taking Taiwan's government to court because he believes access to a livable, cooler environment is a basic human right for his generation and those to come.

At the same time, urban heat expert Tzu-ping Lin is developing practical solutions such as wind corridors, greener buildings and heat mapping to make cities more resilient.

In scorching Taipei, locals seek ways to survive urban heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the world's most threatened animals speaks up

Conservationists and storytellers are finding new ways to connect people with endangered wildlife in South Africa by helping audiences imagine the world through the eyes of a pangolin.

The cute, AI-powered creature speaks South Africa's 11 official languages, answers questions, reacts realistically and ultimately highlights the threats facing the world's most trafficked mammal, which is poached primarily for its meat and scales.

The initiative is driven by a desire to inspire empathy and action, showing that protecting biodiversity starts with understanding the species we share our planet with.

World.title: India: CJP-Government to return to talks as protests grow
World.content:
07/25/2026 July 25, 2026 PM Modi 'thanks friends' in another late night video

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi uploaded yet another reel overnight — this time thanking "friends" for their suggestions over a Gen-Z style video posted late the night before.

"I had a chance to meet you all late last night. The response to the video I posted, the insightful suggestions... thank you everybody," he said in the latest video.

In the previous reel, the prime minister had appealed to the nation that the government had taken several steps to counter the paper leak issue. It was one of his lesser-produced videos shot in a less-than ideal angle, seemingly in an attempt to connect with the youth.

Many protesters on ground read the video as a "desperate attempt" to manage the students' anger as protests began to spread nationwide. "He suddenly woke up and posted a panic reel because they didn't expect the protests to reach this stage," one protesters told DW, asking to stay anonymous over fear of backlash.

Meanwhile, social media did what it does best and made memes.

The Prime Minister appears to have acknowledged that he is watching and learning.

World.title: Iran war: Houthis vow response to 'dangerous escalation' by Saudi Arabia
World.content:
07/25/2026 July 25, 2026 Yemen's Houthis vow retaliation for Saudi strikes

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have accused Saudi Arabia of targeting civilian infrastructure, amid an escalating flare-up with Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia on Friday hit the Houthi-held port city of Hodeida with strikes, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, in response to the rebel group attacking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as part of a maritime blockade.

"The Saudi enemy's targeting of civilian facilities in Hodeida and Kamaran island constitutes a dangerous escalation," the Houthis' Ansarollah media posted on Telegram.

"We affirm that these recent crimes will not go unanswered."

Houthi-run Al Masirah television said on Saturday that Saudi strikes had targeted facilities belonging to the state telecommunications corporation and Kamaran island, off Yemen's western coast.

The broadcaster reported that one worker was wounded in Hodeida while a woman was also injured on Kamaran Island.

The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, claimed that it hit "Houthi military sites" and destroyed targets that were posing a threat to commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

Riyadh said it would do everything necessary to protect its ships, warning the Houthis that if they continued "hostile acts then there will be no hesitation in responding."

For Saudi Arabia, a top oil producer, the Red Sea had emerged a critical shipping alternative to the ​war-blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Trump addresses rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner
World.content:
The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by the alleged attempted assassination of Donald Trump. His hourlong speech combined jokes with attacks on members of the press.

US President Donald Trump addressed hundreds of journalists at a scaled-down and rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner on Friday night.

The gala was held amid heightened security measures, three months after the original event was cut short by an alleged attempt to assassinate Trump.

Trump delivered the speech at Washington's Waldorf Astoria, a smaller venue that held only about 700 people, instead of its usual venue, the Washington Hilton.

Trump jokes about possible third term

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better," Trump said. "And the third time will be better yet."

"I'm only kidding," he added.

Trump has repeatedly suggested that he would entertain the idea of a third term, despite the 22nd Amendment of the US Constitution barring a president from being elected more than twice.

US press freedom no longer a matter of course under Trump To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump makes light of shooting incident, praises Secret Service officer

Trump also joked about the incident during April's gala, when a gunman tried to storm a security checkpoint before he was stopped by security personnel before making it into the ballroom where the dinner was being held.

"After hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, 'Get down! Get down!', which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking. Do you believe it? Get down!" Trump said.

The president also praised Victor Gonzalez, the Secret Service officer who was shot during the April confrontation with the suspect. "What he did was amazing," Trump said. "We salute you and we thank you with all of our hearts."

What else did Trump say during the White House Correspondents' Dinner?

This year's events were the first Trump has attended as president. He did not appear at any correspondents' dinners during his first term.

Trump said he had not attended previous dinners because the press has treated him "unfairly," although he promised to come back next year.

The US president has long had a hostile relationship with many journalists and media outlets .

During his speech, he attacked some journalists, including CNN's Kaitlan Collins — whom Trump repeatedly complained about not smiling enough — and Josh Dawsey of The Wall Street Journal. Both were honored with journalism awards at the gala.

Despite those barbs, Trump ended his speech, which lasted over an hour, by saying that he has "tremendous respect" for the reporters attending the dinner.

"I have tremendous respect for the people in this room. Sometimes I don't feel you treat me fair. Maybe you do. I don't know," Trump said.

Trumps say comedian Jimmy Kimmel should be fired To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump vs the media

The Trump administration has filed lawsuits against multiple media outlets, barred the Associated Press from the White House ​press pool and limited journalists' access ‌to the Pentagon, among other measures.

Trump has maintained that the measures aim to improve accountability and address media bias.

Speaking in the Oval Office on Friday, he defended federal subpoenas — which were later withdrawn — issued to New York Times journalists over their reporting on the security of the new Qatari-donated Air Force One.

"We're not after journalists. We're after leakers. We're after people that are cowards, people that are unpatriotic, people that ⁠are treasonous in many cases. And the way ​you find them is through the journalists," Trump said.

World.title: Starship completes 1st test flight since SpaceX IPO
World.content:
Starship splashed down in the Indian Ocean to complete its 13th test flight and its first since Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket completed a test flight on Friday, the first since Elon Musk's company went public on Wall Street in June.

The ship splashed down into the Indian Ocean, which was celebrated by SpaceX employees watching along from the firm's headquarters in Starbase, Texas.

"Starship is intact, floating in the ocean and transmitting telemetry!" Musk said on X.

This was the world's most powerful rocket's 13th flight.

Previous tests had ended with Starship in flames or exploding at splashdown, or breaking up in midair.

What do we know about the latest SpaceX Starship test?

Starship, which is around 122 meters (400 feet) tall, deployed 20 Starlink satellites into suborbital space.

After ​briefly contacting SpaceX's network of around 10,000 orbiting satellites, they reentered Earth's ​atmosphere and burned up as planned.

It was the 13th test flight and the second this year of the third-generation Starship, dubbed V3 Image: Eric Gay/AP Photo/picture alliance

The hourlong test "will provide critical data as we prepare to expand our Starlink constellation" of the company's satellite internet service, SpaceX said.

By the end of 2026, SpaceX aims to use the Starship rocket to expand its Starlink network with the latest V3 satellites, providing coverage in remote areas where traditional cellular networks are unavailable.

World.title: Paramount agrees to delay Warner Bros. merger amid lawsuit
World.content:
Paramount has agreed to freeze its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery until as late as June 2027. Twelve states have argued that the deal would create a "media behemoth" that would harm the US entertainment industry.

Paramount on Friday agreed to delay its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery as a lawsuit from a dozen US states seeking to block the deal altogether moves forward.

In a court filing, Paramount said it would pause the $110 billion (€96.69 billion) deal until June 2027.

Friday's agreement is a "significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence," according to Paramount, which was bought by Skydance last year.

"This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers and good for creators," the company added.

Judge pauses Paramount and Warner Bros megamerger

The move comes just days after a US federal judge temporarily blocked the proposed merger following a lawsuit brought by 12 states.

The states raised "serious questions" about the deal's potential to "substantially lessen competition," the judge said in her ruling, adding that "the balance of equities and public interest tip sharply in favor of the Plaintiff States."

The Trump administration approved the merger of Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Ellison family who are close allies of US President Donald Trump, and Warner Bros. Discovery, the parent company of CNN and HBO, on June 12 without demanding any changes.

States suing to block merger welcome decision

Twelve states led by California filed a lawsuit on July 13, arguing that the deal would create a "media behemoth" that would damage the US entertainment and media industry.

"We are eager to continue to make our case in court and celebrate another tremendous win in our effort to ensure this unlawful merger never sees the light of day," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement on Friday.

The other 11 states joining the lawsuit — all of them Democratic-led — are Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

"From the workers and artists who bring stories to life to the families who buy tickets at the box office, Paramount's illegal takeover of Warner Bros. is a bad deal for all those who count on a competitive entertainment industry," said New York Attorney General Letitia James on Friday .

World.title: ICC votes to dismiss Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan
World.content:
Members of the International Criminal Court have voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied the accusations.

International Criminal Court members voted on Friday to dismiss Karim Khan as prosecutor ​following allegations ​of sexual misconduct.

The ICC's oversight body, the Assembly of States Parties (ASP), found that Khan had committed "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty," ASP President Paivi Kaukoranta said.

What do we know about the Khan allegations?

A British barrister, Khan was accused of sexual misconduct by a female aide, allegations which he has repeatedly denied.

He had been temporarily removed from his duties at the ICC in June, following a report by the executive committee of the court's oversight body that found he had committed "serious misconduct."

In all, 82 of the court's ​125 member states voted in favor of Khan's removal, while 13 voted against and 15 countries abstained.

Khan, 56, made headlines in 2024 when he successfully applied for arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over the Gaza war, as well as leading members of the Hamas militant group who have since been killed. Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel.

All active ICC warrants will remain in place despite Khan's dismissal, because only ICC judges have the authority to withdraw warrants.

What were the reactions to Khan's dismissal?

Khan's lawyer, Tayab Ali, said Khan would challenge his dismissal.

"Mr. Khan will challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the decision, though all available legal mechanisms," Ali wrote in a post on X.

Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch and now a visiting professor at Princeton University, wrote on X that the ICC states did "the right thing" by removing Khan.

Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, criticized Khan, suggesting the barrister had thought that the arrest warrants against Israeli officials, which Danon called a "political witch hunt," would "distract from serious sexual misconduct allegations."

"He was wrong," Danon said.

ICC prosecutor suspended: can the court still serve justice? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Khan suspension comes as Trump administration wants to 'dismantle' ICC

The move to dismiss Khan also comes at a time when the US President Donald Trump's administration is seeking to weaken and undermine the ICC. The court, based in the Dutch city of The Hague, investigates and prosecutes individuals for genocide and other crimes against humanity.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently said that the US had begun a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty."

The State Department said countries that enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella are "called upon to reject the ICC's purported authority to prosecute American officials and servicemen." The State Department is also mulling "visa revocations and travel bans for ICC personnel" along with "increased sanctions against the ICC and affiliated organizations."

Neither the United States nor Israel is a member of the ICC.

Venezuela announces it will withdraw from ICC

Meanwhile, Venezuela said it would withdraw from the ICC on Friday. The move comes after Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro was abducted and overthrown by the US earlier this year and replaced by interim leader Delcy Rodriguez, who has been willing to comply with the Trump administration's demands.

Notes from Caracas — Venezuela and the US intervention To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia said the "court's actions reflect a demonstrated geographical bias, which disproportionately concentrated its work on African and Latin American countries, to the detriment of the Global South."

Plasencia said the withdrawal was at the instruction of Delcy Rodriguez.

World.title: Última hora de los incendios forestales, en directo | El fuego en Madrid continúa activo y sin controlar tras una noche de trabajo intenso
World.content:
El servicio de emergencias de la región informa de que su evolución “vendrá determinada por el régimen de vientos que se den en las próximas horas” | La bajada de las temperaturas y los vientos ayudan a contener la zona norte del incendio de Ávila

Momentos clave Momentos clave Hace 2h 35 carreteras cortadas por los incendios

El fuego que arrasa la esquina suroeste de la Comunidad de Madrid y ya ha calcinado más de 6.000 hectáreas continúa activo y sin controlar este sábado. El servicio de emergencias de la región ha informado de que “el fuego sigue activo” y que su evolución “vendrá determinada por el régimen de vientos que se den en las próximas horas”. Los bomberos han trabajado “con intensidad” durante toda la noche, aprovechando tres factores que, según el delegado del Gobierno en Madrid, Francisco Martín, abrían una “oportunidad” para intentar controlar las llamas: bajas de temperaturas, menos viento y aumento de la humedad, muy baja durante toda la jornada de ayer. En Ávila, la noche ha sido positiva: han bajado mucho las temperaturas y los vientos han ayudado a contener la zona norte del incendio. La zona más conflictiva sigue estando hacia el sur, con la posibilidad aún presente de que se junte con el gran foco de Madrid. El Ministerio del Interior cifró anoche en más de 60.000 las personas evacuadas o confinadas entre ambas provincias, sin que se hayan registrado hasta el momento daños personales.

World.title: ‘Nekonomics’ o la gran economía gatuna japonesa
World.content:
El gasto en estos animales es de casi 16.000 millones de euros y tiene una cara oculta: el creciente número de estas mascotas sin hogar

El cariño que sienten los japoneses por los gatos se traduce en un gasto que este año ascenderá a 2,9 billones de yenes (unos 15.980 millones de euros), una cifra casi igual al impacto económico de la Exposición Universal de Osaka 2025. Pero esta cantidad no incluye la cara oculta de la economía gatuna: el cuidado de los felinos que se quedan sin hogar.

Las estadísticas de las mascotas japonesas han ocupado un lugar prioritario desde principios de este siglo cuando el número de gatos y perros empezó a superar a la población infantil. En 2025, Japón tenía 8,8 millones de gatos y 6,8 millones de perros, un total de 15,6 millones de mascotas, que superó en dos millones a los 13,6 millones de niños menores de 15 años, según cifras de la Asociación Japonesa de Alimentos para Mascotas y la Oficina de Estadística de Japón.

La magnitud de la economía gatuna es calculada desde 2015 por Katsuhiro Miyamoto, profesor emérito de la Universidad de Kansai y autor de un término ya habitual en los informativos nipones: Nekonomics, acrónimo de neko, gato, en japonés, y economics. El novedoso cómputo incluye el gasto directo en alimentos, servicios veterinarios o vacunas. También suma las cafeterías para sentarse acompañado de gatos, los videojuegos y otros productos audiovisuales, además de excursiones a 14 islas donde abundan los gatos.

La previsión para este año se acerca a los tres billones de yenes aportados a la economía en 2025 por la Exposición Universal de Osaka, el evento de seis meses en el que participaron 158 países y regiones de todo el mundo. “De esas cifras no nos llega nada a nosotras”, declara a EL PAÍS Naomi Furukawa, directora de Chiyoda Nyan to Naru Kai, una ONG situada en el distrito de Chiyoda, en Tokio, que en 100 metros cuadrados acoge 49 gatos rescatados en la calle o abandonados.

“Mientras las ganancias de Nekonomics benefician a quienes comercian con la imagen de los gatos, organizaciones de rescate como la nuestra dependen de donaciones y subvenciones públicas que casi nunca son suficientes”, explica la responsable del refugio. El céntrico distrito de Chiyoda alberga el Palacio Imperial de Japón y, a pesar de ser la sede de grandes corporaciones y bullir de gente durante el día, es el menos poblado de Tokio, con menos de 70.000 residentes. En 2011 fue el primer distrito en Japón en haber reducido a cero el sacrificio de los gatos callejeros o abandonados, el procedimiento más común para controlar la superpoblación de esos animales hasta finales del siglo pasado. Para la gestión actual de gatos callejeros la administración de Chiyoda recurre al método TNR (siglas inglesas para Trap, Neuter, Return), equivalente al CER (captura, esterilización, retorno) usado en España.

Gran longevidad

El distrito de Chiyoda paga también unos 150.000 yenes (unos 810 euros) para el examen veterinario obligatorio de los felinos cuyo amo ha fallecido y deben ser llevados a convivir con otros animales en un refugio. Al igual que la población humana nipona, considerada una de las más longevas del mundo, los gatos japoneses domésticos viven más años y entre los que se quedan sin amo muchos padecen enfermedades crónicas que encarecen su cuidado.

“El gasto en atención veterinaria por gato asciende a unos 200.000 yenes (1.010 euros) y a menudo tenemos que financiarlo nosotras”, añade Furukawa. Explica que los gatos callejeros han dejado de ser el problema más acuciante. “Ahora el problema es el aumento de gatos que son dejados por personas mayores que ingresan a un hogar de la tercera edad o fallecen”, añade. Su ONG también organiza jornadas de adopción que tienen éxito relativo debido a la preferencia por los gatitos. Cuenta que los vecinos más influyentes del barrio, la familia del emperador Naruhito y la emperatriz Masako, han aceptado en palacio gatos callejeros rescatados por su ONG en dos ocasiones.

“Que figuras públicas adopten gatos mestizos de refugio en lugar de comprarlos en tiendas, contribuye a normalizar la adopción de los animales rescatados”, concluye Furukawa.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Thousands cross finishing line as Nijmegen Vierdaagse ends
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmegense Vierdaagse (four-day march) ended on Friday, with tens of thousands of walkers being welcomed with flowers by well-wishers.

British walker Simon Brownlee crossed the finishing line ahead of the rest of the walkers for the 27th time, local media reported. Brownlee, who completed the distance before 10am, told local broadcaster Omroep Gelderland that the walk “felt like home”. “I’m happy it is over and I can now relax,” he said.

Wheelchair participant Ronald van Dort was the very first person to finish, picking up his seventh medal for completing the event.

Over 45,000 walkers from 70 countries took part in this year’s series, which is proving increasingly popular among the young. Ten years ago, 7.5% of the walkers were aged 21 to 30, but this year their number rose to over 20%.

This year the event was marred by a fatal shooting just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place. One man has been arrested.

The shooting, and other crowd problems, led the organisers to cancel performances by urban scene artists such as Ronnie Flex and Lil’ Kleine because their presence was “attracting the wrong sort of people”, the AD reported.

World.title: Dozens of women forced into prostitution by Romanian gang
World.content:
Dozens of women may have been forced into working as prostitutes in Amsterdam’s red light district by a Romanian gang, Dutch police confirmed on Friday.

The statement follows a joint Dutch and Romanian campaign against human trafficking in the area earlier this month. Seven men were arrested during a string of raids on July 14 – four in the Netherlands and three in Romania. All were Romanian nationals.

Shortly after the arrests, police issued a video interview with one of the victims speaking Romanian, which has led more women to come forward and has resulted in other information reaching the police, the statement said.

Police now say they have spoken to several victims and say they believe more women have been trafficked. They too are said to be Romanian.

The women were lured to Amsterdam with the promise of high earnings but found themselves forced into working in brothels and handing over their earnings to the gang. They were also forced to pay “rent” for their rooms.

None of the men had jobs but were big spenders, buying expensive clothes and cars and gambling heavily, the statement said. The gang also treated part of the red light district as their “personal kingdom”.

Four men remain in custody in the Netherlands, one of whom was extradited from Romania. Another man may also be extradited soon, RTL said. They are all suspected of human trafficking and forming a criminal organisation.

According to the Parool, two of the suspects are half brothers aged 44 and 45 who have earlier convictions for trafficking in women in Romania.

More arrests have not been ruled out.

A year ago, Dutch and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a joint investigation into human trafficking and the forced prostitution of Romanian women, mainly in and around Amsterdam.

World.title: Singer Sophie Straat cleared of discrimination over mosh pit
World.content:
Discrimination hotlines in both the Netherlands and Belgium have concluded that Dutch singer Sophie Straat did not discriminate when she asked “all white men to step back” during two of her recent performances.

Last month at the Best Kept Secret festival in Beekse Bergen, Straat — real name Sophie Schwartz — asked for space for women, queer people and people of colour in the “mosh pit”, an area in front of the stage where fans dance chaotically.

She made the same request on Monday during a performance in Ghent, Belgium.

The Dutch discrimination hotline Discriminatie.nl said it received hundreds of complaints but maintains that Straat’s comments do not amount to discrimination against white men based on their colour or gender.

“The call only concerned one short, one-off mosh pit for these groups,” said the hotline. “Therefore, visitors were not refused entry to the concert.”

Belgian authorities reached the same conclusion after receiving some 200 complaints following her performance in Ghent.

“Although the statement may be perceived as polarizing or offensive, in this context it must be seen as a symbolic and artistic expression,” a spokesperson for the Belgian discrimination hotline Unia told the Flemish broadcaster VRT.

“According to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, artistic and political expressions enjoy broad protection under freedom of expression, even when they provoke, shock or offend.”

Hate messages and death threats

Straat wrote on Instagram earlier this month that she has received “a wave of sexist, antisemitic hate messages and (death) threats, some more explicit and creative than others”.

She has also questioned where the left-wing media has been in all this, saying the public narrative is being controlled by the right.

The singer, who was raised in a Jewish home in Amsterdam’s de Pijp neighbourhood and is known for her protest songs, has said she never wanted to exclude anyone but rather wanted to make room for people who feel unsafe in a mosh pit.

World.title: Youngster arrested for participating in sadistic online network
World.content:
Police have arrested a young man from Noord Holland who they suspect of being part of the sadistic online Com network “764”.

The public prosecution department reported the arrest on Thursday, saying the suspect encouraged underage girls to cut themselves and write his online name on a wall with their own blood—so-called “bloodsigns”.

He also is said to have prompted them to write his name on their bodies with a marker, known as“fansigns”. Both are practices within the Com movement—short for The Community—for members to gain prestige.

The suspect himself, who was also charged with aggravated assault, exploitation of underage girls and possession of images of sexual child abuse, was a minor at the time of the alleged crimes. Because of that, no further details are being released.

The Com network consists of various chat groups where members recruit vulnerable young people and force them to commit acts including assault, sexual abuse and murder.

The members, from all corners of the globe, then share images of these acts online in private chat groups, using such platforms as Telegram and Discord.

According to NOS, at least 70 Dutch people are involved in this movement known as “nihilistic extremism” because the incitement to commit such extreme violence doesn’t have a clear ideological motive.

The phenomenon is especially attractive to young men.

World.title: Dangerous drivers face extra surveillance under points system
World.content:
The police and justice ministry officials are working on a system which would see traffic offenders being given points for dangerous driving – which will lead to persistent offenders coming under extra surveillance.

Motorists who have collected six points for using a mobile phone while driving or not wearing a seatbelt would come under the tougher regime, RTL Nieuws reported on Friday. No start date has yet been set.

The points will be awarded in addition to regular fines. The number of points will depend on the seriousness of the offences and speeding tickets recorded by camera will not be included.

The new system is being devised in an effort to tackle persistent offenders who do not change their behaviour despite being fined multiple times, RTL said. Last year, almost 30,000 people would have had at least six points if the new system had been in existence.

“Research shows that people who don’t stick to the rules are often responsible for accidents,” Achilles Damen from the public prosecution department told the broadcaster.

The privacy implications of monitoring specific individuals are still being assessed, RTL said.

World.title: Ajax beat Vojvodina in Conference League qualifier, Twente lose
World.content:
Ajax kicked off their European football campaign with a 4-1 win over Serbian club Vojvodina in the second qualification round of the Conference League competition in Novi Sad on Thursday evening.

The simple win sets the Amsterdammers up in a strong position ahead of the return match next week. If Ajax win again, they will meet either Irish side Shelbourne FC or Estonian club Nõmme Kalju in the third qualification round for the third-tier European competition.

The Amsterdam goal total included one for 16-year-old debutant Mohamed Abdalla, who became the youngest player to score for a Dutch club in Europe.

There was disappointment for FC Twente, who are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the Europa League. They lost 1-2 at home to Hungarian side Ferencváros and will have to pull out all the stops during the away leg next week to remain in the competition.

If they do lose, Twente will move down to the qualification rounds of the Conference League.

PSV Eindhoven and Feyenoord have qualified directly for the Champions League while NEC is taking part in the qualification competition. AZ, as winners of the KNVB Cup last season, will take part in the Europa League competition.

World.title: Unilever backs London for food division secondary listing
World.content:
Unilever’s food division, which is being sold to US sauce and spice producer McCormick, will have a secondary listing on the London stock exchange, despite an intensive lobbying campaign to list in Amsterdam.

Unilever itself has been based in London, and listed there, since 2020.

Unilever said in a statement that the secondary listing is separate to McCormick’s plans to establish an international headquarters in the Netherlands and maintain Unilever Food’s R&D facilities and operations in Wageningen.

This “reflects its commitment to the European market and the critical role the Netherlands will continue to play in the combined company”, the statement said.

Economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert said in a reaction to the sale when it was announced in March that the cabinet had already discussed developments with Unilever and would talk to the new owner “such as about a listing on the Amsterdam stock exchange”.

Unilever’s ice cream arm, spun off in 2024, is listed on the Amsterdam stock exchange as the Magnum Ice Cream Company and is headquartered in the Dutch capital.

The sale of the food arm means there is nothing left of the original Dutch part of Unilever, which was set up in 1930 through the merger of the Dutch Margarine Unie and British soap maker Lever Brothers. Unilever now focuses on personal care and household cleaning products.

World.title: Poland bans chaining of dogs and cats
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. World.title: Police and park rangers step up joint patrols in Poland’s Tatras after series of tourist offences
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. To było jedno z miejsc, do których chcieliśmy dotrzeć podczas tej podróży i wszyscy znajomi oraz przyjaciele mówili, że… pic.twitter.com/tA9shZ6Rqk — Pigułka 💊 (@informacyjnie) May 23, 2026 This season has already seen a number of high-profile cases of transgressions of the park’s strict rules. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. A national park in Poland’s southern mountains has completed testing of an electric bus that could replace horse-drawn carriages carrying tourists to a famous lake.
