MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs denies claims — including from the Chinese ambassador to Manila Jing Quan — that a confidential 2024 agreement means construction isn’t allowed in Ayungin Shoal.

Rappler’s Bea Cupin walks you through what we do (and what we don’t) know about the Provisional Understanding between Manila and Beijing. – Rappler.com

World.title: Home still temporary for some students displaced by 2024 Quito fire in Puerto Princesa
World.content:
SCENES AT NIGHT. Dim lights illuminate a quiet night scene along the narrow, unpaved pathway of the Quito fire victims' temporary shelter compound in Barangay San Pedro, Puerto Princesa City, Palawan.

More than two years after the fire, students continue pursuing their education while living in a temporary shelter. They are still waiting for a place they can permanently call home.

PALAWAN, Philippines – Shan Christian Cabanillas usually begins his day by collecting water.

For a fourth-year engineering student, Cabanillas’ mornings are unlike those of many of his classmates. Instead of waking up in a permanent home, he prepares for school inside a temporary shelter near the Puerto Princesa City Coliseum in Barangay San Pedro, where his family has lived for almost a year and a half.

Before leaving for class, the 21-year-old helps buy supplies for their small store, feeds their dogs, and lines up for water from the communal faucet. Only after finishing these chores does he begin his trip to Palawan State University.

This has become Cabanillas’ normal routine, day in and day out. But it was not supposed to be like this.

A night that changed everything

In the early morning of February 7, 2024, Cabanillas was asleep when their two dogs suddenly started barking nonstop. His mother woke up after hearing someone outside their gate shouting that there was a fire. She immediately woke Cabanillas and his older sister. Caught by surprise, the family rushed outside with barely enough time to save anything.

“Sa pagkataranta namin, kung ano ‘yong suot naming damit, ‘yon lang [‘yong] nasalba namin,” Cabanillas recalled. (In our rush, we saved nothing else but the clothes on our backs.)

With nowhere to go, Cabanillas’ family sought temporary refuge at the homes of his mother’s therapy clients. They first stayed with one client for 15 days before transferring to another client’s property, where they remained for almost a year rebuilding their lives.

The family later moved into a temporary shelter provided by the city in April 2025. There, they started operating a small store to help support their daily needs.

SURVIVAL. A resident stands beside covered trays of home-cooked meals at Cabanillas’ mother’s carinderia, a small eatery serving their community in the temporary shelter. Photo by Vic Albert Bagaan/Rappler

Located only a few kilometers from where the fire happened, the temporary shelter was among Puerto Princesa City’s immediate responses to the fire, which displaced around 920 families (500 from Barangay Bagong Silang and 420 from Barangay Pagkakaisa, two barangays in the Quito area).

The site, built to house fire victims temporarily, was designed to accommodate just 221 families while they wait for permanent relocation. The city government began constructing the shelter in February 2024, and it was completed in April 2024.

Learning to live in a temporary home

The temporary shelter was originally established to provide safe, immediate refuge for vulnerable residents displaced by disasters such as storms and flooding, or domestic crises like fires, while long-term housing is being prepared.

Today, rows of small shelter units stand side by side near the coliseum. Families share communal comfort rooms and water faucets, while children play along the narrow pathways between the houses. Every morning, residents line up with buckets to collect water before going to work or school.

SHARED. A temporary housing facility featuring rows of numbered wooden doors along a damp, dimly lit corridor. Photo by Vic Albert Bagaan/Rappler

Cabanillas admitted that adjusting to life in the shelter was difficult.

“Dati, may mga pagkakataong nahihirapan akong pumasok sa klase,” he said. “Ngayon, hindi na, dahil nakasanayan na.” (There were times in the past when I’d find it difficult to go to class. I’ve since grown accustomed to these conditions.)

Cabanillas’ experience is not unique. Chilling Gonzaga’s family was among those who transferred to the temporary shelter in April 2024 after losing their home to the fire. She said the first few months after the fire were the most difficult.

“Sa tulong ng mga nagdo-donate ng goods, at malaking tulong din ang mga kaklase ko kasi sila ang maraming naitulong sa amin,” Gonzaga said. (We got by with the help of those who donated goods, and my classmates, who also significantly contributed.)

Despite the challenges, she continued her studies and recently graduated from the same university with a degree in business administration.

Like many families who remain in the shelter, Gonzaga longs for a day when her home will no longer be temporary.

Still waiting

In July 2025, local news reported that the Puerto Princesa city government had ordered the clearing of the temporary shelter. According to the report, personnel from the City Housing Office and the Anti-Squatting Office were initially set to padlock the shelter. The residents appealed to Mayor Lucilo Bayron and were granted a three-month extension until October.

While many families continue to wait for permanent housing, the city government has identified them as among the priority beneficiaries of the Tandikan Ville housing project in Barangay Irawan under the national government’s Pambansang Pabahay para sa Pilipino Program.

However, local news reported in December 2025 that there was still no confirmed turnover date for the project due to construction delays. Acting City Information Officer Aries Jade del Rosario said families staying in the temporary shelter would continue to receive priority, although the final selection of beneficiaries rests with the PAG-IBIG Fund.

Cabanillas said residents initially believed the housing would be free, but during a meeting with city officials, they were informed that they would have to pay a monthly amortization of around P3,000 for the housing units.

He said many families, including theirs, decided not to relocate because they could not afford the monthly payments.

As for Gonzaga’s family, she acknowledged the assistance they received from the city government immediately after the fire, including water and free electricity in the shelter. However, she said their family still hopes to receive a permanent place where they can rebuild their lives.

“Sana kahit lupa na lang ang maibigay nila para kahit papaano makapagsimula kaming magpatayo ng maliit na bahay,” she said (I hope they could give us at least land where we could build even just a small house.)

As of this writing, at least 366 occupants continue to live in the temporary shelter in Barangay San Pedro, according to the City Urban Development and Housing Office (CUDHO).

The CUDHO said the remaining occupants cannot be relocated yet because there is no available relocation site ready to accommodate them. Instead of transferring families in batches, the city plans to carry out a simultaneous relocation once the housing project is completed and ready for occupancy to ensure an orderly transition for all beneficiaries.

Holding on to a dream

When his family eventually relocates, Cabanillas hopes for simple things: a home with its own water connection, its own comfort room, stable electricity, and enough space to study. For now, the temporary shelter remains both his home and the place where each school day begins.

More than two years after losing their house to the Quito fire, Cabanillas chooses to move forward. Every morning starts with collecting water instead of simply getting ready for school. Every evening ends in a shelter that was meant to be temporary.

Yet despite the uncertainty, he continues to pursue the same goal he had before the fire: to finish his engineering degree and build a better future for his family.

Home, for now, is temporary, but his dream is not. – Rappler.com

Vic Albert Bagaan is a petroleum engineering student at Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. The development communication editor of Pioneer Publication, he is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

World.title: Maypajo, Caloocan furniture makers strive to sustain their craft
World.content:
Many furniture makers in Caloocan have spent decades dedicated to a craft that some of them would not encourage their children to pursue

MANILA, Philippines – Before Caloocan officially became a city in 1962, it was already known for its thriving furniture industry.

Along A. Mabini Street in Maypajo, a row of furniture shops seeks the attention of passers-by. Made of wood, metal, or polyester, the furniture wait for their new owners to bring them home.

Manong Jun, as he wished to be called, is 58 years old and has been in the furniture resale business for decades. While he observed a decline in their sales, he said customers keep coming back because they trust the quality of furniture made in the city.

WAITING FOR CUSTOMERS. Furniture on display in front of the furniture shops. Photo by Eunicito Barreno/Rappler

Caloocan isn’t the furniture capital of the Philippines — the distinction goes to Cebu, particularly Mandaue City — but it has been around for decades and has survived trying times. The question is, for how long?

Manong Jun inherited the business from his mother and he believes it will end with him. He said he wants his children to pursue a different path, hinting at employment in a more stable industry.

Furniture sales are low from February to August, but usually picks up come the “ber” months. The COVID-19 pandemic as well as online shopping, however, had taken a toll on the local industry, observed Barangay 21 Secretary Ferdinand Dado.

“Malakas dati ‘yan. Walang problema diyan lalo na ‘pag September. Ang lalakas na ng benta niyan. Noong tumuntong ang [COVID-19 pandemic], bawal lumabas ang mga tao. Isa-isang nagsara, walang bumibili. Isa ‘yun sa mga dahilan. Pangalawa, ‘yung mga nag-o-online,” Dado said in an interview.

(Those shops’ sales used to be strong, there was no problem especially when September came. Sales boom. When the COVID-19 pandemic happened, people couldn’t go outside their homes. The shops shut down one by one; no one was buying. That’s one of the reasons. Second is the online businesses.)

But despite these, the shops continue to exist, asserting both their cultural and economic significance to the city.

‘Tatak Caloocan’

As you enter the alleys of the street just behind the shops, the sounds of hammers, saws, and sanders would welcome you, along with sawdust and the smell of varnish and cigarettes. Deeper into the alley, carpenters worked on their trade, a few of them without shirts to cope with the heat.

This was the daily routine of 42-year-old furniture carpenter and seller Edward Marukot for most of his life. He began working in the industry as a varnish painter in sixth grade, saving his money, and observing his uncles who were furniture makers until he eventually became one of them.

Today, Marukot’s furniture are not only found in Metro Manila, but also fnd their way in Mindoro, Cebu, Bohol, Zamboanga, and as far as the southernmost island-province of the country, Tawi-Tawi.

“Tawid-dagat ‘yan (That furniture crosses the sea),” his wife volunteered.

Marukot doesn’t have a physical store and sells furniture through online platforms, keeping up with competitors who had already navigated the digital world. He said he wants to tap TikTok too, to widen his reach.

Asked if he would encourage his children to follow his path, like Mang Jun, Marukot said: “Depende sa sitwasyon ngayon. Mahirap ang [buhay] ngayon, talagang hindi natin alam kasi sila ‘yung may buhay noon e. Hindi ko rin [pinipilit] sa kanila e pero tinuturuan ko rin naman sila paano mag-furniture.”

(It depends on the situation now. Life is difficult now and we really don’t know because it’s their lives. I don’t force them but I also teach them the business somehow.)

Marukot is fortunate as he has yet to experience a decline in sales. He is proud of the city furniture makers’ “King Louis” sala set which, he said, is “Tatak Caloocan” or proudly made in Caloocan. He said he would like the furniture industry in Caloocan, especially their signature sala sets, to be better promoted.

‘A better life for our children’

Dante Acain has been working in Caloocan’s furniture industry for the last 30 years, beginning at the age of 18. He would start work at 7 am, and end his day depending on the need to go overtime. Usually, he earns P700 per day, which he said is small but enough to meet his family’s needs.

HARD AT WORK. Dante Acain at work. Photo by Eunicito Barreno/Rappler

Acain observed that customers flock to the shops around December, apparently in preparation for the holiday celebrations.

He has also never seen his industry receiving government support but he would be happy if workers like him would get any form of government “ayuda (aid),” especially at this time. For now, the only bonus he gets is in December — a Christmas bonus from his boss, furniture shop owner Jerry dela Cruz.

Dela Cruz said the furniture industry used to receive support from the now-defunct National Cottage Industries Development Authority. NACIDA was mandated to promote cottage industries, including assistance in financing, production, and marketing.

Asked if he would like his children to become part of the industry, Acain said he would rather encourage them to pursue whatever job they wanted.

“Siyempre, mahirap na trabaho ‘to. Tama na ‘to sa naranasan ko.… Gusto ko ‘yung magandang trabaho [para sa kanila], hindi maalikabok,” Acain said, noting that the amount of saw dust in their shop.

(Of course this is difficult work. It’s enough that I experienced it. I want a good job for them, not where you get exposed to dust.)

ONE NAIL AT A TIME. A furniture maker in their work shop in Caloocan City. Eunicito Barreno/Rappler

Caloocan has furniture workers and shop owners who have strived to preserve the city’s cultural heritage. Most of them have spent decades dedicated to a craft that some of them would not encourage their children to pursue. What can be done to prevent the industry from fading away? – Rappler.com

Eunicito Barreno is a 2026 Aries Rufo Fellow. He is a senior journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman, where he is also news staffer at the Philippine Collegian, the university’s official student publication.

World.title: Inside the impeachment court, students watch the testing of democracy
World.content:
WEEKLY AFFAIR. Classmates Sandara Villon and Renz Carl Bayanay tell Rappler they will try to attend the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte every Wednesday.

'Everything can be manipulated on the internet. But when you're there physically, you can feel everything, you can see everything. You can judge [on] your own,' a student says of the impeachment trial

MANILA, Philippines – Sandara Villon and Renz Carl Bayanay, both 21-year-old students, are familiar with the atmosphere of the Senate.

The two currently study public administration and belong to a student-led parliamentary organization that is active in lobbying bills to senators.

They have seen the Senate halls, have listened to committee hearings. But now, they also got the chance to watch the plenary hall turned into a court, where senators conduct the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

At the impeachment court, members of the House of Representatives put on their prosecution hats for the trial. Senators wear their red robes to transform themselves as senator-judges. Duterte, who has not shown up in court, is represented by lawyers mostly from the prominent law firm Fortun, Narvasa and Salazar.

But the plenary hall is not just for these three groups and their respective staff. Every trial day, some 61 seats are reserved at the gallery for the Filipino public.

“We are very super excited to come here,” Villon told Rappler in Filipino after the trial on Wednesday, July 22. “I mean, even if it’s already our third time coming for the impeachment trial, the excitement was not lost on us.”

Their excitement was rooted in learning how impeachment as a constitutional process works, and seeing in person, the personalities of the political body.

But Bayanay also said he is disappointed.

While the impeachment process may be fascinating, Bayanay expressed how he feels let down that the country has to see an impeachment trial in the first place. “[There is] some mix of disappointment,” he said, seeing a top elected leader having to be tested for the allegations pointing towards the betrayal of public trust.

Sara Duterte, who has been impeached twice, is facing charges of culpable violation of the Constitution, bribery, graft, corruption, betrayal of public trust, and other high crimes.

‘History in the making’

To attend the trial, the public can register online through the Senate Visitor Management System a day before their preferred date. For the past three weeks, the trial was scheduled from Monday to Wednesday afternoons.

It’s on a first-come first-serve basis, with individuals filling out their details, including submitting a copy of their government ID. And it fills up fast, according to the four people interviewed by Rappler.

Agatha Apostol, 20, failed to secure a slot last week, so she attempted a walk-in to the Senate building. That was a no-go.

So the environment science student tried again for Wednesday’s trial day. Her registration a success, she came in, wearing a black coat, burnt orange top, and black slacks.

Curiosity in the impeachment process led Apostol to the Senate plenary hall. She felt honored to be in the presence of senators, and to witness the rare opportunity that is an impeachment trial.

“There’s some intimidation but I find it really amusing, regarding their interactions with each other,” she said of all parties involved in the trial.

“I’ve been kind of studying law because we have a subject regarding the Constitution. So there’s some kind of familiarity within it but also it’s something new to me as well,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Apostol was not alone, she was with her brother, 27-year-old law student Kyle Orsos, during their Senate visit.

TRIAL ATTENDANCE. Siblings Agatha Apostol and Kyle Orsos talk with Rappler along the Senate’s “legacy wall” after attending the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026. Photo by Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler

“This is history, history in the making. And also as a law student, it’s a big help to watch how our Constitution and laws really work in action,” Orsos said in a mix of English and Filipino.

The trial’s political side

In the past three weeks, the impeachment court was filled with objections, legal jargon, and arguments as the prosecution presented witnesses and documents to present their first case — the grave threats Duterte made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

The complexity of impeachment was not lost on Orsos, who is a second-year law student.

“Since impeachment [is also] political, so sometimes the judges, they cannot help but be political,” he said, noting that the court rules he learned from law school were not strictly followed in the exercise.

Villon expressed disappointment with some senator-judges for, in her mind, seemingly showing bias. She said maybe Filipinos could reach out to senators, even through social media, to compel them to do their duty and remain impartial.

And for her, attending the trial in-person would help many Filipinos to know which senator-judges are genuinely working.

“Everything can be manipulated on the internet. But when you’re there physically, you can feel everything, you can see everything. You can judge [on] your own,” she added.

Will they go back?

With her curiosity already quenched, Apostol is inclined to monitor the trial through the livestream instead. Her brother is slightly hesitant to return.

“One thing that might push me to come back here would be the evidence that they will prepare,” Orsos said.

Prosecutors will bare their pieces of evidence for the remaining articles of impeachment, which tackle allegations of confidential funds misuse, unexplained wealth, and monetary gifts.

Public administration students Bayanay and Villon are eager to maximize their half-day on-the-job training during Wednesdays.

For Bayanay, their presence at the Senate gallery is their way to say that the trial “should also be a conversation of the people.” They actually post their experiences on their social media accounts.

“We go to the Senate to post awareness to the people that we can observe the impeachment trial, we can see how the senators as senator-judges act, and that it’s also a test to our democracy, to the integrity of our institution,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino.

However, they have observed that the trial becomes more technical as the weeks go by. The 61 seats for the public at the gallery seem to be unfilled as well. And they saw that it’s usually law students who are there at the Senate.

It has been only nine days out of the 92-day trial schedule. According to a poll by Momentum Research, only 13% of Filipinos are closely monitoring Duterte’s impeachment trial.

“Nagiging malayo po siya sa mga normal na ordinaryong Pilipino. Hindi na po maintindihan, minsan po nalilihis. Kaya hindi natin masisi [ang] mga Pilipino kung bakit nagbabase sila sa mga memes, sa mga kung sino may malaking makinarya na Facebook social media page diyan,” Villon said.

(The trial has become distant to ordinary Filipinos. It has become more difficult to understand, sometimes it’s being sidetracked. That’s why we cannot blame Filipinos for basing on memes and on Facebook pages with huge machinery.)

She suggested the chamber try to reach out to local government units to invite ordinary people to watch and provide free transportation if they have to.

The student made this appeal to the Senate: “Try to diminish the huge gap between the Senate being seen as a place for the elites, and try to bridge that gap and try to welcome normal Filipino people so that they will join in here.” – Rappler.com

Some quotes are translated to English for brevity.

World.title: Warnings lifted as Typhoon Kiyapo moves away, but monsoon rain persists
World.content:
KIYAPO. Satellite image of Typhoon Kiyapo (Noul) outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of July 25, 2026, 10 am.

Typhoon Kiyapo (Noul) is heading for China, while the southwest monsoon is still affecting parts of the Philippines on Saturday, July 25

MANILA, Philippines – Rainfall and wind warnings due to Typhoon Kiyapo (Noul) were lifted at 11 am on Saturday, July 25, as the tropical cyclone continued to move outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), heading for China.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Kiyapo was last spotted 465 kilometers west of Basco, Batanes, at 10 am.

The typhoon is moving northwest at 25 kilometers per hour, still with maximum sustained winds of 120 km/h and gustiness of up to 150 km/h. It had left PAR at 2 am on Saturday.

PAGASA said in its 11 am bulletin that Kiyapo may strengthen in the next 12 hours, ahead of its expected landfall in China. But it may weaken quickly once it moves further inland there.

In the Philippines, Kiyapo made landfall as a tropical storm in Camiguin Island, Calayan, Cagayan, at 2:10 pm on Friday, July 24. It brought moderate to intense rain to Northern Luzon, and Signal No. 3 was the highest tropical cyclone wind signal raised.

While Kiyapo is no longer posing a threat to any part of the Philippines, the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms across the country. The following provinces are currently the most affected:

Saturday noon, July 25, to Sunday noon, July 26

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Pangasinan, Zambales, Bataan, Occidental Mindoro

Sunday noon, July 26, to Monday noon, July 27

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Pangasinan, Zambales

Floods and landslides can still occur.

The southwest monsoon and the typhoon’s periphery or outer bands are also bringing strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Saturday, July 25

most of Luzon, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Northern Samar, Zamboanga del Norte, Davao Oriental

Sunday, July 26

Batanes, Cagayan, Ilocos Region, Zambales, Bataan, Quezon, Mimaropa

Monday, July 27

La Union, Pangasinan, Zambales, Lubang Islands, Kalayaan Islands

Meanwhile, conditions at sea are starting to gradually improve, although travel remains dangerous for small vessels in certain seaboards.

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Seaboard of Batanes – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboard of Babuyan Islands; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Northern seaboards of Isabela and Ilocos Sur; western seaboard of Kalayaan Islands; remaining seaboards of mainland Cagayan and Ilocos Norte – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboard of Zambales; northern seaboard of La Union; western seaboards of Pangasinan, Bataan, Calamian Islands, and Occidental Mindoro including Lubang Islands; eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining seaboards of Isabela, Ilocos Sur, and Kalayaan Islands – waves up to 2 meters high

Kiyapo was the Philippines’ 11th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the fourth for July alone. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Newspoint] A brewing emergency
World.content:
Still, while not yet fully inactivated and still president, he cannot escape taking a position on an issue like Sara Duterte, an issue not just political and legal, but moral — indeed, an issue that poses an existential danger to the nation’s well-being

When Ferdinand Marcos Jr. goes to Congress on Monday, July 27, to report on the state of the nation, the air will be filled with foreboding of an emergency, one so grave and so imminent that what he has to say now and what he has to do from now on will define his presidency.

Everything will turn on how the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, his archenemy, goes. If she survives it, her path to the presidency, which she openly covets, becomes paved with dark intentions. And the curse is not just on him but on the entire nation. The only consolation is he gets it first.

The Senate, as an impeachment court, is now trying Duterte on four charges: one involves a death threat on Marcos, his wife, and his first-cousin the former Speaker Martin Romualdez; the others, embezzlement of taxpayer pesos in the hundreds of millions, unexplained wealth in the billions, and kickbacks to her office from anomalous contracts with suppliers.

Evidence in the embezzlement case is set to be presented at the trial. As for the death threat, the presentation has gone quickly. The prosecutors said the case was “rather straightforward.” Sure enough, the defense, in all those hours of cross-examination, did not so much as suggest that its client had not made the threat, because that would be a lie.

In fact, she did it publicly, at a press conference, and footage of the event has been making the rounds in cyberspace profusely. In it she says, “I have already talked to someone” who would kill the three “once I died,” presumptuously laying the culpability for her hypothetical death squarely on them. She even adds superfluously, “No joke, no joke.”

The Dutertes are never known to be less than serious when it comes to those things. During an investigation into death-squad killings in Davao City, Leila de Lima, chair of the Commission on Human Rights at the time, found herself right inside the lion’s den where Sara’s father, then-Davao mayor Rodrigo Duterte, was the pride male. She was marked for death herself, according to a confessed Duterte hitman. The hit went unconsummated — De Lima took an unplanned detour, thus frustrating the pre-positioned hit squad — but Rodrigo Duterte, upon assuming the presidency, had his hitmen in the Department of Justice, in Congress, and the courts carry on. They put De Lima, a senator by this time, in detention on concocted drug charges. She spent nearly seven years in jail, let out only to appear at her trial and set free only after Duterte had left the presidency.

Duterte himself is now detained in The Hague, the Netherlands, awaiting trial by the International Criminal Court on charges of “crimes against humanity” for thousands of extrajudicial killings in his war on drugs during his presidency. Marcos’ police chief had arrested him on a warrant issued by that court and delivered by the Interpol, and put him on a plane on the same day for the 6,000-plus-mile flight.

Now, it’s his daughter’s turn at a reckoning, in her home country, where patronage is currency and her family has built a considerable herd following. If opinion polls were a determinant and the presidential election were held today, she would be a shoo-in. In fact, without regard for the law — although admittedly, it has proved toothless across the board — she prematurely declared for the next presidential election, in 2028, and has been campaigning vigorously since — and with some success, judging again by the polls. A relentless barrage of propagandistic falsehoods on social media tends to swamp revelations about her true gangster character.

The only thing that will stop her in her tracks is a guilty verdict by the senator-judges. It removes her automatically as vice president and bans her from taking public office ever again. But that requires a two-thirds vote, although that threshold looks less formidable now that the Duterte bloc has lost control of the Senate after a few defections. A further thinning of its ranks is in prospect as the law begins to catch up with members charged with non-bailable crimes; once their cases go to trial, they could be held in detention for its duration and become ineligible for impeachment duty, thus unable to vote. But the trial, being nationally televised, thus exploitable as a political platform, pro-Duterte senator-judges work it for the purpose to the hilt, shamelessly acting as if they were themselves counsels for the defense. And, very suspiciously, the presiding senator-judge, who happens to be one of the defectors from the Duterte camp, indulges them.

At any rate, If Sara Duterte is acquitted and goes on to be elected president, a review of Rodrigo Duterte’s regime should make for a fair warning of what’s coming: cronyism, plunder, vice crimes, weaponization of the law, the security agencies, and the courts; vengeful targeting, and promotion of communist China’s expansionist designs. As I’ve said, it’s all too obviously in the blood.

Anyone dreaming of a somewhat chastened Duterte II presidency is bound to be rudely roused. Ferdinand II himself, for all his benignness, has yet to come to terms with the bald fact of his father’s own notoriety, but, like him or not, there’s just no taking away from the son’s fairly responsive presidency.

But what has he got in response to the brewing emergency? Surely, he wants to do something, if only for her family’s sake. But what?

So far, President Marcos has tried, it seems to me, to stay above the impeachment fray, while much of the nation is in or onto it anxiously, like me. I guess he is careful to be seen as uninvolved or impartial, to be consistent with his apparent wish to look good, although I also suspect he is implicitly replying to Duterte’s persistent portrayal of her case as something put up at his urging — “politically motivated.” But who cares! Who cares if helping stop a Sara Duterte serves whosever political interest?

In his case, anyway, Marcos is being tested by the circumstances — by the fates, if you like. Never mind whether or not he’s looking to be redeemed from his own notorious legacy. To the Dutertes, Marcos is not just a lame duck, but a dead one. Still, while not yet fully inactivated and still president, he cannot escape taking a position on an issue like Sara Duterte, an issue not just political and legal, but moral — indeed, an issue that poses an existential danger to the nation’s well-being.

That’s why Marcos is expected to work his political will by doing what he can by law and by conscience to stop Sara Duterte. That’s also why I can’t wait to know what he has to say in this, his penultimate and possibly last relevant, State of the Nation Address. – Rappler.com

World.title: Iloilo City flooding eases; 35 barangays still inundated as Kiyapo exits
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

ILOILO CITY — Floodwaters have begun to recede in several parts of Iloilo City after Tropical Cyclone Kiyapo (international name: Noul) intensified into a typhoon and exited the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR), but at least 35 barangays remained flooded while more than 500 residents continued to be affected as of 6 a.m. Saturday, July 25.

The Iloilo City Emergency Operations Center (ICEOC), in its Situation Report No. 3, said a total of 45 barangays had experienced flooding since the onset of heavy rains. Floodwaters have already subsided in 10 barangays, leaving 35 barangays still inundated.

Authorities have placed the city’s Emergency Operations Center under Blue Alert as response operations continue.

Article continues after this 

READ: Wind signals lifted as Kiyapo heads towards Southern China on Saturday

The city government reported that 132 families, or 508 individuals, were affected by the flooding. Of these, 73 families composed of 221 individuals were staying inside four evacuation centers located in nine affected barangays.

The evacuation centers are serving residents from Calubihan and San Vicente in Jaro; Ticud in La Paz; Alalasan and Don Esteban in Lapuz; Airport in Mandurriao; and San Antonio, Compania Central and Infante in Molo.

Initial assessment by the City Social Welfare and Development Office (CSWDO) also showed three partially damaged houses affecting five families or 15 individuals. The damaged houses were located in Barangay Airport in Mandurriao, Barangay Compania Central in Molo, and Barangay San Vicente in Jaro.

Strong winds associated with the weather disturbance also uprooted five trees, with incidents recorded in Jaro, La Paz and Mandurriao. No toppled electric posts were reported.

Article continues after this 

Among the areas still experiencing flooding were portions of Arevalo, City Proper, Jaro, La Paz, Lapuz, Mandurriao and Molo, with flood depths ranging from a few inches to as much as 48 inches in parts of Ticud, La Paz. Several areas in Sinkway, Lapuz remained under 24 to 36 inches of floodwater, while Don Esteban in Lapuz and Desamparados in Jaro each recorded flood depths of 36 inches.

Meanwhile, several previously flooded barangays had already reported receding waters, including Kahirupan and Ortiz in City Proper; Timawa Tanza 2 and Inday in City Proper; Bantud in La Paz; Oñate de Leon and Navais in Mandurriao; Calumpang, South San Jose and West Timawa in Molo.

Article continues after this 

Rainfall during the past 12 hours remained generally light to moderate, with the highest accumulation of 11 millimeters recorded at the West Visayas State University monitoring station. Wind speeds reached up to 50 kilometers per hour at the Lapuz Depot weather station.

Despite improving conditions in Iloilo, the city continued emergency operations, including 24/7 monitoring, flood surveillance, public information campaigns, evacuation assistance, declogging operations, and coordination with barangay officials and response agencies.

The ICEOC also recommended the implementation of the asynchronous alternative delivery mode for students at all levels in Iloilo City on July 25 as a precaution against the lingering effects of flooding.

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), Kiyapo had intensified into a typhoon before moving outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility early Saturday.

World.title: Pangilinan on survey of front-runners for next polls: Too early for 2028
World.content:
Sen. Francis Pangilinan. — Photo from Senate Social Media Unit

MANILA, Philippines — Following the release of a Pulse Asia survey on voter preferences ahead of the 2028 elections, where Sen. Robinhood Padilla topped the senatorial race, Sen. Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan took to social media to say it’s too early to name the front-runners.

In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Pangilinan said the 2028 elections are still in the distant future.

“Malayo pa ang 2028. Walang bibitiw!! [2028 is still a long way off. No one is backing down!],” he said

Article continues after this 

He also posted photos of a pre-election survey from April 20 to 24, 2025, where he ranked in the 16th to 18th place, only 4 percent shy of being included in the top 12. He highlighted that the survey had a ±2 margin of error, implying that the Senate race was “anybody’s ball game”.

READ: Sara Duterte, Bong Go top bets for President, VP in 2028, survey says

“We aren’t on the list on page 1; we are on page 2. We are ranked 16th to 18th, trailing the top 12 by 4 percent, while the margin of error is plus or minus 2 percent. As the saying goes, it’s anyone’s game, and the race for the 12th through 18th spots is a tight contest,” he said in Filipino.

Pangilinan recalled the previous year’s survey result ended with Sen. Bam Aquino as the second preferred senate candidate from being in the rank 11th to 18th bracket during the pre-election survey, while he placed fifth.

“The important thing is, we did not give up and fought hand to hand until the end. The result? Bam came in number 2 and we came in number 5. While Risa’s Akbayan Partylist came in number 1 and Leila also won the ML Partylist. Remember. The people did not abandon us and I am confident that the people will not abandon us,” he added.

Article continues after this 

Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson expressed support for Pangilinan, adding that surveys are mere “snapshots of voters’ preferences” during specific periods.

““Yes, Sen. Kiko. We may have run under different alliances, but I am happy that you and Sen. Bam not only made it but won strong and big. That being said, surveys are nothing but snapshots of voters’ preferences during specific timeframes,” he said.

Article continues after this 

The Pulse Asia survey, conducted from June 28 to July 6, showed that Padilla was the top preferred candidate at 48.4 percent, followed by Pasig City Mayor Vico Sotto at 47.9 percent.

Meanwhile, other senators included in the Magic 12 bracket were Sen. Raffy Tulfo in 2nd to 5th places at 43.9 percent, Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano at 43.2 percent ranked 3rd to 5th places, Sen. Loren Legarda at 40.3 percent also ranked 3rd to 5th places, Sen. Manny Pacquiao at 35.6 percent ranked 6th to 7th places, Makati City Mayor Nancy Binay at 32.4 percent ranked 6th to 7th places, Education Sec. Sonny Angara at 27.2 percent ranked 8th to 9th places, Sen. Mark Villar at 26.1 percent ranked 8th to 9th places, and Ben Tulfo at 20.7 percent ranked 10th to 12th places. /jpv

World.title: Biliran Bridge restores full 15-ton load capacity after repair
World.content:
t0726visbreak3: Biliran Bridge restores full 15-ton load capacity after repair of expansion joints

TACLOBAN CITY — The Biliran Bridge has been cleared to accommodate all types of vehicles again after the completion of repair works that restored its original 15-ton maximum allowable load capacity, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) said.

DPWH-Biliran District Engineering Office District Engineer Irwin Antonio said the lifting of vehicle-type restrictions followed the replacement of the bridge’s expansion joints, which had been identified for repair after the structure was placed under restrictions following a bridge-swaying incident in December 2024.

READ: Biliran Bridge rehabilitation nears completion

Article continues after this 

All vehicles may now cross the bridge, provided their total load does not exceed 15 tons, beginning on July 23, Antonio said.

However, motorists must strictly follow safety rules while crossing the structure. These include avoiding gear shifting, allowing only one vehicle at a time to cross and maintaining a speed of 15 to 20 kilometers per hour.

Antonio urged motorists to comply with the regulations to help ensure their safety and protect the structural integrity of the bridge.

The Biliran Bridge, built in 1976, is the only road link connecting Biliran Island to Leyte and the rest of Eastern Visayas. It serves as a critical route for the movement of residents, agricultural products, commercial goods and essential services.

The bridge had been under a 15-ton load restriction since December 2024 after a viral video showed the structure visibly swaying, prompting authorities to conduct a structural inspection. Vehicles exceeding the allowable weight were prohibited from crossing and were required to use barge services between Biliran and Leyte.

Article continues after this 

While the repair works have allowed the bridge to resume normal vehicle access, the DPWH is pursuing longer-term measures to preserve the aging structure.

The agency proposed a P266-million retrofitting project under its 2027 budget request. The project would include installing additional support systems and reinforcing aging steel components.

Article continues after this 

Plans are also advancing for a proposed P1.72-billion parallel bridge project, with funding support from the Asian Development Bank. The project remains subject to feasibility studies and other pre-engineering activities.

Despite the proposed new bridge, authorities said the existing Biliran Bridge will be preserved as an important landmark and enduring symbol of the province’s connection to Leyte and the wider Eastern Visayas region. /jpv

World.title: BI denies spreading false info on Romualdez’s alleged bid to leave PH
World.content:
Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez appears at the Independent Commission for Infrastructure, Fort Bonifacio, Taguig City on October 14, 2025, to attend hearings on alleged flood control project anomalies. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Immigration (BI) on Saturday stood by its statements regarding former House Speaker Martin Romualdez’s alleged travel plans, saying it did not disseminate false information on the matter.

BI’s statement came after the lawyers of Romualdez demanded an apology from the agency over its alleged fake reports that the lawmaker was attempting to leave the country.

In a statement on Friday, Romualdez’ spokesperson Ade Fejardo said that the Solis Media Fajardo & Malilong Law Offices sent a demand letter addressed to BI Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado stating that the information on the lawmaker’s plan to leave the country is “patently false.”

Article continues after this 

READ: Romualdez camp to BI: Apologize over fake news on attempt to leave PH

According to Viado, the agency responded to legitimate media inquiries, emphasizing that it only provides factual information within the agency’s mandate.

“The Bureau respectfully rejects the allegation that it disseminated false or fabricated information. We remain committed to providing honest, accurate, and responsible public information while respecting due process and the constitutional rights of all persons,” Viado said in a press release.

Viado noted that the information the BI gave regarding alleged travel plans that did not push through pertains to a supposed trip in April 2026.

The statement from Romualdez’ spokesperson said that the demand letter was prompted by a July 21 statement by BI spokesperson Dana Sandoval, which said that the BI “received information that there were plans that did not push through.”

Article continues after this 

The information was cited by the Office of the Ombudsman, which accused Romualdez of attempting to leave the country as plunder and money laundering complaints were being prepared against him.

“The Bureau’s response referred to information available to the Bureau at the time and was issued solely in response to legitimate media inquiries. The Bureau did not initiate the public discussion on the matter,” Viado added.

Article continues after this 

Romualdez’ camp also said that the information given by the BI “unfairly created the impression” that he was attempting to flee the country to evade the pending criminal investigation against him.

In April 2026, Romualdez’ request to travel out of the country for his angioplasty follow-up checkup was granted by House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and Secretary General Cheloy Garafil.

World.title: Police see no foul play in elderly Calapan man’s death
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police dismissed claims that the home of an elderly couple was ransacked, saying initial investigations found no signs of foul play or forced entry.

In a telephone interview on Saturday, July 25, Calapan City Police Station chief Lt. Col. Michael Caraggayan said Scene of the Crime Operatives (SOCO) found the couple’s personal belongings, including their cell phones and wallets, untouched inside the house.

“Based on our investigation, the male senior citizen’s body was already in an advanced stage of decomposition, indicating that he may have died several days to a week before he was discovered,” Caraggayan said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Calapan City’s sixth most wanted arrested in Oriental Mindoro

The body of the 85-year-old man was found on Friday inside the couple’s home in Barangay Suqui after neighbors reported a foul odor coming from the residence.

His 86-year-old wife, who is suffering from Alzheimer’s disease, was found unconscious inside the house.

She was rushed to the Oriental Mindoro Provincial Hospital and remains under medical treatment.

Police said the investigation is ongoing. /das

World.title: Whirlwind damages homes, displaces families in Pagadian City
World.content:
Houses in Barangay White Beach, Pagadian City, were damaged after a whirlwind (ipo-ipo) struck the coastal community on Friday afternoon, July 24, 2026. — Photo courtesy of village councilor Merryhill Rabanos

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — A whirlwind (ipo-ipo) tore through coastal communities in Barangay White Beach here on Friday afternoon, July 24, destroying houses and displacing dozens of residents.

City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO) chief Engr. Vince Quipot said response teams were immediately deployed to assess the damage and ensure the safety of affected families.

Initial assessments showed that three houses were destroyed while five others were damaged after the whirlwind, which struck amid heavy rains and strong winds.

Article continues after this 

No injuries or fatalities were reported.

READ: Whirlwind damages 20 houses in Negros Occidental town

Quipot said damage assessment is continuing in coordination with concerned local government offices to determine the extent of losses and facilitate assistance for affected residents.

Village councilor Merryhill Rabanos said at least 50 people were displaced and are temporarily staying with relatives in nearby areas.

She added that the barangay hall also sustained damage during the incident.

Article continues after this 

“Even the displayed plaques were destroyed by the strong winds. Luckily, the building itself remained intact,” Rabanos said.

The village council said it is coordinating with the city government to secure assistance for affected families as recovery efforts continue. /das

World.title: 258 evacuated as Kiyapo-triggered rains swell rivers in Cagayan
World.content:
The Taytay–San Isidro Bridge in Baggao, Cagayan, is submerged in floodwaters after heavy rains brought by Typhoon Kiyapo on Friday, July 24, 2026. — Photo courtesy of the Baggao Information Office

TUGUEGARAO CITY — At least 258 people from 57 families were displaced in Cagayan after heavy rains spawned by Typhoon Kiyapo (international name: Noul) triggered flooding and heightened the risk of landslides in several northern towns, provincial disaster responsed officials said on Saturday, July 25.

A report from the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO) showed the evacuees came from 13 barangays in the towns of Allacapan, Buguey, Santa Teresita, Camalaniugan, and Gonzaga.

Of the total, 243 individuals from 54 families are staying in seven evacuation centers, while 15 people from three families have sought temporary shelter with relatives or neighbors.

Article continues after this 

READ: Wind signals lifted as Kiyapo heads towards Southern China on Saturday

The evacuations were carried out as rivers swelled and flooding threats persisted on Friday despite Typhoon Kiyapo moving away from the country.

No casualties have been reported.

The PDRRMO said it continues to coordinate with municipal disaster risk reduction and management offices to consolidate reports, while the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council and the Task Force Lingkod Cagayan–Quick Response Team (TFLC-QRT) remain on alert to ensure immediate response to emergencies.

TFLC stations in Gonzaga, Lal-lo, Ballesteros, and Sanchez Mira have been placed on red alert to enable rapid deployment if needed.

Article continues after this 

Authorities urged residents to remain vigilant and follow advisories issued by their local government units, particularly in areas still experiencing heavy rainfall.

Several bridges were submerged due to rising floodwaters, including the Taytay–San Isidro Bridge in Baggao and the Nanguillatan Bridge in Peñablanca, disrupting travel in affected areas. /das

World.title: Discover Stories Behind Kazakhstan’s Most Unique Mosques
World.content:
47125

ASTANA – From soaring modern landmarks to centuries-old sanctuaries carved into rock, Kazakhstan’s mosques reflect the country’s rich spiritual heritage and architectural diversity. While modern mosques attract visitors with their monumental domes and soaring minarets, many of the country’s oldest mosques continue to captivate travelers with their unique construction techniques, legends and historical significance.

According to the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Kazakhstan, the country had 2,888 active mosques as of January 2025. Data from the Bureau of National Statistics shows that 20 new mosques were commissioned in 2025, a 54% increase compared to the previous year.

Yet beyond these growing numbers lie centuries of history. Scattered across Kazakhstan are mosques built from clay, carved into rock faces, or designed in architectural styles. Some have served generations of worshippers for more than 150 years.

Oiyl Mosque

Located around 300 kilometers from Aktobe in the Oiyl district of western Kazakhstan, the Oiyl Mosque is one of the country’s most unusual architectural monuments.

Built in 1869 by local merchants, the single-story mosque has served as the district’s main place of worship for more than a century. Its distinctive silver-colored triangular minaret and reddish earthen walls set it apart from many other historic mosques in Kazakhstan.

What makes the mosque particularly remarkable is its construction technique. Instead of using water, builders mixed mare’s milk and sheep’s wool with red sand brought from the nearby Barkhyn Desert to produce durable clay bricks. Local residents say this traditional mixture has helped preserve the mosque’s exterior for generations, with the façade largely retaining its original color.

Mangystau’s underground mosques

The Shopan Ata underground mosque forms part of a larger necropolis carved into rock. It is located around 60 kilometers from Zhanaozen.

The complex is considered one of the largest underground religious sites in Mangystau and remains an important destination for pilgrims.

Nearby stands a sacred mulberry tree that local tradition associates with healing. According to popular belief, elderly visitors who walk beneath its branches may find relief from back pain.

Around 57 kilometers from Fort-Shevchenko in the Tupkaragan district lies the Sultan-Epe underground mosque, one of Mangystau’s oldest pilgrimage sites.

Historians date the mosque to between the ninth and 13th centuries. The complex consists of 11 chambers connected by a central gallery supported by stone columns. Openings in the ceiling allow sunlight to illuminate the underground rooms.

Visitors descend a steep stone staircase before entering the galleries, where some narrow passages require people to crouch, or even crawl, to reach secluded prayer cells once used by Sufi devotees.

A nearby well is believed by pilgrims to contain healing water, while local tradition holds that the mosque offers spiritual protection to travelers embarking on long journeys.

Outside the mosque is the Sultan-Epe necropolis, where visitors often tie small pieces of cloth to poles near graves as symbols of prayers and wishes. Another local tradition says that walking around the burial site seven times before tying a ribbon may help one’s wishes come true.

The Shakpak Ata Underground Mosque is one of Kazakhstan’s most significant religious and architectural monuments. Located near the village of Tauchyk in the Mangystau Region, the mosque was carved into a massive chalk cliff overlooking a dramatic canyon landscape.

Although commonly referred to as an underground mosque, the sanctuary is actually hewn into the side of a rock formation rather than buried beneath the ground.

Scholars disagree on its exact age. Most date the monument to between the 10th and 13th centuries, while others believe parts of the cave may have existed much earlier and were adapted into a place of worship during the medieval period.

For centuries, Shakpak Ata served as a spiritual center for Sufi followers. Local legends say the saint after whom the mosque is named possessed healing powers and spent his final years in seclusion, helping people who sought relief from illness and personal hardships. Pilgrims continue to visit the site today.

The Shakpak Ata mosque is one step closer to UNESCO World Heritage status as the country’s nomination is being reviewed at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, South Korea.

No journey through Mangystau’s sacred sites is complete without a visit to Beket Ata, one of Kazakhstan’s most important pilgrimage destinations.

Located in the remote Oglandy area near the Ustyurt Plateau, around 115 kilometers from the village of Senek, the complex is associated with the 18th-century scholar, Sufi teacher and spiritual leader Beket Ata.

Historical records indicate that Beket Ata established four underground mosques during his lifetime across western Kazakhstan. The mosque at Oglandy, where he is buried, is the largest and most visited.

Every year, thousands of pilgrims travel across Kazakhstan and neighboring countries to pray at the shrine, which is regarded as one of the country’s holiest Islamic sites.

Zharkent Mosque

At first glance, the Zharkent Mosque hardly resembles a traditional mosque. Its sweeping tiled roofs, colorful wooden carvings and pagoda-like silhouette are inspired by Chinese architecture, making it the only mosque of its kind in Kazakhstan.

Located in the town of Zharkent near the Chinese border, the mosque was completed in the late 19th century under the direction of Chinese architect Hong Pik, who blended Chinese construction techniques with Central Asian decorative traditions.

The building was constructed entirely from Tian Shan spruce without the use of nails, a remarkable engineering achievement for its time.

Intricately carved wooden beams, vibrant floral motifs and richly decorated ceilings reflect the craftsmanship of artisans representing the region’s diverse ethnic communities, including Kazakhs, Uyghurs, and Dungans, among others.

Today, the mosque houses an architectural and art museum displaying artifacts that showcase the cultural heritage of the peoples who have lived in southeastern Kazakhstan for generations.

Kunanbai Mosque

The Kunanbai Mosque in the Karagandy Region is closely connected to one of the most influential figures in Kazakh history, Kunanbai Oskenbaiuly, the father of the renowned poet and philosopher Abai Kunanbaiuly.

Built between 1849 and 1853 with Kunanbai’s personal funds while he served as the senior administrator of the Karkaraly District, the mosque became one of the first major Islamic religious buildings in northern and central Kazakhstan.

In 1920, its minaret was demolished, and the building was repurposed as a school and later as a warehouse. For decades, it remained closed to worship.

Restoration efforts began in the 1980s, and by 1991 the mosque had regained its original function as a place of worship. Because much of the original structure had been lost, specialists reconstructed the building using archival photographs, historical descriptions and surviving documentation.

Despite the extensive reconstruction, several authentic elements from the 19th-century mosque were preserved. Among the most significant are original wooden beams from the first building, now incorporated into the ceiling of the imam’s room.

Nearby stands the Abai and Kunanbai monument by sculptor Saken Dauletbayev. Rising more than four meters high, it depicts the young Abai returning from a madrasa and meeting his father, a symbolic representation of the transmission of knowledge, family values and spiritual guidance across generations.

World.title: Kazakhstan Strengthens Organ Donation Awareness as 4,739 Patients Await Life-Saving Transplants
World.content:
55869

ASTANA – Kazakhstan is intensifying efforts to raise public awareness of organ donation and improve its transplant system as 4,739 patients, including 126 children, remain on the national transplant waiting list, with transplantation representing the only chance of survival for many of them.

Documentary raises public awareness

A documentary film, “4739,” produced by the Khabar Agency, premiered in Astana on July 21 to highlight the importance of organ transplantation, the work of transplant specialists, and the experiences of patients awaiting donor organs.The title reflects the number of people currently on Kazakhstan’s transplant waiting list. More than 350 patients die each year before receiving a suitable organ. Through the stories of transplant recipients, their families, and medical professionals, the film aims to encourage informed public discussion while respecting different personal and ethical views on organ donation, reported the Prime Minister’s press service.

The documentary will be broadcast on the 24KZ TV channel on July 24 at 7:30 p.m.

Government reaffirms support for transplant medicine

Opening the premiere, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Culture and Information Aida Balayeva said protecting citizens’ lives and health remains a government priority in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s policy of strengthening healthcare and developing high-tech medicine.

She said Kazakhstan has made significant progress in transplant medicine, with domestic specialists performing increasingly complex operations requiring advanced technology and multidisciplinary expertise. The government will continue to develop the national transplant system, strengthen the capacity of medical institutions, and expand public awareness efforts, she added.

Balayeva also wrote on her Facebook account that she has officially registered her consent to posthumous organ donation.

“One person’s decision can give another the opportunity to continue living despite everything. That is why we must discuss this issue not through the prism of fear, but with understanding, responsibility, and deep respect for human life. Human life is the highest value, and every step taken to preserve it can be of enormous, sometimes decisive, significance. Every person awaiting a transplant lives with the hope of a second chance. Preserving that hope is our shared human responsibility,” she wrote.

Transplant activity expands, as waiting list remains high

According to the National Center for Coordination of Transplantation and High-Tech Medical Services, 4,739 patients are currently awaiting organ transplantation, including 4,208 people waiting for kidney transplants, 293 for liver transplants, 208 for heart transplants, and 30 for lung transplants. The waiting list includes 126 children.

Since Kazakhstan established its modern transplant service in 2012, doctors have performed 3,270 organ transplants, including kidney, liver, heart, lung, corneal and pancreas transplant procedures. Overall, 82% of operations have relied on living donors, while 18% have been performed using organs from deceased donors.

Over the past five years, approximately 1,500 organ transplants have been carried out in Kazakhstan, with every fourth operation performed in 2025. Last year alone, doctors completed 310 kidney, liver, heart and lung transplants. This year, the country also performed its first pediatric heart transplant.

Deceased organ donation increases

Health officials reported a significant rise in deceased-donor transplantation. The number of transplant operations using organs from deceased donors increased from 23 in 2024 to 68 in 2025, while the number of actual deceased donors rose from six to 18 during the same period, reported Kazinform.

According to the national donor registry, 16,109 people have formally consented to posthumous organ donation, while 156,174 have officially registered their refusal. Officials noted that one deceased donor can save the lives of up to seven patients, depending on the condition of the donated organs.

Regulatory changes are being considered that would make a person’s officially registered consent for organ donation legally sufficient after death, eliminating the current requirement to obtain additional permission from relatives.

Health officials emphasized that medical staff treating patients do not have access to information about a person’s donor status. Such information is available only to three national transplant coordinators and is disclosed only after brain death has been formally confirmed. Authorities also stressed that hospitals receive no financial incentives for deceased organ donation and that every donation case undergoes strict medical and legal oversight.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan Expand Strategic Partnership Through Trade, Transport and Regional Agreements
World.content:
131969

ALMATY – Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan signed regional and commercial agreements worth more than 80 billion tenge (US$146 million) on July 24 as the two countries advanced cooperation in trade, transport, industry and cross-border development during a series of meetings in Aktau.

The agreements were concluded following the 23rd meeting of the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan Joint Intergovernmental Commission and the inaugural Council of Regional Leaders, co-chaired by Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov.

The leaders reviewed implementation of agreements reached by Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev. They discussed priorities for expanding cooperation in trade, investment, industrial production, transport, regional development and cultural ties.

“Thanks to the joint efforts of our heads of state, multifaceted cooperation between our countries continues to develop dynamically and today serves as a successful example of partnership for the entire Central Asian region,” Bektenov said.

Aripov said the governments remain committed to implementing the tasks set by both presidents during their meetings in Bukhara, Astana and Turkistan this year.

“I am ready to take all necessary measures to fulfill these instructions. I am confident that today’s negotiations will contribute to the further development of trade, investment, industrial, transport, interregional and cultural cooperation,” he said.

Transport and logistics

Transport connectivity featured prominently in the discussions as both countries seek to strengthen regional trade corridors. According to Bektenov, rail freight between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan increased 16% in 2025, reaching 32.3 million tons. The two governments have adopted a joint action plan to increase railway corridor capacity from 35 million to 60 million tons.

The prime ministers also visited the Aktau International Sea Trade Port, Kazakhstan’s largest maritime hub and a key component of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR). Covering 44 hectares, the port can handle nearly 12 million tons of cargo annually and provides year-round connections to the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Caspian region.

According to Bektenov, Kazakhstan completed dredging works at the Kuryk Port in 2025, becoming the first Caspian state to do so. Similar dredging at Aktau is expected to finish by the end of this year, allowing fully loaded vessels to enter the port safely while increasing cargo capacity.

According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy Chairman Yelzhas Otynshiyev, the combined capacity of the Aktau and Kuryk ports now stands at 22 million tons annually.

He highlighted that container transit through Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports along the TITR has increased 3.8 times between 2022 and 2025. To support further growth, Kazakhstan has launched the first phase of a new container hub at Aktau with an annual capacity of 140,000 TEU, which is expected to expand to 240,000 TEU after completion of the second phase in 2027-2028.

The country has also ordered six new container vessels, four scheduled for delivery in 2027 and two in 2028, while modernization continues on the Shalkar-Beyneu and Beyneu-Mangystau railway sections to improve cargo access to Aktau and Kuryk.

Cargo handled through Aktau and Kuryk on behalf of Uzbekistan increased by more than 60% in 2025, supported by favorable tariffs and improved transport infrastructure.

“Our task is to provide Central Asian cargo with fast and reliable access to the markets of the Caucasus, Türkiye and Europe. Kazakhstan is ready to expand transit of Uzbekistan’s export cargo through the ports of Aktau and Kuryk,” Bektenov said.

Trade and investment cooperation

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan continue to deepen economic integration, with bilateral trade reaching $4.8 billion in 2025. During the first five months of 2026, trade increased 37% year-on-year to $2.3 billion.

Bektenov highlighted Kazakhstan’s export potential in metallurgy, mechanical engineering, petrochemicals, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, transport equipment and construction materials, while emphasizing implementation of a $7.8 billion investment and trade roadmap designed to diversify bilateral trade and attract new investment.

Industrial cooperation remains one of the partnership’s fastest-growing areas. The two countries are jointly implementing 80 projects worth more than $1.8 billion. Fifteen projects valued at $227 million have already been launched, creating nearly 5,000 jobs, while six additional projects worth $102 million are under active implementation. Authorities are also developing 59 new initiatives totaling approximately $1.5 billion.

World.title: Kazakh FM Urges More Practical SCO as Global Turbulence Reshapes Regional Priorities
World.content:
144457

ALMATY – The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is increasingly shifting from a platform centered on political dialogue and regional security toward one that places greater emphasis on economic resilience, trade connectivity and practical cooperation, as member states respond to growing geopolitical and supply-chain disruptions.

That transformation was at the center of discussions during the July 24 meeting of the SCO Council of Foreign Ministers in Cholpon-Ata, the Kyrgyz Republic, where Kazakhstan called for stronger coordination on trade security, transport connectivity, climate resilience and water management ahead of the organization’s summit in Bishkek on Sept. 1.

Speaking at the meeting, Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev said that the rapidly changing geopolitical environment is making economic resilience an urgent priority for the region.

“Geopolitical turbulence, increasingly spilling over into the military sphere, is seriously affecting the stability of international trade relations. Today, the security of supply chains is becoming an ever more pressing issue, including for Kazakhstan,” he said.

Kosherbayev cited attacks by unidentified unmanned systems on energy infrastructure and tankers chartered by Kazakhstan to transport oil as an illustration of growing vulnerabilities affecting international logistics. He said that these risks underscore the need for the SCO to make the protection of regional trade routes one of its strategic priorities.

The emphasis on supply-chain security reflects a broader shift in Kazakhstan’s regional diplomacy. As global trade routes face growing disruption from geopolitical tensions and attacks on critical infrastructure, Astana is increasingly framing transport connectivity not only as an economic objective but also as a strategic security issue.

Analysts say Kazakhstan’s priorities reflect broader changes taking place within the SCO itself. According to Manarbek Kabaziyev, deputy chairman of the board of the Foreign Policy Research Institute under Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry, the organization itself is undergoing a broader transformation.

“The SCO is indeed going through a stage of qualitative transformation. While its primary task in the early years was strengthening trust and ensuring regional security, today its agenda has become much broader. The focus now includes trade and economic cooperation, transport and logistics connectivity, digitalization, energy, food security and technological cooperation,” he said.

That assessment closely aligns with Kazakhstan’s own priorities within the organization. Alongside transport security, Kosherbayev called for deeper cooperation on climate adaptation and sustainable water management, reiterating Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations and an SCO Water Issues Analysis Center.

The minister also emphasized that the SCO should continue adapting its institutions to contemporary challenges, reflecting Kazakhstan’s broader push to make regional organizations more responsive to economic and technological change.

For Kazakhstan, Kabaziyev said, the shift toward project-oriented cooperation carries particular strategic significance.

“Kazakhstan’s geographic position and its role as one of Eurasia’s key transit hubs objectively make the country one of the main beneficiaries of projects aimed at developing transport connectivity, digital logistics and regional value chains,” he said.

According to him, whether the SCO succeeds in making that transition will likely become one of the defining questions for the organization over the coming years.

Attention will now shift to the Sept. 1 SCO summit in Bishkek, where the organization’s heads of state are expected to define the bloc’s strategic priorities. The extent to which leaders embrace Kazakhstan’s calls for stronger economic coordination and practical cooperation may offer an early test of whether the SCO is indeed evolving beyond its traditional security agenda.

World.title: Kazakhstan Rises to 53rd in Updated Global Investment Risk and Resilience Index
World.content:
122201

ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 53rd out of 150 countries in the May 2026 Special Edition of the Global Investment Risk and Resilience Index (GIRRI), improving from 70th place in the original 2025 ranking, as the updated index reflects the impact of recent geopolitical and economic developments on global investment risk.

The updated ranking was released by Henley & Partners in cooperation with AlphaGeo and incorporates Country Risk Premium (CRP) data as of April 1, allowing the index to combine long-term structural resilience with real-time market assessments of sovereign risk.

The Global Investment Risk and Resilience Index evaluates countries using two core dimensions: structural resilience, which measures long-term economic, institutional and environmental strengths, and sovereign risk, reflecting exposure to political, financial and external shocks, according to Henley & Partners.

The May 2026 Special Edition does not revise the original methodology or resilience scores. Instead, it serves as a stress test of the existing framework by keeping structural resilience unchanged while updating the risk component with current market data.

According to the report, the revised rankings provide a risk-adjusted view of the global investment environment, showing how geopolitical and economic developments have reshaped investor perceptions.

The report notes that changes in country rankings reflect relative shifts in position compared with other countries rather than absolute improvements or deterioration in risk or resilience. The update is intended to illustrate how the global investment landscape is evolving as markets respond to current geopolitical and economic conditions.
