World.title: Federal government says fuel supply 'solid and secure' as prices climb again
World.content:
The federal government is moving to reassure motorists about Australia's fuel supply as petrol prices rise amid renewed clashes in the five-month-old war in the Middle East.

During the week oil prices crept over $US100 ($143) a barrel for the first time since May.

It follows a fresh escalation in the conflict between the United States and Iran, with US President Donald Trump promising "major military punishment" for Tehran over attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near the Red Sea.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

The expansion of the conflict along with reduced output from the US has prompted warnings from some analysts of "more sustained" price pressure over the months ahead.

Today federal energy minister Chris Bowen said motorists could have confidence in Australia's fuel supplies despite the uncertainty in the Middle East.

"One thing Australians can be certain about is that our fuel supply continues to be solid and secure," he said.

"I can tell you that we have 42 days' worth of petrol, 38 days' worth of diesel, and 32 days' worth of jet fuel.

"All of these figures are more than we had on the day Iran was first bombed, on February 28th."

The federal government's fuel excise cut was halved this month and expires on August 2. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

He said in addition to the 6.2 billion litres of fuel in stock, 51 ships were on the water with 3.1 billion litres locked in for delivery over the next month.

"Obviously, as we've said consistently, we want to see the situation in the Middle East return to normal," Mr Bowen said.

"In the meantime, we'll continue the efforts and the work with our trading partners, with our refiners, to ensure that Australians can have confidence in our fuel supply."

Oil prices jump back over $US100 a barrel The entry of the Houthi rebels into the war between the US and Iran has threatened another vital shipping route through the Middle East.

Mr Bowen gave no indication whether the fuel excise discount due to expire on August 2 would be extended again, but it has previously not been ruled it out.

The cut was halved from 32 cents per litre to 16 cents per litre this month, with the discount to the Heavy Vehicle Road User charge also trimmed.

On Friday NMRA spokesman Peter Khoury said he believed the federal government was keeping the option of extending the excise open and could make an announcement in coming days.

At lunchtime today the national average price of unleaded 91 was $1.88 per litre, with diesel at $2.30 per litre.

Sydney had the lowest average capital city price for unleaded 91 at $1.83, more than 10 cents below the average price per litre in Darwin.

World.title: Trump mixes jokes with barbs at press freedom dinner
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has poked fun at the press during a redo of the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner after a shooting forced the suspension of the original event in April.

The president, whose administration has often been at odds with the press, mostly stuck to the warm and relaxed tenor of the evening, noting that his speech for the original event "was going to be a doozy".

"I was so psyched, I was going to rip people," he said during his hour-long speech.

"Your lives were really in danger the last time … but on the plus side, your careers were saved."

Mr Trump alternated between friendly jokes and pointed criticisms of what he called the "fake news media".

He also could not resist taking cracks at his adversaries in the press and show business, singling out journalists, politicians and celebrities, including Bruce Springsteen and Jane Fonda.

"I know it was not easy finding shoes to go along with your bulletproof vest, which many people didn't want to wear because they'd rather die than look 20 pounds heavier," Mr Trump said.

Donald Trump said his speech had been toned down since the first event. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

At one point he said he was "probably being a little bit oversensitive" with regard to negative press, but said: "I really do think that some of you don't like me."

Press freedom advocates have criticised the Trump administration over lawsuits it has filed against media organisations, restrictions on some journalists' access, and threats of action against broadcasters.

The president has previously rejected the criticism, saying his administration is promoting accountability and addressing bias.

Ahead of his speech, Mr Trump sat through more than an hour of awards presentations, including for journalists who published stories critical of him and his administration in the last year.

Trump sues Murdoch over Epstein birthday greeting report It comes hours after The Wall Street Journal reported on a 50th birthday greeting to Jeffrey Epstein that Donald Trump allegedly sent in 2003.

A team of Washington Post journalists were awarded the Katharine Graham Award for Courage and Accountability for their reporting on a lewd sketch signed by Mr Trump that was included in a compilation of birthday messages for convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The president laughed and threw his hands up in a shrug when it was acknowledged he sued the outlet over the story.

Mr Trump made his first presidential appearances at the event this year after boycotting it during his first term.

"Time goes by, time passes, and you sort of look at life differently," he said of his change of heart.

Mr Trump promised to return next year.

Heightened security

The black-tie gathering of journalists, politicians and administration officials on April 25 was called off after a man tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired a shotgun outside the ballroom where Mr Trump and members of his cabinet were taking their seats.

ABC reporter at Trump dinner when shots rang out The ABC's Americas editor was inside the ballroom when a shooting suspect was stopped by the Secret Service.

In May, Cole Allen pleaded not guilty to a number of charges, including attempting to assassinate the president.

The dinner was rescheduled for July 24 and moved to the smaller Waldorf Astoria.

One of the first messages of the night was defiance in the face of the assault.

"Tonight, our message is this: We are back," outgoing White House Correspondents' Association president Weijia Jiang said.

"We will not be intimidated. We refuse to let an act of violence have the final word."

Mr Trump later said: "We do not yield to political violence … no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that."

Security was tightened for the second event. (AP: Cliff Owen)

The event also honoured the Washington Hilton staff who assisted guests after the attack in April, as well as Secret Service officer Victor Gonzales, who was shot at a security checkpoint outside the ballroom.

Mr Gonzales, who was wearing a protective vest and was the only person wounded that night, is credited with stopping the attack.

The gala has been an annual fixture on Washington's calendar for more than a century. It raises money for journalism scholarships and celebrates press freedoms as guaranteed by the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

It normally features a comedian who pokes fun at the president and the press, but this year's entertainment came from mentalist Oz Pearlman.

At one stage during his speech, Mr Trump ribbed Pearlman, who correctly guessed the name of White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt's unborn baby at the first dinner, for not foreseeing the attack.

"How the hell he didn't see that coming?" Mr Trump asked to laughter.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Two new bird flu cases suspected in SA, including first on a metro beach
World.content:
Two additional suspected cases of H5 bird flu have been detected in South Australia, including one on a metropolitan beach.

A greater crested tern was found near Robe on South Australia's Limestone Coast, while another greater crested tern was found at a beach ramp near the Semaphore Surf Life Saving Club, north-west of Adelaide.

If confirmed, Semaphore will be the first metropolitan case in the state.



SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke said the bird found in Robe was located 4 kilometres from the location where the first Australian seabird confirmed to have the H5 strain of bird flu was found.

"Unfortunately, we are finding that these two cases are in our local [bird] species, so we need to send these tests off now to Geelong for them to have confirmation at that centralised location that they are, or are not, the H5 high strand of this disease," Ms Bourke said.

Previous confirmed cases involved migratory birds from the sub-Antarctic region.

Minister Emily Bourke says the two latest suspected H5 cases in South Australia are in local bird species. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the results from testing at the CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness in Geelong were expected early next week.

"I do understand that these birds were deceased so they may be degraded samples but the CSIRO lab will do everything they can to check the sequencing," Ms Collins said.

"We have no evidence of any transmission in Australia in terms of the H5 bird flu at this point in time. We have no mass mortalities been recorded, we have no bird flu in our poultry or agricultural systems and the risk to human health remains low.

Lab testing is underway on samples from greater crested terns found in Robe and Semaphore, SA. (ABC Goldfields & Esperance: Tara de Landgrafft)

"As soon as we have any results we will make them public. What we’re doing here today is we’re being as up-front with the Australian community at the earliest opportunity, as we have at every occasion with these bird flu incursions."

South Australia's first confirmed case was found in a giant petrel found on the Fleurieu Peninsula, on June 14.

Nationally, there are currently 18 confirmed cases of bird flu in Australia, five of which are in South Australia.

Queensland confirmed its first case of H5 bird flu today, after a dead petrel was found on Moreton Island, east of Brisbane.



The public's vital role in detection

South Australia's latest two suspected H5 cases were found by members of the public.

"These two tests have come about because community members called the hotline, did the things that we've been saying: avoid record and report," Ms Bourke said.

" It's exactly what's happened here: people walking on the beach, people reporting, people recording, and people doing the right thing in South Australia. "

Ms Collins said 8,000 calls had been made nationally to the hotline and through the Australian government's bird flu (Avian influenza) website.



"In terms of the reporting, the recording, and avoiding any dead birds and we have literally done hundreds of tests across the country so we are monitoring this incredibly closely."

Ms Collins said the community was the "first line of defence when it comes to biosecurity".

World.title: Here's what you need to know about Woodside's Federal Court case
World.content:
Questions of ministerial bias, unseen text exchanges, and climate change arithmetic have gone under the microscope in a landmark legal fight over the life of Australia’s biggest gas project.

Federal Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt made international headlines last year when he gave Woodside Energy the green light to keep operating its North West Shelf facilities off Western Australia until 2070.

This week, his approval faced two opponents in Federal Court.

Claims of 'apprehended bias'

The proceedings in Melbourne heard simultaneous challenges from the Friends of Australian Rock Art (FARA) and the Australian Conservation Foundation (ACF).

Their legal grounds thrust at the heart of Mr Watt's decision and the way he approached the 40-year extension.

Lawyers for Murray Watt defended his decision in Federal Court. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

ACF barrister Angus Scott KC told the court an "extraordinary amount of engagement" between Mr Watt's staff and Woodside ensured the company received a workable solution.

He claimed a reasonable observer could interpret the dialogue — revealed in nearly 200 texts and emails traded by the minister's office and the oil and gas giant — as pre-judgement.

Justice Catherine Button later described ACF's suggestion as one of a "chumminess or cosiness between the department and Woodside".

In one text put before the court in written submissions, a government official opened a communication channel with a senior Woodside executive about "environmental law reform".

"Let's wait till [the] current matter is cleared and then we'll move onto the next thing!" the recipient wrote back.

Another sent by a Woodside representative celebrated the end of negotiations with their opposite number.

"Thanks Rachel! We got there!" they said.

ACF CEO and former federal Greens leader Adam Bandt rallied demonstrators outside the Federal Court. (Supplied: ACF)

FARA said Mr Watt's "closed mind" meant he "cherry-picked" the North West Shelf's economic advantages, such as jobs, and neglected counterarguments.

Barrister Sashi Maharaj KC even contended he "copy and pasted" a summary of benefits provided by Woodside consultants into his published reasons.

Minister says he defied Woodside

Mr Watt ultimately attached 48 conditions to the approval, having amended them after Woodside warned his initial proposal would "amount to a refusal".

Woodside barrister Damian Clothier KC said the concessions demonstrated the strength of Woodside's persuasion rather than any bias by the minister, who did not — in any case — need to remain "neutral".

The meaning behind Murujuga's petroglyphs Ahead of UNESCO releasing its final assessment of the area's world-heritage potential, the Burrup's traditional owners tell the stories behind the landmark rock art.

Representing the minister, Stephen Lloyd SC went further, stating it was unlikely Mr Watt was aware of "innocuous" messages sent by his juniors.

He said Mr Watt plainly disagreed with the energy giant on whether industrial emissions were damaging thousands of sacred Indigenous rock carvings in the nearby Murujuga World Heritage Site.

"Woodside's position was that air emissions don't have any impact on the petroglyphs, and the minister didn't accept that — he said that they did," said Mr Lloyd.

" The minister found impacts that Woodside denied, and proposed conditions to mitigate those impacts. "

Browse proposal looms large

Another project off WA's Kimberley region cast a long shadow over the court battle: Woodside's $30 billion proposed expansion into the Browse basin, Australia's largest undeveloped gas reserve.

Mr Scott said the minister was wrong to factor plans for Browse into his North West Shelf decision, given the former is subject to a separate and ongoing approval process.

Woodside hopes to process the gas it would draw from the reserve — enough to power 800,000 homes every year — using its main North West Shelf plant near Karratha.

A company spokesperson said the project would contribute to the region's economic prosperity and energy security while managing environmental concerns.

"Stakeholder feedback has helped shape the project from reducing the infrastructure footprint around environmentally sensitive areas like Scott Reef, to designing additional safeguards to help protect marine life," the spokesperson said.

Protesters wore colourful costumes and held up signs highlighting Browse's proximity to the Scott Reef. (Supplied: ACF)

Only rating a brief mention in court was the unprecedented intervention of United Nations envoy Astrid Puentes Riaño, who made submissions in support of ACF and FARA.

Mr Watt's legal team maintained the minister did not have to account for the North West Shelf's near 4 billion tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions, a position Ms Riaño denigrated as "purely arithmetical" in her own filings.

The special rapporteur said it "did not consider the specific risk and the significant harm that the action would have had, as mandated by international law".

Justice Button has reserved her judgment for a later date.

World.title: NRL LIVE updates: Kikau sets up Burton as Bulldogs strike first against Warriors

World.title: AFL LIVE: Star Hawk and Bomber cop injury blows early at the ’G; Swans off to a dominant start over Giants
World.content:
Gold Coast’s nightmare season has continued, losing to inspired Carlton by 13 points at Marvel Stadium for a ninth-straight defeat.

Trailing by 12 points at the final break, the Suns opened the last quarter with three clutch goals to reclaim the lead.

But the final term followed the script of the first three quarters – Gold Coast start strongly, before the Blues break away late in the term.

George Hewett stepped up with a huge goal, while off-season recruit Will Hayward sealed the 16.14 (110) to 15.7 (97) win for the Blues with five minutes remaining.

Premiership favourites early in the season after a superb start in March, as well as coming off a semi-final appearance last year, the Suns’ campaign has descended into chaos.

The pain of it all: Gold Coast’s Matt Rowell. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Two weeks after coach Damien Hardwick prematurely declared Gold Coast’s season over, this time he might be right.

The Suns have crashed to 7-12 and 14th on the ladder, two games away from a wildcard spot with only four rounds left.

But Carlton, who began the season at 1-8 and dealt with the departure of coach Michael Voss, have jumped to 10th with a 9-10 record to give them a serious chance of featuring in finals.

The Blues’ midfield brigade battered Gold Coast for most of the day, captain Patrick Cripps, Hewett (three goals, 24 disposals), Jagga Smith (31 touches) and Sam Walsh (31) all immense in deciding the result.

The Suns’ stars had their moments, but were never able to sustain it for long enough.

Suns captain Noah Anderson stepped up, slotting a goal of the year contender in the second term when he dodged through traffic and slipped two tackles to finish superbly.

But Anderson’s influence in the second half waned, as his opposing captain – Cripps – went to another level.

Cripps had a colossal 15 clearances from his 30 possessions to go with an important goal in the third quarter.

In his 150th game, veteran Carlton defender Nic Newman had an early finish after hurting his hamstring when wildly attempting to kick a loose ball.

AAP

World.title: Tumultuous week for Tigers ends on a low with sixth straight loss
World.content:
Canberra 56 Wests Tigers 10 SportNRLNRL 2026 Tumultuous week for Tigers ends on a low with sixth straight loss Adrian Proszenko July 25, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

When is it a good time to blood a rookie playmaker? The answer, if you’re Wests Tigers, is to hand the No.7 jersey to a teen after bumping Adam Doueihi to lock, prompting the regular halfback to stand down from playing duties, while the five-eighth’s head appears elsewhere, the team is going through a major form slump and their opponents have their number. Loading Welcome to first grade, Javon Andrews. After a week of turmoil in Tiger town – in other words, a week like most others – long-suffering supporters were looking for a reason to get out of bed on Saturday morning. It’s unfair to expect it to come in the form of Andrews, a 19-year-old thrown in due to a raft of absences.



Few would have thought Doueihi would have been one of them, particularly after earning one of the rarest of wins, on a Tuesday night at the judiciary. But faced with the prospect of wearing the No.13 jersey or none at all, Doueihi chose the latter. It’s unclear where the Lebanese international watched Saturday’s match, which ended in a 56-10 humiliation, or whether he witnessed it at all. He wasn’t at GIO Stadium, and we’ll never know for sure what sort of difference he would have made. But based on what his teammates dished up, it’s likely it would have been negligible. Tigers players wait for a try conversion Getty Images After all the turmoil off the field, attention turned to what the Tigers would produce on it. When big back-rower Ethan Roberts, once an aspiring jockey, crashed over early to hand the visitors the lead, there was a flicker of hope. But it’s the hope that kills you. That’s as good as it got for the Tigers. Jarome Luai threw three passes that missed their mark in the first half-alone, by which time his team had leaked five tries. By that stage, some of the hearty Tigers souls that had made the trip up the Federal Highway had left early for the long commute home.



They were spared watching any more from a frustrated and fractured playing group. Are they on Team Benji? Team Jarome? Team Doueihi? They may be wearing the same colours, but they don’t remotely look like they’re playing for the same team. Under this backdrop, it was difficult for the newbie to leave his mark. Andrews kicked reasonably well and his large frame – he’s already 190cm and 98kg – was too busy making tackles to have the opportunity to bust any. Hopefully he won’t be scarred by what he has just endured. Tigers coach Benji Marshall looks on. Getty Images The Raiders deserve to be more than the footnote to the story. Opposing halfback Ethan Sanders had easily his best game, which included a solo try. It was one of several spectacular long-range efforts, highlighted by fullback Kaeo Weekes finishing another coast-to-coast effort for the second successive match. The Tigers clocked off early. To their credit, despite having the result well within their grasp before half-time, the Raiders didn’t. Daine Laurie, playing against his former club, scored a second-half hat-trick.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Knights marquee man Dylan Brown does ACL, Dylan Lucas also out for season For the Tigers, things could get worse before they get better. Patrick Herbert was placed on report for slamming an opponent’s head into the ground, before seemingly butting his own head against it. The joint-venture outfit started the day as a mathematical possibility of making the play-offs, but after their sixth successive loss, there’s not an abacus on earth that gives them a chance. Next up, it’s Luai against one of his future employers, Parramatta. And if you thought the halves debate was a hot topic last week, strap yourself in for what’s to come. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: McDonald back on the double to cap record-equalling season
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing McDonald back on the double to cap record-equalling season Craig Kerry July 25, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Champion jockey James McDonald was calculating just how much he was in his wife’s good books after Astronomix was part of a winning double at his first meeting back at Randwick on Saturday. McDonald, about to tie 1960s legend George Moore with a record 10th Sydney jockeys’ premiership and eighth straight, had not ridden at home since May 27, and he eased back into action following a month-long break with five rides at the penultimate NSW city meeting of the season. James McDonald winning on Hawker Hall at Randwick on Saturday. Getty Images The John O’Shea and Tom Charlton-trained Astronomix ($3.90), a last-start winner at Canterbury, was McDonald’s second ride back and came with a wide run to wear down Nullarbor Jane by a length in the 1300m benchmark 72 handicap for three-year-olds. “He’s fitter than me, I know that,” McDonald quipped.



“He might be a progressive little horse. Now is his time, he likes the wet ground. He’s no world-beater, but he tries his heart out.” James McDonald. Getty Images The comeback victory was even sweeter given McDonald’s wife, Katelyn, is a part-owner of the horse. First prize plus the BOBS bonus of $38,500 took the total windfall for connections to $121,000. “I think it was BOBS race, too,” he said smiling. “It’s actually a good pay. She’ll be over the moon.”



McDonald later rated Kris Lees-trained Hawker Hall ($6.50) well out front in the 1100m benchmark 88 to beat Istolea Merc by a long head. The brace took him to 90 winners for the NSW metro season, 12 clear of next best Zac Lloyd. Astronomix gave O’Shea and Charlton a double on the day, after Lloyd won on Scintillation. The I Am Invincible filly, a $7.50 chance, raced in third spot before taking over at the 250m mark and winning the two-year-old 1100m handicap by three-quarters of a length from Suasion. Stable representative Jordan O’Shea said the group 3 Quezette Stakes (1100m) at Caulfield on August 15 was a likely second-up start for Scintillation. Alysha Collett was suspended three meetings (August 2-7), reduced from seven, for careless riding on Suasion when shifting in on Iced Fury at the 150m mark. Lees, meanwhile, said he would space Hawker Hall’s runs into the spring after the first-up win.



“He’s going to have to keep stepping up, but he’s certainly up to open company, that listed type level,” Lees said. Widdup excited about new year potential Hawkesbury trainer Brad Widdup labelled the rise of Satono Jasmine through the grades as incredible after she made it four on the trot with a last-to-first win at Randwick. The three-year-old swept to victory in the 1800m benchmark 78 for fillies and mares, beating Horizons by a length and a quarter. Her winning streak started with a Gosford maiden and continued through a Hawkesbury benchmark 68, Warwick Farm fillies and mares benchmark 72 and then a career-best run on Saturday. “I don’t know where it’s coming from,” Widdup said.



“I thought she could win a maiden and maybe a class one, but not many do what she’s doing. “I’ll give her a break. I won’t be charging into the spring now. I’ll probably try and win a couple of races after Christmas and see where that leads to.” Sly Boots on the right ground for Waterhouse-Bott Sly Boots capped a big week for the Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott yard with an overdue win at Randwick on Saturday. The five-year-old, having his sixth start this preparation, was tough late to hold out Perfect Justice by a half neck in the 1800m benchmark 78 handicap for the boys.



It was a first win for Sly Boots since saluting at Randwick in December and came after Waterhouse and Bott won the race to secure the vacant 65-box Leilani Lodge stables on-course at track on Thursday. Bott was relieved to get the win after Sly Boots struggled on heavy ground last start when third after getting a gun run. “His last start was very good, but he just laboured a bit in that ground,” Bott said. “He’s hit a few heavy tracks, he’s had some tough draws and has been caught wide. “Up to 2000 might be as far as he wants it, but he can be really effective at a mile and he’s got a pretty good record here at Randwick.”



Asked if Sly Boots could be a Big Dance horse, Bott said: “Could be. I’m not sure how many more runs we can get this prep to qualify him. That’s probably the hardest part.” The win was part of a double for Rachel King, who also rode Sir Les to victory. Sir Les rewards Carmody for hard yards Sir Les gave Randwick trainer Craig Carmody a satisfying win when he stormed clear in the 1100m benchmark 72 handicap. The three-year-old, named after trainer Les Bridge and comedian Barry Humphreys’ character, Sir Les Patterson, won his first two starts before coming fifth at Rosehill. Carmody, an 11-time group 1 winning jockey, then gave Sir Les a let-up to work on his racing manners firsthand.



The 58-year-old rode him extensively in work to get him to settle better, and it paid off with a three and a half-length win over Benevac. “He likes to go a little bit keen, he’s a bit aggressive, so I did a lot of slower work,” Carmody said. “When he tried to get ahead of me, I’d get him back to virtually a trot, a slow canter, and eventually he would give in to me. So just repetition, day after day, got it through his head that you don’t have to run through the bridle. “All that effort was well worth it.” Carmody said he would spell Sir Les before bringing him back in the late summer, early autumn.



Bittersweet Highway double for Scone trainer Related Article Horse racing Race-by-race preview and tips for Muswellbrook on Sunday Scone trainer Cameron Crockett described it as “bittersweet” when Leovanni ($7) scored back-to-back Highway wins at Randwick on Saturday. The former Annabel and Rob Archibald-trained mare wore down Moon Sweeper as a $20 chance two weeks earlier at Randwick for a breakthrough city win, and this time lead throughout under Alysha Collett for a three-quarter length victory. Crockett paid $40,000 online for Leovanni a year ago but had to carry the load himself after struggling to find owners. That was until she broke through for him at Tamworth, before the Highway double.



“I sold 75 per cent of her before she won her last Highway,” Crockett said. “I thought if I don’t sell her now, she’ll get beat and no one will want her.” Crockett said he will give the four-year-old a freshen up before finding another target.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: She’s the voice that inspires the Diamonds, but she can’t stand hearing herself speak
World.content:
There are few athletes that command a huddle like Kate Moloney.

With fire in her eyes and voice loud, Moloney has for years taken the lead in the seconds before her Melbourne Vixens or Australian Diamonds hit the court in big moments.

Vixen Kate Moloney shows her passion. Getty Images

TV directors quickly picked up on Moloney’s knack for revving up her teams and as such there are several famous videos such as her “throw everything you have” speech before the final minutes of last year’s Super Netball grand final win.

When the Diamonds reach the toughest moments in their quest for gold in Glasgow, you can bet Moloney will be urging her side on.

“I’ve always played off a lot of passion – what I love about netball is that it is a team sport and I get to go out and play with the girls around me,” Moloney said.

“I’m extremely competitive and I guess those sorts of things are how I’m feeling in the moment. There is not much else to it and no planning towards it.”

In many sports, the captain would be the person leading such huddles but when it comes to the Diamonds, skipper Liz Watson is happy to let her long-time teammate and vice-captain Moloney fire away.

“There is full trust within the relationship,” Moloney said.

“We back each other to the end and I think that’s what makes it work.”

Watson is the poise and living, breathing standard for the Diamonds; Moloney is the voice and the passion. The combination of their leadership styles works.

“They are two very different leaders in the best way,” Diamonds mid-courter Jamie Lee Price said.

“Liz definitely leads by her actions. She doesn’t chat too much but says things when she feels like she has to.

“Then she just goes on court and does it and everyone just wants to follow her because she’s so inspiring and has that never-give-up mentality – when she does speak, everyone is like “OK, let’s go”.

Diamonds captain Liz Watson and vice-captain Kate Moloney have different leaderships styles but full trust in each other. Ruby Alexander

“Kate is one of those players, she has so much passion in her voice. I feel like I can hear her from anywhere and it creates a lot of energy.

“I feel like she narrates the game and that allows us all to feed off that energy.”

Watson and Moloney have been playing together since they were teenage stars at City West Falcons in the Victorian Netball League.

They graduated into the Vixens roster and then the starting side playing together in Super Netball titles in 2014 and 2020 until Watson crossed to Sunshine Coast Falcons for the 2024 season.

Watson’s leadership style is based on example and using her voice when it’s most needed.

“It’s probably close to 15 years together and we were in a few state teams as well,” Watson said.

“I try to lead by actions and let them speak louder than words.

Kate Moloney and Liz Watson have been playing together for years. The pair were all smiles after the Vixens won the 2020 grand final. Getty Images

“Because I don’t say it a lot, it probably has a better impact when I do but this group is awesome, there is not a lot of rev-ups or yelling. It’s more a reminder of what we are good at and what we need to stick to.”

Watson added she took on the way previous leaders like Caitlin Bassett and Laura Geitz had fostered a culture where hard work on the court was combined with fun and camaraderie off it.

“The biggest thing I want to do is create the environment where it is fun and we work hard because it is the memories and the moments that you remember,” Watson said.

While teammates and fans alike love to hear Moloney’s final words, the player herself often has no ideas what she has said and cannot stand to hear it back should she come across a video of herself post game.

“If I ever saw one coming up, I would turn it off straight away, I hate hearing myself speak,” Moloney said.

“It makes me cringe a little bit, usually I can’t remember what I said, so I like to keep it that way.”

World.title: NRL LIVE updates: Kikau sets up Burton as Bulldogs strike first against Warriors
World.content:
A Bulldogs penalty turns into a Bulldogs blunder, as Matt Burton fails to find touch thanks to a diving effort over the sideline by Alofiana Khan-Pereira, who bats the ball infield.

The Warriors regain possession and go on the attack in the Bulldogs’ half, but Taine Tuaupiki spills the ball while attempting a pass and Canterbury are let off the hook.

The Dogs then have more success with a bomb in the next set, Dallin Watene-Zelezniak leaping high but unable to bring the ball down cleanly and Viliame Kikau grabs it for Canterbury.

A few tackles later Kikau produces his second offload of the game, and this one is a beauty – unleashing Matt Burton in space for the game’s opening try.

Bulldogs 6, Warriors 0 after six minutes

World.title: AFL LIVE: Star Hawk and Bomber cop injury blows early at the ’G; Swans off to a dominant start over Giants
World.content:
Gold Coast’s nightmare season has continued, losing to inspired Carlton by 13 points at Marvel Stadium for a ninth-straight defeat.

Trailing by 12 points at the final break, the Suns opened the last quarter with three clutch goals to reclaim the lead.

But the final term followed the script of the first three quarters – Gold Coast start strongly, before the Blues break away late in the term.

George Hewett stepped up with a huge goal, while off-season recruit Will Hayward sealed the 16.14 (110) to 15.7 (97) win for the Blues with five minutes remaining.

Premiership favourites early in the season after a superb start in March, as well as coming off a semi-final appearance last year, the Suns’ campaign has descended into chaos.

The pain of it all: Gold Coast’s Matt Rowell. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Two weeks after coach Damien Hardwick prematurely declared Gold Coast’s season over, this time he might be right.

The Suns have crashed to 7-12 and 14th on the ladder, two games away from a wildcard spot with only four rounds left.

But Carlton, who began the season at 1-8 and dealt with the departure of coach Michael Voss, have jumped to 10th with a 9-10 record to give them a serious chance of featuring in finals.

The Blues’ midfield brigade battered Gold Coast for most of the day, captain Patrick Cripps, Hewett (three goals, 24 disposals), Jagga Smith (31 touches) and Sam Walsh (31) all immense in deciding the result.

The Suns’ stars had their moments, but were never able to sustain it for long enough.

Suns captain Noah Anderson stepped up, slotting a goal of the year contender in the second term when he dodged through traffic and slipped two tackles to finish superbly.

But Anderson’s influence in the second half waned, as his opposing captain – Cripps – went to another level.

Cripps had a colossal 15 clearances from his 30 possessions to go with an important goal in the third quarter.

In his 150th game, veteran Carlton defender Nic Newman had an early finish after hurting his hamstring when wildly attempting to kick a loose ball.

AAP

World.title: Tumultuous week for Tigers ends on a low with sixth straight loss
World.content:
Canberra 56 Wests Tigers 10 SportNRLNRL 2026 Tumultuous week for Tigers ends on a low with sixth straight loss Adrian Proszenko July 25, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

When is it a good time to blood a rookie playmaker? The answer, if you’re Wests Tigers, is to hand the No.7 jersey to a teen after bumping Adam Doueihi to lock, prompting the regular halfback to stand down from playing duties, while the five-eighth’s head appears elsewhere, the team is going through a major form slump and their opponents have their number. Loading Welcome to first grade, Javon Andrews. After a week of turmoil in Tiger town – in other words, a week like most others – long-suffering supporters were looking for a reason to get out of bed on Saturday morning. It’s unfair to expect it to come in the form of Andrews, a 19-year-old thrown in due to a raft of absences.



Few would have thought Doueihi would have been one of them, particularly after earning one of the rarest of wins, on a Tuesday night at the judiciary. But faced with the prospect of wearing the No.13 jersey or none at all, Doueihi chose the latter. It’s unclear where the Lebanese international watched Saturday’s match, which ended in a 56-10 humiliation, or whether he witnessed it at all. He wasn’t at GIO Stadium, and we’ll never know for sure what sort of difference he would have made. But based on what his teammates dished up, it’s likely it would have been negligible. Tigers players wait for a try conversion Getty Images After all the turmoil off the field, attention turned to what the Tigers would produce on it. When big back-rower Ethan Roberts, once an aspiring jockey, crashed over early to hand the visitors the lead, there was a flicker of hope. But it’s the hope that kills you. That’s as good as it got for the Tigers. Jarome Luai threw three passes that missed their mark in the first half-alone, by which time his team had leaked five tries. By that stage, some of the hearty Tigers souls that had made the trip up the Federal Highway had left early for the long commute home.



They were spared watching any more from a frustrated and fractured playing group. Are they on Team Benji? Team Jarome? Team Doueihi? They may be wearing the same colours, but they don’t remotely look like they’re playing for the same team. Under this backdrop, it was difficult for the newbie to leave his mark. Andrews kicked reasonably well and his large frame – he’s already 190cm and 98kg – was too busy making tackles to have the opportunity to bust any. Hopefully he won’t be scarred by what he has just endured. Tigers coach Benji Marshall looks on. Getty Images The Raiders deserve to be more than the footnote to the story. Opposing halfback Ethan Sanders had easily his best game, which included a solo try. It was one of several spectacular long-range efforts, highlighted by fullback Kaeo Weekes finishing another coast-to-coast effort for the second successive match. The Tigers clocked off early. To their credit, despite having the result well within their grasp before half-time, the Raiders didn’t. Daine Laurie, playing against his former club, scored a second-half hat-trick.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Knights marquee man Dylan Brown does ACL, Dylan Lucas also out for season For the Tigers, things could get worse before they get better. Patrick Herbert was placed on report for slamming an opponent’s head into the ground, before seemingly butting his own head against it. The joint-venture outfit started the day as a mathematical possibility of making the play-offs, but after their sixth successive loss, there’s not an abacus on earth that gives them a chance. Next up, it’s Luai against one of his future employers, Parramatta. And if you thought the halves debate was a hot topic last week, strap yourself in for what’s to come. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: McDonald back on the double to cap record-equalling season
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing McDonald back on the double to cap record-equalling season Craig Kerry July 25, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Champion jockey James McDonald was calculating just how much he was in his wife’s good books after Astronomix was part of a winning double at his first meeting back at Randwick on Saturday. McDonald, about to tie 1960s legend George Moore with a record 10th Sydney jockeys’ premiership and eighth straight, had not ridden at home since May 27, and he eased back into action following a month-long break with five rides at the penultimate NSW city meeting of the season. James McDonald winning on Hawker Hall at Randwick on Saturday. Getty Images The John O’Shea and Tom Charlton-trained Astronomix ($3.90), a last-start winner at Canterbury, was McDonald’s second ride back and came with a wide run to wear down Nullarbor Jane by a length in the 1300m benchmark 72 handicap for three-year-olds. “He’s fitter than me, I know that,” McDonald quipped.



“He might be a progressive little horse. Now is his time, he likes the wet ground. He’s no world-beater, but he tries his heart out.” James McDonald. Getty Images The comeback victory was even sweeter given McDonald’s wife, Katelyn, is a part-owner of the horse. First prize plus the BOBS bonus of $38,500 took the total windfall for connections to $121,000. “I think it was BOBS race, too,” he said smiling. “It’s actually a good pay. She’ll be over the moon.”



McDonald later rated Kris Lees-trained Hawker Hall ($6.50) well out front in the 1100m benchmark 88 to beat Istolea Merc by a long head. The brace took him to 90 winners for the NSW metro season, 12 clear of next best Zac Lloyd. Astronomix gave O’Shea and Charlton a double on the day, after Lloyd won on Scintillation. The I Am Invincible filly, a $7.50 chance, raced in third spot before taking over at the 250m mark and winning the two-year-old 1100m handicap by three-quarters of a length from Suasion. Stable representative Jordan O’Shea said the group 3 Quezette Stakes (1100m) at Caulfield on August 15 was a likely second-up start for Scintillation. Alysha Collett was suspended three meetings (August 2-7), reduced from seven, for careless riding on Suasion when shifting in on Iced Fury at the 150m mark. Lees, meanwhile, said he would space Hawker Hall’s runs into the spring after the first-up win.



“He’s going to have to keep stepping up, but he’s certainly up to open company, that listed type level,” Lees said. Widdup excited about new year potential Hawkesbury trainer Brad Widdup labelled the rise of Satono Jasmine through the grades as incredible after she made it four on the trot with a last-to-first win at Randwick. The three-year-old swept to victory in the 1800m benchmark 78 for fillies and mares, beating Horizons by a length and a quarter. Her winning streak started with a Gosford maiden and continued through a Hawkesbury benchmark 68, Warwick Farm fillies and mares benchmark 72 and then a career-best run on Saturday. “I don’t know where it’s coming from,” Widdup said.



“I thought she could win a maiden and maybe a class one, but not many do what she’s doing. “I’ll give her a break. I won’t be charging into the spring now. I’ll probably try and win a couple of races after Christmas and see where that leads to.” Sly Boots on the right ground for Waterhouse-Bott Sly Boots capped a big week for the Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott yard with an overdue win at Randwick on Saturday. The five-year-old, having his sixth start this preparation, was tough late to hold out Perfect Justice by a half neck in the 1800m benchmark 78 handicap for the boys.



It was a first win for Sly Boots since saluting at Randwick in December and came after Waterhouse and Bott won the race to secure the vacant 65-box Leilani Lodge stables on-course at track on Thursday. Bott was relieved to get the win after Sly Boots struggled on heavy ground last start when third after getting a gun run. “His last start was very good, but he just laboured a bit in that ground,” Bott said. “He’s hit a few heavy tracks, he’s had some tough draws and has been caught wide. “Up to 2000 might be as far as he wants it, but he can be really effective at a mile and he’s got a pretty good record here at Randwick.”



Asked if Sly Boots could be a Big Dance horse, Bott said: “Could be. I’m not sure how many more runs we can get this prep to qualify him. That’s probably the hardest part.” The win was part of a double for Rachel King, who also rode Sir Les to victory. Sir Les rewards Carmody for hard yards Sir Les gave Randwick trainer Craig Carmody a satisfying win when he stormed clear in the 1100m benchmark 72 handicap. The three-year-old, named after trainer Les Bridge and comedian Barry Humphreys’ character, Sir Les Patterson, won his first two starts before coming fifth at Rosehill. Carmody, an 11-time group 1 winning jockey, then gave Sir Les a let-up to work on his racing manners firsthand.



The 58-year-old rode him extensively in work to get him to settle better, and it paid off with a three and a half-length win over Benevac. “He likes to go a little bit keen, he’s a bit aggressive, so I did a lot of slower work,” Carmody said. “When he tried to get ahead of me, I’d get him back to virtually a trot, a slow canter, and eventually he would give in to me. So just repetition, day after day, got it through his head that you don’t have to run through the bridle. “All that effort was well worth it.” Carmody said he would spell Sir Les before bringing him back in the late summer, early autumn.



Bittersweet Highway double for Scone trainer Related Article Horse racing Race-by-race preview and tips for Muswellbrook on Sunday Scone trainer Cameron Crockett described it as “bittersweet” when Leovanni ($7) scored back-to-back Highway wins at Randwick on Saturday. The former Annabel and Rob Archibald-trained mare wore down Moon Sweeper as a $20 chance two weeks earlier at Randwick for a breakthrough city win, and this time lead throughout under Alysha Collett for a three-quarter length victory. Crockett paid $40,000 online for Leovanni a year ago but had to carry the load himself after struggling to find owners. That was until she broke through for him at Tamworth, before the Highway double.



“I sold 75 per cent of her before she won her last Highway,” Crockett said. “I thought if I don’t sell her now, she’ll get beat and no one will want her.” Crockett said he will give the four-year-old a freshen up before finding another target.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: She’s the voice that inspires the Diamonds, but she can’t stand hearing herself speak
World.content:
There are few athletes that command a huddle like Kate Moloney.

With fire in her eyes and voice loud, Moloney has for years taken the lead in the seconds before her Melbourne Vixens or Australian Diamonds hit the court in big moments.

Vixen Kate Moloney shows her passion. Getty Images

TV directors quickly picked up on Moloney’s knack for revving up her teams and as such there are several famous videos such as her “throw everything you have” speech before the final minutes of last year’s Super Netball grand final win.

When the Diamonds reach the toughest moments in their quest for gold in Glasgow, you can bet Moloney will be urging her side on.

“I’ve always played off a lot of passion – what I love about netball is that it is a team sport and I get to go out and play with the girls around me,” Moloney said.

“I’m extremely competitive and I guess those sorts of things are how I’m feeling in the moment. There is not much else to it and no planning towards it.”

In many sports, the captain would be the person leading such huddles but when it comes to the Diamonds, skipper Liz Watson is happy to let her long-time teammate and vice-captain Moloney fire away.

“There is full trust within the relationship,” Moloney said.

“We back each other to the end and I think that’s what makes it work.”

Watson is the poise and living, breathing standard for the Diamonds; Moloney is the voice and the passion. The combination of their leadership styles works.

“They are two very different leaders in the best way,” Diamonds mid-courter Jamie Lee Price said.

“Liz definitely leads by her actions. She doesn’t chat too much but says things when she feels like she has to.

“Then she just goes on court and does it and everyone just wants to follow her because she’s so inspiring and has that never-give-up mentality – when she does speak, everyone is like “OK, let’s go”.

Diamonds captain Liz Watson and vice-captain Kate Moloney have different leaderships styles but full trust in each other. Ruby Alexander

“Kate is one of those players, she has so much passion in her voice. I feel like I can hear her from anywhere and it creates a lot of energy.

“I feel like she narrates the game and that allows us all to feed off that energy.”

Watson and Moloney have been playing together since they were teenage stars at City West Falcons in the Victorian Netball League.

They graduated into the Vixens roster and then the starting side playing together in Super Netball titles in 2014 and 2020 until Watson crossed to Sunshine Coast Falcons for the 2024 season.

Watson’s leadership style is based on example and using her voice when it’s most needed.

“It’s probably close to 15 years together and we were in a few state teams as well,” Watson said.

“I try to lead by actions and let them speak louder than words.

Kate Moloney and Liz Watson have been playing together for years. The pair were all smiles after the Vixens won the 2020 grand final. Getty Images

“Because I don’t say it a lot, it probably has a better impact when I do but this group is awesome, there is not a lot of rev-ups or yelling. It’s more a reminder of what we are good at and what we need to stick to.”

Watson added she took on the way previous leaders like Caitlin Bassett and Laura Geitz had fostered a culture where hard work on the court was combined with fun and camaraderie off it.

“The biggest thing I want to do is create the environment where it is fun and we work hard because it is the memories and the moments that you remember,” Watson said.

While teammates and fans alike love to hear Moloney’s final words, the player herself often has no ideas what she has said and cannot stand to hear it back should she come across a video of herself post game.

“If I ever saw one coming up, I would turn it off straight away, I hate hearing myself speak,” Moloney said.

“It makes me cringe a little bit, usually I can’t remember what I said, so I like to keep it that way.”

World.title: Questions asked after monsoon-like rains sweep Wellington
World.content:
Questions are being raised about the cause of flooding in parts of the capital.

Wellington residents reported torrents surging down Tinakori Road in Thorndon on Saturday morning and rising around parked cars, with some joking a boat or kayak lane was needed on the busy street.

MetService issued a Severe Thunderstorm Warning for Wellington for the morning, including for torrential rain, after thunderstorms were detected near the city and airport, moving east-northeast. The formal alert was extended during the morning, before later being lifted.

Wellingtonian Rebekah Ward described watching floodwaters rising towards the doors of shops in Tinakori Road, while having breakfast there.

She said the "river" of water rose to the bottom of parked cars and even knocked over a scooter, prompting fears her own vehicle could be swept away.

The timing of the downpour was an "ironic" reminder of the monsoon she would soon experience on a trip to India, Ward said.

"There were cars parked along Tinakori Road and the water was getting higher and higher and higher... and I could see that the water was getting up to the level of the bottom of the car door, and I was thinking 'oh gosh, am I going to have a car when this is finished?'

MetService meteorologist Paris Marshall said multiple reports and observations of hail and intense rainfall were logged across the capital on Saturday morning as the storm moved east toward Lower Hutt.

The intensity was at a level where flash flooding around streams, gullies and urban areas were possible, and instruments recorded 40 millimetres of rain in half an hour at MetService's Kelburn station, near Tinakori Road, Marshall said.

Fire and Emergency NZ said it had no weather-related callouts from the downpours.

Responding to commentary on social media, Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty said three-water provider Tiaki Wai should investigate what went wrong, adding that the area had not flooded significantly during heavy rain events earlier in the year.

Tiaki Wai was approached for comment.

However, Tiaki Wai did issue an alert that heavy rain had lead to a discharge of fully treated wastewater into the Waiwhetū Stream, in Lower Hutt, which empties into Wellington Harbour.

This could make the water discharge appear cloudy or murky or mean it has an odour, they warned, and all recreational water users should follow Land Air Water Aotearoa (LAWA) advice and stay out of the stream the next two to three days.

The LAWA website had all swimming spots on the north and east of Wellington Harbour as well as Oriental Bay marked as unsuitable for swimming, on Saturday.

Snowfall warnings issued for high parts of the country, strong wind watch for Auckland

Elsewhere in the country, MetService issued snowfall warnings for the Desert Road (SH1) and Lewis Pass (SH7), while strong southwest winds prompted a yellow Strong Wind Watch for Auckland, through till 7pm Saturday.

Snow was expected to settle on Desert Road from late Saturday afternoon and into the evening, with 2 to 4cm possible near the summit and light flurries down to 800m.

World.title: How learning te reo Māori in her 70's transformed one Pākehā grandmother's view of Aotearoa
World.content:
"Open your heart."

Those are the kupu one Pākehā grandmother hopes will encourage more New Zealanders to take their first step toward te reo Māori and te ao Māori.

Gael Finlayson-Davis, grandmother of six and great-grandmother of two, now in her 70s, became an unexpected symbol of this year's Matariki celebrations after speaking through tears at the national hautapu ceremony at Takaparawhau.

Her emotional kōrero, in which she described learning te reo Māori as part of her hope for "a better future for our country", resonated with thousands.

Although learning te reo is something she wishes she had embraced decades earlier, she hopes her story shows it is never too late.

"If I can do it in my 70s, anyone can," she told RNZ.

"Open your heart. Just listen and learn. There is so much generosity in the Māori community that if you take a step forward, you will be met."

Even learning basic greetings and taking the time to pronounce Māori place names correctly, she believes, is an act of respect.

"You would do that in countries overseas, so why would you not try in your own country?"

Finlayson-Davis was a probation officer and later a clinical psychologist. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Raised on a farm near Dargaville, Finlayson-Davis describes her childhood as a typical rural upbringing of the 1950s and 60s, surrounded by whānau and generations living side by side.

Although there were few Māori at her school, one experience stayed with her for decades.

"I remember going on a marae visit when I was about 12, and I remember just being blown away and thinking there's something here that I feel very drawn to. I didn't understand it and I didn't know how to access it, but it was an important experience in my young life."

That feeling never disappeared.

Throughout her career as a probation officer and later as a clinical psychologist, she worked alongside many Māori. Witnessing the inequities many of her clients faced only deepened her desire to better understand te ao Māori, she said.

"I saw so many young Māori offenders who'd had a very tough time in their lives, often through children's homes and borstal. It seemed like things could have been very different for them if they'd had different opportunities, and that really affected me."

She enrolled in her first te reo Māori class while in her 30s, but raising two daughters, building a career and family life meant the language had to take a back seat.

Only after retiring did she finally return to learning through Selwyn Community Education.

"It's been really hard. I'm not a natural linguist and I will never be fluent, but I've learnt such a lot, such a tremendous amount. As a person very interested in language, written language and meaning, I love the whakataukī and the waiata and the significance for different iwi, so it has unlocked something important for me as a Pākehā that I would not have had otherwise."

RNZ / Richard Tindiller

Learning te reo became a way of understanding Aotearoa differently, she said.

"Though it will never be my language or my culture, by learning the reo you unlock so much about the culture that you're unaware of if you don't speak the reo."

"Māori have such a beautiful way of honouring the natural world, the whenua, the awa and the moana. I just really appreciate all of that."

One of the greatest lessons, she said, was recognising that her experience of learning te reo as a Pākehā is fundamentally different from the experience of Māori reclaiming their own language.

"I'm very aware that for a Pākehā to learn te reo and for a Māori to learn te reo, they're two extremely different experiences."

"The anguish of Māori who are having to reclaim their own language rather than being brought up with it and being fluent in it... I feel very humbled by the effort that that takes and the emotional toll it takes."

"Whereas for me it's quite different. I come with curiosity and an openness, but I don't have that emotional anguish that I'm reclaiming something I should never have lost."

She said learning more about Aotearoa's history had also been confronting.

"Yes, it is confronting. It is. And it's confronting in a way that needs to be experienced."

While Finlayson-Davis said while Aotearoa has come a long way, she believes there is still work to do.

"I have been very disturbed by recent attempts to remove the reo, and aspects of Māori representation on councils, and I find that disheartening... we've struggled hard to get to this point, which is some way, but to see that being dismantled has been heartbreaking actually.

"Clearly there are people who feel antagonistic towards Māori and I don't really understand it, because we have a partnership, and to honour that would make us very strong.

"We could do better than we're doing at the moment."

Aucklander Gael Finlayson-Davis was one of the many Pākehā New Zealanders watching this year's Matariki hautapu ceremony at Bastion Point - she said it was a beautiful and emotional experience. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

She said too often people viewed Māori success as coming at someone else's expense.

"People seem to think that if Māori thrive, then Pākehā will suffer."

"No. Māori don't want to make a country that's better just for Māori. They want to make a country that's better for everyone. That would be taking care of climate and whenua and waterways and people, so everyone would thrive."

She points to the way marae respond during times of crisis as an example of the country Aotearoa could be.

"We only need to look at what happens in a crisis, and marae open and manaakitanga is extended to anyone who turns up. That's a strength in our community."

"We could be so much better with both Pākehā and Māori working collaboratively rather than in some sort of contest, as if [when] someone gets something it's taking away from someone else. No. We're adding to it for everyone."

Finlayson-Davis said she is not alone in this way of thinking, and said there are many others like her embracing Māori culture. She attends a waiata Māori kaupapa every Monday, where she says up to 20 Pākehā wāhine attend each week.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/586724/growing-numbers-of-pakeha-seeking-to-understand-te-tiriti-o-waitangi

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-ao-maori/532750/the-pakeha-project-a-tangata-tiriti-led-push-for-tino-rangatiratanga

"I don't consider myself unusual in thinking that there are many Pākehā who are well disposed towards Māori being fully represented and acknowledged within our nation in ways that are appropriate to them, and that seems to me that could make us a special country."

As a grandmother and great-grandmother, she said she feels hopeful seeing younger generations learning te reo Māori, tikanga and waiata from their earliest years at school.

World.title: ACT wants hunters in charge of game animals on conservation land, not DOC
World.content:
The ACT party wants to give hunters a "real stake in managing and looking after our conservation estate".

The party wants to transfer the responsibility for game animals on conservation land from the Department of Conservation (DOC) to the Game Animal Council.

ACT's spokesperson for conservation, Cameron Luxton, said the party's policy for hunters is about recognising them as the "conservationists they are".

The party would also recognise game animal and game-bird species as "natural resources to be sustainably managed" in legislation, and designate certain game herds, such as Stewart Island whitetail deer, as "Herds of Special Interest".

The party would reward hunters for verified conservation outcomes, improve hunting access to public land and protect lawful hunting by creating infringement offences for interfering with hunts. Interference could include the use of drones and helicopters.

ACT deputy leader Nicole McKee announced the policy at the Hunting & Wildlife Expo on the weekend.

Speaking to RNZ, Luxton said giving hunters a "real voice" in managing the conservation estate was "well overdue".

He explained the Game Animal Council was established in 2013, with the purpose of being a voice for hunters and to be involved in decisions around game animals.

But ACT wants the council to be empowered beyond just consultation, and to be funded by the money currently available to DOC for managing these animals.

"It's time government stopped getting in hunters' way and started trusting them with the responsibility they've earned."

Luxton said that DOC could not manage the country's estate alone, adding that hunting groups were already providing hundreds of hours towards conservation efforts, "looking after tracks, maintenance on huts, and importantly predator control".

He said introduced species became pests when unmanaged, but also held deep value to New Zealanders, be it "cultural value, historic value, and even meat value for the table".

"Any virtue taken too far becomes a vice, but managing our valued species is incredibly important."

He used deer that were already in the conservation estate as an example, and the ability for hunters to manage them in a way that made sense for communities that utilised them, but also for the environment they lived in.

"Hunters aren't out there trying to do damage to the environment.

World.title: Christchurch landlords ordered to pay $400 for broken water feature
World.content:
When Shuo Chang and Min Wu moved into their rental, they expected to enjoy the view of two water features outside their window.

Instead, they were "denied the pleasure" of one water feature and had to look out at a giant urn-like feature that was bone dry because their landlords could not get it to work.

Now Christchurch landlords Lisa Smart and Jeremy Smart, as trustees of the Smart Family Trust, must pay Chang and Wu $400 in compensation for the non-working feature after the tenants took their case to the Tenancy Tribunal.

Chang told Open Justice that the case was never just about a fountain.

"We moved into a home with existing defects, spent two years reporting recurring maintenance problems, and then faced claims seeking to make us pay for the property's wear and repair costs," Chang claimed.

"When we reported water ingress, it was not treated as urgent; after we left, the same issue became the basis of claims totalling $14,000. Those claims were dismissed, but we left the tribunal feeling that we had not been heard on equal terms."

He said both he and the landlords were appealing the decision.

Both the tenants and landlords had applied to the tribunal regarding several issues during the now-ended two-year tenancy.

The tenants sought compensation and exemplary damages for various alleged breaches of the landlords' obligations and repayment of the bond, while the landlords sought compensation for the tenants' alleged failure to allow proper access to the premises and for loss and expense relating to their attendance at the hearing.

Tribunal adjudicator Ross Armstrong said in his recently released decision that there were two water features in the garden of the property.

When the tenancy began, one worked and one did not.

The one that did not work was black and shaped like an urn. When filled with water and working, the water overflowed and cascaded down its exterior, where it was collected and recirculated.

The landlords were unable to get it to work during the tenancy.

The tenants told the tribunal the property manager had told them before the tenancy began that both water features worked.

"They say that they have been denied the pleasure of looking out the kitchen window and seeing the water spilling out of the urn and running down its surface," Armstrong said.

He accepted the tenants were entitled to have two working water features, and as they were part of the premises, the landlords were required to provide and maintain them in a reasonable state of repair.

"From my assessment of the messages relating to the water feature, I accept that the tenants wanted it to work. I also accept that they would have taken pleasure from seeing it working when they were looking out the kitchen window or when they were out enjoying the garden.

"In my view, I must assess the value of the loss of a working water feature based on how it would affect the average person. That is a person who is not indifferent to it or one who is especially enamoured by it.

"It is a small part of what comprises the amenity and enjoyment of the premises, but some compensation is warranted."

He ruled $400 was appropriate.

The tenants also applied for compensation for claims regarding flickering lights, a heat pump that they said was faulty, an alleged mice infestation, a broken garage door, a leak in the ensuite, a breach of quiet enjoyment and having to do garden work they deemed "forced labour".

In his decision, Armstrong said there was a lack of evidence to support those claims and they could not be proved.

Landlord's claims also dismissed

The landlords applied for compensation regarding the ensuite leak, claiming the tenants prevented them from completing repairs until after they moved out.

The tenants notified the landlord of the leak and insisted that only the landlords' qualified contractor could attend to investigate the situation and limited the visit to 30 minutes.

The landlords' builder attended and subsequently reported that there was unlikely to be a leak, and if there was, there was no urgency to deal with it. The landlords left it until after the tenants had vacated.

They then fixed the problem, including regrouting the shower and ensuite floor with waterproof grout.

The landlords claimed $4000 for the cost of the work and $10,000 in lost rent, saying the tenants had delayed the work by asserting they would not allow it to be done while they were living in the property.

Armstrong dismissed the claim, finding that the tenants had correctly reported the apparent leak and that the landlords had decided to leave the work until after the tenancy ended because it was considered non-urgent.

The landlords also claimed losses and expenses arising from the litigation, but the claim was denied.

Armstrong also ordered the tenants' $4000 bond be refunded.

It was not the first time this tenancy had ended up before the tribunal. In early 2025, the landlords claimed compensation for damage to a kitchen worktop and a contribution towards the cost of an electrician replacing lights.

The tenants claimed compensation for interference with their quiet enjoyment and for a breach of the landlords' maintenance obligations.

The tenants' claims included allegations that the lights in the premises flickered and at times failed to work altogether, and that a water feature did not function, issues that were also raised in the latest application.

At the time, all claims were dismissed.

Armstrong was able to consider the claims regarding the faulty lights and non-working water feature but only for the period ending with the previous hearing on 27 January, 2025.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Civil Defence website crash during tsunami alert due to third-party problems - minister
World.content:
The Emergency Management Minister has been told problems with third party services crashed the Civil Defence website during a tsunami alert.

And work is underway to speed up an emergency map system that was too slow.

The website went down during last week's Fiordland earthquake and tsunami event.

Mark Mitchell met with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) on Tuesday.

He said it told him it had extensively strength-tested the website over the last year.

"But issues with third party services led to Thursday's outage."

This was an "unfortunate combination" of a problem with the firewall - that has since been fixed - and a global outage affecting the software controlling the failover to NEMA's backup site.

NEMA was working with the third party responsible for the failover software and had put in place manual processes meantime to function in an emergency.

"I have instructed NEMA officials to provide me with regular reporting as permanent fixes are progressed," Mitchell said in a statement.

A second piece of emergency tech also failed to perform as it should, both in the tsunami alert and in the earlier Wairoa evacuation alert, when the new emergency mobile alert map did not update as quickly as it should.

"The current feed is proving too slow for live alerts, and NEMA is now redesigning how the map handles the data behind the scenes so it can refresh more regularly," Mitchell told RNZ.

Text alerts went to residents in both events, and the map is mostly for media or friends and family outside the area to know where alerts apply to.

It was still in the testing phase. "These recent events have been valuable in helping NEMA to identify improvements," the minister said.

World.title: Live: Hawks avalanche overwhelms Dons as Swans dominate listless Giants
World.content:
Jarman Impey picked up an equal game-high 18 disposals in the first half against Essendon. (Getty Images)

Sam Durham almost misses his boot with a set shot from 20m out on a slight angle, and that pretty much sums up Essendon's half of football.

Durham's miss is at least the fourth gettable shot on goal that the Dons have fluffed, and it's why they find themselves in a 45-point hole at the half.

The competitive first quarter feels like a distant memory right now after Hawthorn piled on 6.3 to 0.2 for the quarter.

They've done it by getting right on top in the clinches. The Hawks lead the clearance count 19-13 and lead the inside 50s 30-22.

Jai Newcombe has 18 disposals, six score involvements and three clearances and has looked like a man against boys at times, although this is probably true given how young Essendon's mids are sans Merrett and Durham.

Newcombe and Jarman Impey lead all players with 18 disposals, while Essendon's high man is Jacob Farrow with 12 touches.

Cam Mackenzie has also put together a really strong half of footy with 12 touches, five score involvements and three clearances.

Might Zach Merrett have been a Hawk right now if Mackenzie was thrown in that deal?

Hawthorn well on its way to yet another percentage-boosting win.

Essendon well on its way to a result that is good for the No.1 pick superfund.

World.title: 'Blight on the sport': Fight cancelled on Tszyu card after weigh-in
World.content:
Luckless Australian boxer Liam Wilson has been dealt another cruel blow, with his scheduled world title eliminator against Stephen Fulton cancelled after the American failed to make weight.

In farcical scenes, Fulton hit the scales at almost 63.5kg on Saturday, almost 4.5kg more than the two-division world champion was originally supposed to fight Wilson at in Sydney.

Fulton and Wilson were supposed to square off at the super-featherweight of 59kg before officials on Friday raised the weight to 60.3kg for the feature bout on the blockbuster Tim Tszyu-Errol Spence Jr card.

Wilson had happily agreed to the late change, saying he was desperate to earn another world title shot with a victory over the former unified super-bantamweight world champion and ex-WBC featherweight belt holder.

But now the American's team is being accused of never truly intending to fight on Sunday.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"This feels like a stitch-up," Wilson's manager and Tszyu's ex-agent Glenn Jennings said.

"If you are serious and you sign a contract at 133 [pounds], there is an expectation that you will deliver.

"It is not only unacceptable, it is a blight on the sport. This is unprofessional, there is nowhere to go for this bloke now."

Undefeated Olympian Paulo Aokuso will move to the main card, taking on Luis Tejeda from the Dominican Republic in a light-heavyweight bout.

Wilson's fight is the second co-main event to be cancelled this week after Fulton's fellow American Jermall Charlo was denied a visa to face rising Australian Koen Mazoudier.

World.title: 'We can all feel it': Bronze medal lifts Aussie gymnasts' outlook
World.content:
Australian gymnast Jesse Moore had a sinking feeling in his stomach: he had seen this movie before.

Four years ago at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, the nation's best male artistic gymnasts fell agonisingly short of bronze by 0.650 points after slipping at the death to Cyprus.

Fast forward to Glasgow and Australia found themselves in a similar position when hosts Scotland mounted a late challenge en route to the final of six apparatuses.

With just one point the difference in the men's final at Glasgow International Stadium, Australia's five-man squad withstood the raucous home crowd and proved their mettle on the pommel horse to avoid history repeating.

Bolstered by a strong start on rings and horizontal bar, Australia clinched bronze with a combined score of 235.650 points.

A near-flawless Canada team won gold (241.400 points), pipping 2022 Birmingham champions England by 3.150 points.

Australia's men won their first team medal since their maiden gold at the 2010 Delhi Games, doing so with four debutants in the five-man squad.

Paris Olympian Moore was the only Australian man to have experience on the Games stage, leading Ritam Malik, James Hardy, Ben Foster and Tru Hagens.

Australia's Ritam Malik flips through the air after performing on the rings. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

Moore, 23, laughed when asked if his mind went back to the 2022 Games.

"You always have that in the back of your mind," Moore said.

"But we have got a job to do. The game's not over yet.

"The way we finished on pommel is pretty extraordinary. It shows how well we've come over the past few years.

"It's a bit weird being one of the oldest and most experienced on the team. I'm proud to be that in this team.

"We're certainly on track, only upwards from here.

"We can all feel it and people back home can feel it as well."

Moore notched Australia's second-best score (13.300) on the apparatus behind Malik (13.500), while 19-year-old Hagens was awarded 13.100 points despite falling.

Pommel horse specialist Hagens had waited through the nearly four-hour final for his only apparatus.

Australia claims six gold on Commonwealth Games opening day Australia claims six gold medals, and 13 overall, to open competition on day one of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Hagens started his 40-second cameo just as Scotland began their last-ditch effort for the podium on the horizontal bar.

Cameron Lynn (13.500) and Reuben Ward (13.150) matched it with the Australians, but crowd favourite Hamish Carter scored 12.900 points.

"I was pretty nervous," Hagens said.

"Not the outcome I wanted, but it was good to get up there, finish it off for the team, to get up a score we needed to get the medal."

A horrific injury to English gymnast Gabriel Langton put a damper on the final.

Langton had to be stretchered from the Glasgow International Arena after falling from the horizontal bar and landing on his head and neck, resulting in a 15-minute pause in competition.

The 19-year-old lay motionless on the ground for several minutes, but gave a thumbs up as he left the arena.
